Research has examined the correlations of charges in particle interactions within Pb-Pb collisions, specifically looking at whether evidence of the Chiral Magnetic Effect (CME) exists in the collision data collected at 2.76 and 5.02 TeV. The study considered all charged particles within specific pseudorapidity and centralization ranges. Analysis involved comparing observed patterns to those generated by Monte Carlo simulations, specifically using ALICE's CMS and FMU detectors, in conjunction with the TESBE and STARLIGHT models. Findings indicate that while there are observable differences and similarities between the two collision energies, the observed patterns do not definitively support the presence of the CME. Instead, the data suggests that CME signals were obscured by background contributions associated with the collision's geometry and charged-particle distribution. Thus, the study sets a upper limit on the CME signal, ranging from 5% to 30% or more depending on the collision conditions and the specific signals being compared. The research also establishes a basis for future investigations into CME signals in collisions at higher energies and with greater precision. Additionally, the study highlights the importance of its results in relation to the properties of quark-gluon plasma and the potential pathways to uncovering the CME signal in electron-ion collisions. Finally, the study effectively links the findings to the queries and recommendations outlined in the original study. Please note that the CME signal and related background contributions were described in greater detail in the original publication. This abstract focuses solely on the constraints imposed on the CME by the study in question. Finally, the study expresses anticipation for the potential outcome of future investigations using charged azimuthal correlations in Pb-Pb collisions at 5.02 TeV as well as in pp collisions at 13 TeV. The study further adds that the data collected at 5.02 TeV using the CMS detector may yield CME signal constraints that align with the theoretical predictions outlined in the original study. Our investigation, spanning multiple platforms including Kickstarter, Indiegogo, and Fundraising Club, reveals that online crowdfunding success relies on specific crowd actions. This study aims to shed light on these actions through a comprehensive analysis of fundraiser pages and their surrounding comment sections. By examining video, text, and image content, along with crowd engagement metrics like likes, comments, and contributors, we identify the critical factors that predict successful fundraising campaigns. Our findings can inform platform designers and fundraisers on how to boost their campaign's chances of success. A replication of our study's methods and analysis is available online. Machine learning (ML) based detection of network attacks has shown effectiveness when tailored to a single organisation, but combining data from multiple sources is challenging due to data format inconsistencies and privacy concerns. To address this issue, this paper introduces a collaborative federated learning framework, allowing multiple organisations to co-create and train a robust ML-based intrusion detection system without compromising their data's privacy. A key feature of the proposed framework is the ability to collect and process network traffic data in a common format to reveal meaningful patterns. Moreover, the federated learning mechanism allows organisations to benefit from shared cyber threat intelligence without needing to share sensitive information, by sharing only model updates through the averaging process. To evaluate the proposed framework's effectiveness, two NetFlow datasets were used and compared to a traditional monolithic learning approach and a baseline federated learning method. The results demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms these methods in accuracy and F1 score, and requires less training data to achieve similar performance. The source code for replicating the experiments is available on GitHub at https://github.com/jdabbas21/FL_IDS. This cyber threat intelligence sharing framework provides a secure and efficient means for organisations to collaborate and share intelligence, reducing attack detection latency and system security breaches. It is suitable for training and testing ML-based intrusion detection systems, offering a privacy-preserving and efficient means of sharing threat information and improving overall security. The proposed framework can potentially replace traditional security information and event management systems, yielding better results. Future research will focus on enhancing the framework's efficiency by adapting it to work with distributed datasets and exploring the potential for integrating new ML algorithms. Moreover, the federated learning mechanism will be further developed to merge the code into a comprehensive cyber-physical system, enabling this cyber threat intelligence sharing service to be integrated into real-world security systems. In particular, this framework can be utilised for training ML models in large-scale transportation systems, and providing a secure means for data providers to benefit from shared intelligence without compromising their privacy. To address this, a novel intrusion detection system will be co-designed and trained using the proposed framework, and validated through simulation with data from a smart transportation system. This will demonstrate that the proposed framework can provide a secure and efficient means of sharing threat information and improving the security of large-scale transportation systems. The issue of scheduling a robot's tasks efficiently is a long-established concern in manufacturing. Solutions have commonly drawn on a variant of the classic Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP), with a focus on achieving the quickest or most time-efficient task sequence. Despite their optimality, these methods face challenges in real-time execution, especially with larger problems. In fast-paced online planning environments where tasks are executed swiftly, the time taken to optimize task ordering becomes a substantial hindrance, even overshadowing the overall task duration. The optimal approach in such cases involves balancing solution quality with total duration, rather than striving for the lowest possible time. The ideal task ordering in this context can be considered a form of clustering, where tasks are grouped into sets based on the order in which they appear in a desirable sequence. We introduce a novel algorithm that uses these clusters to introduce significant improvements in task ordering quality, using a greedy method that incorporates cluster information to evaluate and discard poorly performing task arrangements. The resulting algorithm achieves rapid execution, with a time complexity of O(nD^2) where n is the number of tasks and D is the maximum number of tasks in each cluster. The algorithm also boasts a relatively low memory requirement, with a complexity of O(n) for storing task ordering information. The results presented here demonstrate that this algorithm is capable of arranging tasks in a manner that closely approaches optimal arrangements, with improvements in solution quality of up to 60% based on the number of tasks and their durations. The algorithm is further validated through applications in industrial settings, where it proves to be a suitable solution for the complex problem of arranging tasks for a multi-point robotic manipulator. The algorithm is now being prepared for integration into the widely used Open Robotics Execution System (ORES), with the aim of providing a practical solution for arranging tasks in online planning environments. When each cluster contains identical systems, synchronized within that group, but operating independently from other groups, this phenomenon is known as group synchronization. Typically, strict conditions need to be met to achieve synchronization, but research has revealed that slight discrepancies in parameters or connections do not necessarily preclude it. Through advanced analysis, it is now possible to identify stable conditions for group synchronization, including the impact of within-group connections. This expanded understanding allows for a more general representation of these complex systems, reducing their stability evaluation to simpler mathematical dimensions. Additionally, the proposed methods can be applied to various models of interacting systems, as demonstrated using a general model of coupled oscillators. Parameters influencing group synchronization were also explored, as well as the dynamic behavior resulting from within-group connections. Ultimately, the proposed framework enables a more comprehensive analysis of this phenomenon, potentially extending the theory of group synchronization to real-world applications. Our study examines the existence of domain-level source diversity bias in video search outcomes by utilizing a virtual agent-based method. The approach entails comparing the outputs of five prominent search engines, as well as a combined aggregate search, for over 1800 queries across nine domains, conducted both in English and additional languages. The analysis reveals significant variation in source diversity according to domain, with English-language searches often yielding less diverse output than non-English language searches. Interestingly, the aggregate search results demonstrate source diversity comparable to that of individual video platforms, suggesting an effective counterbalance against domain-level bias. The findings stress the importance of understanding and addressing implicit biases affecting video search outcomes, with implications for designing and outsourcing search functions. Despite the exceptional performance of Graph Neural Networks in semi-supervised node classification, they face significant challenges when dealing with an extremely limited number of labels. The semi-supervised pseudo-labeling method is often employed to mitigate this issue, which aims to supplement the training set with high-confidence, pseudo-labeled nodes in a self-training cycle. Nevertheless, current pseudo-labeling techniques have several shortcomings. They tend to produce a substantial number of noisy pseudo-labels, which can significantly hinder the network's ability to learn from the model's high-confidence predictions. Moreover, they typically disregard the invaluable knowledge hidden within the graph structure. To address these limitations, we propose Informative Pseudo-Labeling, which focuses on assigning pseudo-labels to nodes that are unlikely to be labeled information propagated from nearby nodes. By doing so, it minimizes the accumulation of noisy pseudo-labels and encourages the network to capitalize on the graph's semantic components. Informative pseudo-labeling enables the reduction of frequent pseudo-label updating, allowing the pseudo-label set to be consistently refined and integrated into the training set. Experimental evaluations on six benchmark datasets demonstrate that our proposed method consistently outperforms existing pseudo-labeling techniques. The code and dataset are publicly available for reproduction of the results. Further analysis confirms that the proposed method can efficiently obtain high-quality pseudo-labels and train the model to achieve superior performance, especially when the number of available labels is extremely scarce. It also offers enhanced robustness against data corruption compared to traditional pseudo-labeling techniques. To validate the proposed method's theoretical foundation, we employed Gaussian Process regression to analyze the relationship between the number of pseudo-labels and the model's test accuracy. The results demonstrate that Informative pseudo-labeling can lead to a more stable and significant increase in the model's performance as the number of pseudo-labels increases. The constant improvement in test accuracy when using the proposed method is attributable to the high quality of pseudo-labels obtained through Informative pseudo-labeling. To confirm that the proposed method efficiently assigns informative pseudo-labels, we conducted an empirical study on three benchmark datasets. The results show that Informative pseudo-labeling produces a substantially higher percentage of correctly assigned pseudo-labels compared to existing pseudo-labeling techniques. Moreover, we used Gaussian Mixture Models to examine the distribution of node distances within the pseudo-labeling set in GraphSAGE. The findings reveal that Informative pseudo-labeling significantly narrows the gap between the smallest and largest eigenvalues, resulting in a more consistent and informative pseudo-label set. In video processing tasks, precise identification of recognizable objects at a low computational cost enables real-time video analysis on devices. We present PatchNet, a highly efficient neural network model for tracking objects across adjacent frames in videos. Unlike traditional pixel-based approaches, PatchNet leverages patch-wise correlation features. This results in a compact network that runs at a remarkably low computational cost of 58MFLOPs, approximately $5\times$ simpler than MobileNetV2. Our research showcases the effectiveness of PatchNet on object detection in videos and visual tracking, yielding substantial performance gains and comparable or better results. Specifically, on benchmark datasets ImageNet VID and OTB2015, PatchNet significantly outperforms other models by reducing their computational costs, achieving a $5.0$ to $6.6$ percentage point improvement in mAP/drift for VID, and a $2.3$ to $6.3$ frame per watt improvement in precision at $80\%$ on OTB2015. Furthermore, experiments on benchmark datasets validate PatchNet's efficiency on other video tasks, including video classification, semantic segmentation, and keypoint detection. Our research demonstrates that PatchNet's design serves as a versatile backbone network, offering significant efficiency gains without compromising performance in various video analysis tasks. We present a generic, classical modeling of electric circuits that describes conventional single-tone microwave optomechanics, where a mechanical oscillator functions as a mobile capacitor within a parallel RLC circuit. This model accurately mirrors the behavior seen in experiments, including the conversion of mechanical oscillations into electrical ones and the inverse process. It also predicts that when the mechanical oscillator's amplitude becomes sufficiently large, there will be a significant back-action force exerted by the electric field, thereby extending the usual regime of tiny "blue" motivations to a larger scope. In addition to the linearized parameters, this model also considers nonlinear coefficients, which are inevitable in real-world applications, and explores their influence on key system characteristics, now developed as intricate current-driven analyses involving Josephson junctions, all consistent with previously documented findings. Furthermore, we examine the behavior of our circuit when its mechanical oscillator has a nonzero damping rate, and analyze the current-driven nonlinear interactions within the circuit, which generate novel effects not seen in linearized scenarios. We also discuss how to achieve mechanical amplification through electrical feedback, and describe specific circuit designs that can realize this mechanism, thereby potentially increasing the typical optomechanical gain by a substantial factor. These designs, predicated on an understanding of voltage transients, can be implemented using advanced techniques such as multi-junction junctions and have already been successfully integrated in experimental settings. Lastly, we explore the behavior of our electric circuit when its mechanical oscillator is driven beyond its linearization threshold, and provide a detailed description of its complex, nonlinear dynamics in terms of current-driven bifurcations, all of which contribute to a deeper comprehension of conventional single-tone microwave optomechanics. We also identify key design elements that contribute to good mechanical feedback coupling, and examine the behavior of our electric circuit when subjected to frequency-stable, distributed-power drives. We demonstrate that these drives give rise to an interaction phenomenon between the mechanical and electrical oscillators when the system is pushed beyond its linear stability limit, and present specific design requirements necessary for achieving mechanical oscillation amplification through electrical feedback. We also present an extensive analysis of our electric circuit's stability when its mechanical oscillator is driven by non-vanishing forces, and identify two distinct stability conditions for the system's hybrid fixed point. We demonstrate the achievement of mechanical oscillator amplification through electrical feedback in our electric circuit, and highlight the significance of scale for realizing this effect. We also examine the effects of scale on our electric circuit when its mechanical oscillator is driven beyond its linearization threshold, and identify three distinct scale dependencies

Employing a robot design proposed by Steve Mesburger and Alfred Hubler in "Chaos in Wall Following Robots", the autonomous entities use a straightforward distance sensor to navigate, with the added limitation of a narrow "phi" field of view. As these agents maintain a consistent forward velocity, they rely on the sensor to adjust their path accordingly: rightward when close to obstacles and leftward when distant from them. In a linear environment, the autonomous entities maintain a consistent distance from their surroundings and proceed along a fixed path. However, when faced with periodic patterns in the environment, such as square, triangular, or sawtooth shapes, and the field of view is narrowed, these agents follow a recurring path. But as their field of view expands, their movements become increasingly chaotic. Laparoscopic surgery has limitations due to a narrow field of view. Smoke produced by laser ablation in such operations obstructs the surgeon's visibility, highlighting the need for smoke removal to ensure a clear view. To apply smoke removal techniques effectively, it's essential to accurately distinguish between smoke and non-smoke images, which poses a challenge as current methods are incomplete. To overcome this issue, we have developed an image enhancement technique that extracts crucial information from RGB images to differentiate between smoke and non-smoke content. Leveraging a weighted least squares optimization framework, we employ statistical features derived from bivariate histograms to create a dimensionality-reduced feature space, which is then classified using a nearest neighbor algorithm. We tested our approach on the Cholec80 dataset and compared it against existing methods, demonstrating that our technique achieves a classification accuracy of 70% without relying on RGB colors, which are often distorted due to surgical camera processing. Additionally, we have made our code available for public use. Furthermore, we have investigated the performance of various RGB color combinations and features in a weighted least squares optimization framework to identify the most beneficial elements for smoke image detection. Our study indicates that combining green and red components, along with statistical features, achieves the highest accuracy in differentiating between smoke and non-smoke content. While this technique reaches 68% accuracy on the Cholec80 dataset, it outperforms other methods and methods without image enhancement, showcasing the benefits of this approach. Furthermore, we have examined various feature sets to determine which ones contribute most to accurate classification, revealing that histograms of green and red colors, along with their combinations, are essential for distinguishing between smoke and non-smoke images. Interestingly, we have discovered that using only the RGB colors extracted from our image enhancement technique can achieve a 57% accuracy without relying on any other features. This research establishes that the eigenvalue density at a matrix's edges influences its asymptotic computational complexity. The hypothesis regarding this density is a more realistic premise than assuming a complete spectral distribution. A novel concept has been introduced where an intralayer particle (formed through light exposure) interacts with particles that can leave the excitonic state to form interlayer charged entities called polarons. Utilizing complex computational models, our study begins with calculating the strength of bonds between particles composed of those from different and the same layers, crucial in the understanding of charged entities' behavior. Predicted features match known patterns for this type of layered material state, indicating changes in these interactions when layers are spaced farther apart will alter their corresponding light response patterns. Additionally, the weight of light-induced components can influence these patterns, resulting in distinct changes to already existing optical behaviors when such components become stable. We have developed a message-passing algorithm designed to accurately determine the location and track of mobile objects within areas with multiple signal paths that may experience blocked or obstructed visibility. The proposed adaptive probabilistic algorithm estimates a mobile device's position by leveraging data from multiple anchors, accounting for the timing and amplitude variations in signal components and incorporating an adaptive uncertainty model that facilitates efficient belief propagation. The performance of this algorithm has been demonstrated through experimental results, which show that it achieves a significant 60% improvement in accuracy compared to a method that doesn't consider signal variations. The obtained results indicate that this approach yields a location error below 30 centimeters and a tracking error below 10 centimeters per second. The proposed algorithm demonstrates effective performance across a range of signal strengths and mobile speeds, making it a versatile solution for localization and tracking applications. These measurements were derived from $139$ fb$^{-1}$ worth of data from proton-proton collisions at a $13$ TeV center-of-mass energy, obtained with the ATLAS detector at CERN's Large Hadron Collider.  $W^{\pm}Z$ candidate events, resulting from the decay of these bosons into electrons and muons, have been used to quantify longitudinally polarized vector boson pair production, an event that is here reported for the first time, occurring at a statistical significance of $7.1$ standard deviations.  Fiducially-integrated joint helicity fractions for these events are $f_{\mathrm{00}} = 0.067 \pm 0.010$, $f_{\mathrm{0T}} = 0.110 \pm 0.029$, $f_{\mathrm{T0}} = 0.179 \pm 0.023$ and $f_{\mathrm{TT}} = 0.644 \pm 0.032$, in concordance with a next-to-leading order prediction from the two-loop QCD matrix element calculation.  Additionally, joint helicity fractions for individual $W$ and $Z$ bosons were quantified, yielding no substantial disparity in joint polarization states between these two particles.   $W$ boson joint polarization states were also used to constrain oblique parameters, specifically $W$ boson wave function normalization and a $4$-fermion coupling, while further, joint polarization states for $W$ and $Z$ bosons have been used to develop further sum rules relating the electromagnetic and weak fine structure constants. We introduce a visual representation system that translates Coq proof scripts into tabular forms, which can be exported as $\LaTeX$ or PDF files. Our tool aims to facilitate learning and proof review by providing an interactive visual representation of each step in a proof. Consequently, this system enables educators and reviewers to utilize the proofs without relying on the Coq program, thereby allowing them to be printed or shared in other forms, as opposed to the more conventional hypertext or markdown formats. Moreover, as the tool can generate proofs in $\LaTeX$ or PDF, it allows educators to incorporate these proofs into examination papers or assignments, thereby giving students additional assistance. Furthermore, this system makes it easier for reviewers to gain a clearer understanding of the proof by allowing them to print the proof or view it without the distraction of hypertext, code or other irrelevant information, as opposed to viewing it in a terminal or IDE. In this paper, we explain the motivation behind our tool, describe its implementation and evaluate its effectiveness through user feedback. Specifically, we used our tool to enhance the review of undergraduate students' projects and receive feedback on the proofs reviewed. In particular, a mathematics reviewer commented, 'I think this could be really useful for understanding the content of any proof', as evidenced by the feedback received. Consequently, we suggest future improvements to this system, as well as its potential applications across a wider range of areas, as it could provide valuable insights into the relationships between different results. In particular, we propose that this visual representation system could be used to illustrate the connections between results by generating a table of priority that shows which results depend on other results. To realising this potential, we plan to explore and implement the following features: (i) extending the tool to allow results to be linked together, as opposed to the current isolated view of each proof; (ii) developing a user-friendly interface for selecting and reviewing groups of related results; (ii) enhancing the tool so that it detects relationships between results, as opposed to requiring manual input. We demonstrate that the fourth moment of holomorphic Hecke cusp forms is limited under the assumption of the Riemann Hypothesis for a specific degree 8 L-function. This is achieved by leveraging Watson's formula, which allows us to recast our investigation as a tractable problem related to L-functions, ultimately facilitating the application of Soundararajan and Harper's methods for deriving sharp bounds on the moments of the Riemann zeta function. Furthermore, in the absence of the Riemann Hypothesis, we provide a theoretical estimate, albeit less stringent, based on the spectral gap between the first two eigenvalues of the Laplace-Beltrami operator on a unit volume hypersurface. This approach also enables us to strengthen Deligne's earlier findings regarding the growth rate of the same expression. Our analysis also reveals that the Riemann Hypothesis is not essential for establishing the asymptotic equivalence between the second moment of Hecke cusp forms and the squared zeta function's first moment, a relationship initially observed by Conrey and Keating. This observation on the Riemann Hypothesis' non-essentiality can be generalized to the investigation of the fourth moment as well. Lastly, in the context of character twists, we prove the asymptotic stability of the fourth moment as the weight increases, a finding previously validated for the second moment by Li and Wang. This observation is primarily the result of our capacity to characterize the range of possible spectral influences on the fourth moment, which, in the character-twist context, is precisely the range of possible influences on the Riemann zeta function's first moment, as per the framework of the quantum period, initially conceptualized by Keating and Suleymanov. Conversely, emerging technologies like intelligent systems frequently result in real-world setbacks despite a lack of record of their failures. Consequently, businesses frequently make mistakes by repeating mistakes already encountered in the industry. A central database of intelligent system failures experienced by industry insiders would help prevent and mitigate these errors. The AI Incident Database, a collaborative effort of industry professionals, collects failures of intelligent systems in a comprehensive and accessible manner. It offers customizable search tools and publicly searchable incidents on its website, aiming to raise awareness of failures and prevent repetitive failures in the industry. However, extending this connection to Yang-Mills theory while maintaining gauge invariance proves to be complex. In a 2012 paper, the challenge of integrating gradient flow into Yang-Mills theory while preserving gauge invariance was explored, and a precise formula for the exact RG flow equation in terms of the time-dependent Yang-Mills theory was proposed. This idea was further developed in a paper presented at the 2019 CERN Summer Student and Research Student Conference, where the time-dependent Yang-Mills theory was related to the RG flow equation, and key properties of the time-dependent theory were outlined. Although the time-dependent Yang-Mills theory has not been widely adopted, it offers a unified description of the RG and gradient flows, and as such, it holds significant theoretical value. In addition to RG and gradient flows, the time-dependent Yang-Mills theory also incorporates aspects of the Bloch equation, which describes the dynamics of Dirac fields in terms of the Yang-Mills field. Building on the principles of this theory, a new action for Yang-Mills theory has been developed, and it was demonstrated that this action leads to the RG flow equation and the Schnitzer equation, a previously established outcome of the RG flow. The new action also holds close analogies to the Wilsonian effective action and the background-field method. Consequently, this new action, as well as the time-dependent Yang-Mills theory, may provide valuable insights for further research in the fields of Yang-Mills theory and scalar field theory. Current business process monitoring methods mainly concentrate on one process model. However, in some scenarios, it is necessary to analyze multiple process definitions at the same time. These specifications can be operational, rule-based, or a combination of both. For example, in the medical field, a treatment guideline might not cover all co-factors a patient can have and therefore supplementary restrictions might need to be considered. Sometimes, these constraints may conflict with existing guidelines, requiring either the guidelines or the constraints to be violated. To address this issue, we suggest a solution to monitor hybrid process definitions expressed through a combination of (data-aware) Petri nets and temporal logic rules. During the process execution, the monitoring system can handle conflicting specifications by possibly violating some of them, and can even provide recommendations for the next course of action based on a violation cost model that minimizes the total cost of violations. Our monitoring solution can also handle limitations such as incomplete or imprecise process information. We have extended the CAMALEO monitoring tool to support the monitoring of complex process definitions, and have shown in practical experiments that the monitoring of hybrid processes is feasible. These experiments have also shown the effectiveness of our approach, particularly in environments where complete process information is available. To illustrate the advantages of our method, we have looked into real-life scenarios from the medical and educational fields. To achieve efficient monitoring, we have adopted a detection architecture with a monitoring filter and a detection component that relies on automated verification techniques, such as (data-aware) automata, temporal logic, and Satisfiability Modulo Theory. This allows for a more efficient distribution of the processing load between these two components. When a process instance triggers an event that requires evaluation according to the specifications, the monitoring system applies this event to a virtual model of the process definition and determines the resulting state. To achieve this, we have developed a virtual process model based on (data-aware) automata, and defined the application of constraints as temporal logic rules. If the resulting state corresponds to a process milestone, and if the advanced state is also a process milestone, and if the difference between these states does not contain any process information that is not relevant to the evaluation of the specifications, then the monitoring system has determined the advanced state as the next process state. Otherwise, the monitoring system has declared the current process state as the next process state. Quipper, a domain-specific language, enables the description of quantum circuits by embedding in Haskell, resulting in a highly functional and practical language. Yet, its embedded nature in Haskell hinders the development of a formal semantics and restricts the type system. The absence of linear types in Haskell makes it simple to write quantum state-cloning violating code. The Proto-Quipper family addresses this issue through research languages designed to ensure the type-safety of quantum circuit fragments. Specifically, this paper examines Proto-Quipper-M, which employs a categorical quantum circuit model and incorporates linear types for compile-time cloning property verification. To establish a semantic framework, we construct a small-step abstract machine semantics by mapping the model to a von Neumann-style machine, thus providing a clear explanation of the quantum circuit execution process. Moreover, we derive a type system from the abstract machine semantics, offering an alternative characterization of the compile-time linear typing system defined within the categorical model. By demonstrating that the two systems align, we ensure that the categorical model offers both sound and efficient compile-time type checking for quantum circuits. The resulting abstract machine semantics can also serve as a runtime validation mechanism for types. The proposed prototype, implemented in Haskell, effectively checks the type correctness of quantum circuits at both compile-time and runtime. As a result, the categorical model can be employed for quantum circuit design-time type checking, while its execution involves the standard Haskell runtime. The abstract machine semantics provide a meaningful validation for the type system used in Quipper, while the type system offers an implementable type-checking tool. Furthermore, the categorical model can be used to develop type-checking tools for other domain-specific languages by modeling and abstracting semantic structures. Specifically, we have successfully applied this approach to design and implement a type system for another quantum programming language, Stratospin. By applying graph abstraction, sequences with no linear connection are eliminated, thereby reducing unnecessary computations and optimizing sequence generation. We implemented this algorithm on top of the Haloparasite genome assembly tool and achieved significant speedup on a single node, up to $38.8\times$ on large genomes, and further demonstrated substantial parallel scalability through comprehensive benchmarks and realistic simulation studies, showing promising results for assembling large genomes. We accurately assembled genomes of up to $202$ million bases in chromosomal regions of $12$ MB, using $62$ nodes, and demonstrated satisfactory overall performance with encouraging potential for parallel assembly of complete genomes. The proposed algorithm offers an efficient and scalable solution for genome assembly, enabling exploration of complete genomes and opening doors for salting-out assembly techniques. The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at an 8.16 TeV centre-of-mass energy. Top quark production was identified in events featuring one isolated electron or muon and four or more jets, from a data set totaling 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity. The measured signal exceeded the five-standard-deviation threshold expected for a background-only hypothesis, and the cross-sectional measurement for top quark pairs was found to be 45 nanobarns with an 8-nanobarn uncertainty, consistent with theoretical predictions based on the five-flavour model. Additionally, the cross-section was found to be uniform across different pseudorapidity regions, and the production of top quarks and individual top quarks was investigated using proton-proton data at 8 TeV. The cross-section for top quark production was found to be 739 nanobarns with a 22-nanobarn uncertainty, and the systematics were analysed for various kinematic variables. The results were found to be in agreement with theoretical predictions at the 10 percent level. A preliminary measurement of the forward collection time for top quark pairs was reported, and future research will focus on measuring the production of top quarks and individual top quarks as a function of the momentum transfer squared. We introduce a new efficient framework for representing functions in graphical models, which serves as a foundation for a variety of computational tasks. Our concise model then leverages this framework, specifically using deterministic finite state automata within a variable elimination approach known as Bucket Elimination. We dub this variant Bucket Automaton Elimination (BAE) and demonstrate that it facilitates the efficient computational resolution of Most Probable Explanation and related optimization problems in complex models, which are often intractable when approached through traditional techniques. Notably, BAE excels at models featuring non-linear conditional relationships and large model datasets, offering substantial time savings when compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. The proposed approach also welcomes the incorporation of external constraints through the introduction of finite state automata encoding custom function behaviours. We showcase the efficacy of our method with detailed empirical analyses showcasing its performance benefits. The developed model and associated algorithmic implementations are made freely available for public use. The code is publicly accessible through our GitHub repository at https://github.com/grasp-lysis/bae and the model can be accessed via the Grasp logical flow library, also hosted on GitHub at https://github.com/grasp-lysis/grasp. Furthermore, a demo showcasing the method in action is available through the Grasp website at grasp.lisy.gr. We invite readers to explore our work and welcome their feedback and suggested improvements. Additionally, we outline plans for future development and research avenues. One anticipated area of enhancement revolves around the integration of external knowledge that may be represented as finite state automata, encompassing domains such as natural language and chemistry. We envision discrete mathematics to play a pivotal role in advancing the advancements within these domains. We intend to delve into these research possibilities in our future work. We describe a novel, efficient framework, specifically tailored for function representation, which we build upon by introducing Bucket Automaton Elimination (BAE). BAE systematically breaks down complex problems into more manageable subtasks by strategically eliminating variables, where each corresponding subtask is tackled using finite state automata within a determinism framework. This framework essentially converts any complex system into a predictable, automaton-based model. We demonstrate the computational efficiency of BAE by showing that it achieves a linear time complexity for evaluating marginal probabilities. We build upon this by transforming optimization and Most Probable Explanation problems into a tractable realm, where subtasks are resolved using finite state automata. We showcase the robustness of our method by successfully applying it to complex systems featuring non-linear conditional relationships and large model datasets, while also incorporating external constraints

A deep learning approach, consisting of two interconnected networks, is designed to locate the falling object in a video, using the mixed sensory inputs. Researchers propose that abrupt shear thickening serves as an initial indicator of a state transition, developing a comprehensive framework for interpreting viscosity through a universal function that bridges the frictionless point of jamming and a state of rigidity influenced by friction, anisotropy, and shear. Studies involving cornstarch and glycerol/water, as well as numerical simulations with spheres and other objects, demonstrate that for mixtures that reach the point of jamming, the ratio of yield stresses to shear thickening stresses follows a consistent, tightly confined range, varying little with particle shape. This theory allows researchers to reevaluate earlier studies, identifying a widespread, particle-scale pattern underlying shear thickening, and revealing that the apparent disparity in the dynamics of fluid-like and rigid states may, in fact, be a result of a single underlying phenomenon viewed from different perspectives. This paper presents an innovative approach to predicting electricity consumption on a hourly basis, set against a backdrop of power shortages. We develop a probabilistic model to estimate consumer behavior during periods of power restrictions. To inform our calculations, two distinct regression models are employed, one based on past consumption patterns and the other incorporating external factors such as temperature and time of day. However, due to the inherent unpredictability of consumer behavior, both models are modified to account for random variability, thus enabling us to estimate probability distributions of hourly electricity consumption. Ultimately, our model is successfully validated using actual data from Argentina's 2001 power crisis. Our analysis reveals that consumer behavior is indeed influenced by external factors, but also exhibits purely stochastic characteristics. Consequently, this model can serve as a useful decision-support tool for policy-makers to guide their decisions on power consumption policies, such as specifying consumption patterns and setting targeted objectives, while also allowing users to assess the effectiveness of such policies in achieving desired outcomes. An area that has not been extensively studied in online search is how personalisation influences the discovery of relevant information. A study has been conducted that addresses this gap, examining how Google's personalised search results can lead to the overlooking of relevant answers. The researchers carried out a comprehensive experiment involving 1500 questions across seven complex topics and found that, on average, Google's personalised results fail to display the most accurate answer for nearly 40% of queries. Furthermore, the study revealed that a substantial 27% of queries have multiple relevant answers that are missed by Google's personalised results. The data also showed that Wikipedia is a primary source of accurate answers that may be overlooked due to personalisation. The study further analyzed the characteristics of queries that may lead to the missed detection of relevant information but found that no such pattern exists across the evaluated data sets. The magnitude of missed information has significant implications and may lead to the dissemination of misinformation in fields such as medicine and law where reliance on search engines is often the sole means of accessing information. The study's findings highlight the need to investigate further the extent to which search engines fail to provide complete answers and the potential risks this poses. The data collected during the study can be utilized to create test cases that may aid in assessing the effectiveness of future non-personalised innovations in Google's Web search. The study's results may also contribute to the development of more efficient methods for evaluating the accuracy of AI-driven information retrieval. The study's findings can potentially be applied to other platforms beyond Google's Web search and may lead to the development of better technologies for providing non-personalised answers and promoting transparency in the algorithms used by modern search engines. The study's results may also shed light on the potential biases inherent in Google's personalised results and the need for increased transparency and deformation methods for enhancing user experience. The study's data can be accessed via a public GitHub repository. The study employed a multi-method approach and relied on the assistance of 780 participants including academics, researchers, and professional lawyers and medicine practitioners distributed across 158 institutions. It distills key mathematical concepts behind each method while showcasing several benchmark climate modeling examples for illustrative purposes. The primary objective is to establish a clear understanding of what reduction methods can achieve in climate modeling. 

Let $X$ represent the phase space governing a climate's behavior, with $X$ being a high-dimensional space. Assuming solutions evolve slowly, we'll examine mechanisms for simplifying this system by mapping it to a lower-dimensional subset of $X$. This process involves identifying a suitable $d$-dimensional subspace within $X$ and a smooth function $f:X^{d} \rightarrow X^{(n-d)}$ to obtain a simplified system $\dot{x} = f(x,\lambda)$, where $\lambda$ denotes the scaling factor. 

We'll examine various reduction techniques, beginning from classical methods like averaging and matched asymptotics to more contemporary techniques such as center manifold reduction, stable reduction, and geometric modeling. Additionally, we will analyze the difficulties and possibilities of combining these methods with two approaches: the dynamical system's weakly interacting basin model and the stable reduction of multistable systems. By reviewing the progress made in this area, we aim to equip readers with the knowledge needed to address reduction-related challenges in climate modeling. 

In particular, we will discuss the implications of using different reduction techniques to model the interaction between slow and neutral components, along with the theoretical underpinnings of these approaches. By exploring the concepts of weak neutrality, non-resonance, and uniform hyperbolicity, we aim to provide a clearer understanding of the underlying mathematical principles. Additionally, we will examine the possibility of obtaining precise, exponentially accurate reductions for certain multistable climate models.

In the final section, we will summarize the main topics covered and highlight their interconnections. Radiation oncologists' goal is to target tumors accurately while shielding surrounding vital organs, specifically the stomach and intestines, from x-ray beams. The incorporation of MR-Linac systems allows real-time tumor positioning, enabling precise radiation dosage adjustments based on shifting cell populations. The manual process of identifying these organs and calibrating X-ray beams can be lengthy, extending treatment times up to one hour a day, making automated segmentation using deep learning techniques appealing alternatives. In our research, a subset of publicly available abdominal CT scans were used to develop and test a deep learning model's ability to automatically identify and segment the stomach and intestines. The results showed that our model could accurately identify these organs in a timely manner, setting a hopeful stage for implementing automated visual recognition in MR-Linac systems. The implementation of automated organ identification could streamline treatments, enabling more patients to receive radiation therapy, and potentially lead to enhanced treatment outcomes. The technical aspects of achieving seamless real-time organ identification during treatments were also discussed. Additionally, the implications of developing this system were explored in terms of clinical outcomes, radiation treatment costs, and overall survival rates. Compositional data analysis is a technique that deals with complex datasets, which consist of several interdependent components summing to a constant value. Common constant values are 1 and 100%. This data structure is found in fields like biochemistry, geochemistry, and the social sciences. Researchers often examine compositional data in "omics" studies with extremely large dimensions. The method involves calculating logratios – the logarithmic expressions of component proportions. The matrix representation, calculation, and interpretation of these logratios present distinct challenges. We will illustrate that the composition of a dataset is solely defined by its matrix factorization, yet this data structure's complexity necessitates special handling due to one-dimensional interpretations of the results. We utilize a matrix perspective to demonstrate that essential characteristics of compositional data are encapsulated by the matrix factorization of the data matrix. This approach allows us to highlight the limitations of traditional statistical models and linear algebra outcomes that fail to acknowledge the data's matrix structure. We also introduce Benjamini-Yekutiel corrections for multiple hypothesis testing, enabling the exploration of large-dimensional datasets with a high number of variables. To facilitate compositional data analysis, we provide a method for visually representing the results of this technique, which can be applied to "omics" studies, as demonstrated using DNA copy number data. In this example, we successfully apply our method to investigate DNA copy number logratios and their associations with cancer types. The techniques presented can be employed for compositional data analysis in diverse applications, ultimately shedding new light on the underlying biology. We investigate how thermal equilibrium is disrupted and the impact on dark matter abundance when a dark particle's interaction with normal matter is mediated by another dark particle. Assuming that the dark particle is produced efficiently at an early time through a random process, such as the decay of a supersymmetric particle, we find that the dark matter candidate's interaction with normal matter can lead to its rapid destruction in two scenarios. Firstly, if the dark matter candidate's mass is roughly twice that of normal particles, its interaction can directly result in its candidate's removal. Secondly, in cases where the dark matter candidate's mass is significantly different from twice that of normal particles, its interaction can lead to the creation of particles that have similar mass to it, ultimately leading to its overall diminishment. We analyze these destruction processes for both a specific type of particle interaction - a force carried by particles with no mass - and a more general type of interaction, representing the exchange of a particle with nonzero mass between dark and normal matter particles. In the latter case, we also consider a scenario in which the dark matter candidate's mass is not precisely known. If the dark matter candidate's mass is not precisely known but its interaction with normal matter is well understood, we find that its inelastic collision can result in its destruction. Furthermore, we identify a type of particle interaction where the dark matter candidate's mass is determined accurately and its destruction due to normal matter interaction is prevented completely. In a specific class of models, we find that the dark matter abundance can result from a combination of its early production and subsequent inelastic collision. Finally, we discuss the potential for a dark matter phenomenon, resulting from an unusual interaction, in which normal matter appears to be surrounded by darker particles that have mass similar to that of normal particles. In particular, we examine the potential for a dark matter phenomenon at normal particle masses around 5 GeV. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) can efficiently solve complex problems that demand memory, error correction, and selection capabilities, mirroring brain circuit behaviors, albeit with limited applicability due to large training demands and memory needs. Brain structures pose constraints such as synaptic distance costs and thus inspired local masking, allowing task-independent predetermined graphs, even with sparsity rates as low as 4\%. We introduce locality-normalization to significantly improve task complexity, empirically verifying our approach with 12 cognitive tasks, demonstrating superior efficiency and adaptability with considerable reductions in training steps and required edge weights in RNNs. Notably, 80\% of the implemented tasks showed at least a 2x improvement in sample efficiency and 40\% showed at least a 4x improvement with comparable or better accuracy when compared to standard fully-connected RNNs, even with 10x fewer edge weights. This development brings neurobiologically-plausible sparse RNNs closer to solving real-world brain-inspired learning paradigms. From an computational neuroscience perspective, our work presents a flexible model of modulation within the brain's cognitive systems, providing a useful proxy for simulating brain circuit behaviors to better understand their mechanisms. A comprehensive set of implemented code and experimental data is available online for verification and extension of these results. We've analyzed the data from a unique binary star system, SDSS J082239.54+304857.19, based on our comprehensive photometry observations taken over 318 days. These observations revealed detailed patterns of dimming and brightness across various stages of the binary's orbit. Utilizing our findings from long-term and ultra-short timescale studies, we've developed an accurate theoretical model of the binary's behavior. According to our analysis, the binary star system consists of two white dwarf stars with a primary white dwarf having a larger size, specifically a temperature of 14,300 K and a radius of 0.031 R sun, while the secondary white dwarf has a temperature of 6,500 K and a radius of 0.012 R sun. Our data and theoretical models both indicate that the binary shares the same orbital plane, exhibiting predictable patterns of dimming and brightness throughout the day. These observations confirm our current understanding of the binary's behavior and offer valuable insights into its internal characteristics and behavior. Additionally, our study provides further evidence of the binary's daily eclipses, reinforcing our current models and offering a deeper understanding of this complex system. Our data and analysis do not indicate any irregular patterns or external factors affecting the binary's behavior, indicating that the binary remains stable and consistent. Overall, our study has contributed to our understanding of the binary's dynamics and offered a more comprehensive perspective on this complex system. Our data and analysis are available for public access.

To address this, a novel, well-established global pooling framework has been established through the lens of optimal transport theory. A unified perspective is provided for various global pooling methods, allowing for a clear distinction between two distinct categories: sampling-based and sample-independent techniques. Sampling-based methods are linked to a specific unitary transformation, whereas sample-independent methods are associated with unique optimal transport maps. Building upon this understanding, theoretical limits of global pooling methods are derived, and existing methods are revisited from this new perspective, leading to the development of an optimal sample-independent pooling method. Furthermore, empirical evidence demonstrates that considering the OT mapping can result in improved inference outcomes in radial neural networks. This proposal gives rise to novel pooling methods for image classification, as demonstrated by the experimental results presented. Additionally, the proposed framework may be extended to additional neural network components, enabling a broader application to models with built-in global pooling layers. Our focus lies on AGN host galaxies which, according to the unified theory, should not exhibit systematic differences depending on AGN classification. We used the SDSS catalogue up to a redshift of 0.2, and the Galaxy Zoo Project catalogue which classifies galaxies into two broad Hubble types, and classified AGNs using emission line diagnostics. Our findings reveal that elliptical galaxies have a significantly higher fraction of Type 1 Seyfert nuclei compared to other AGN types, and the transition from Seyfert 1 to LINER, Type 2 Seyfert, and composite nuclei corresponds to a rise in spiral galaxies. These findings indicate that the unified theory may need to be supplemented by additional mechanisms, and that there may be significant dependencies on the host galaxies between different types of nuclei. Furthermore, our findings also suggest distinct orientations of jet relative to the major axis of the host galaxy for Seyfert 1 and LINER nuclei. These results could be compromised by variability of nuclei and uncertain host galaxy classifications, and significant uncertainties need to be taken into account when interpreting these findings. Furthermore, distinct jet orientations between Seyfert 1 and LINER nuclei may indicate differing accretion modes or black hole masses. The ability to create complex, engaging stories about the characteristics and behaviors of time-series data is extremely important in fields like geology, meteorology, epidemiology, finance, trade analysis, stock market monitoring, and sales forecasting. Currently, domain-specific time-series narration methods rely on predefined templates that ensure consistency but often produce mechanical, uninspired narratives. In contrast, we introduce TCube, a neural framework that can describe time-series data in a universal way without being tied to a particular domain. TCube represents essential time-series elements using a knowledge graph, which is then translated into coherent, engaging stories by leveraging the strengths of pre-trained language models. Since there's a scarcity of labeled data for time-series, TCube incorporates a knowledge graph to make the translation process feasible. This innovative approach marks TCube as the first exploration of neural methods for time-series narration, according to our current knowledge. In our comprehensive evaluations, we demonstrate that TCube significantly improves the variety of words in the generated stories, while also maintaining correct grammar, by up to 65.38%. Furthermore, an expert review of 21 professionals showed that 76.2% of them preferred TCube as a viable system for time-series narration because of its richer narratives, despite being auto-generated. TCube's open-source code and supporting materials are publicly available for anyone to reproduce our results and build upon our work. Additionally, we've introduced a new benchmark called STS, which consists of a dataset with 1,935 human-generated stories and 1.92 million word-level annotations to support future research in neural time-series narration. This dataset is tailored to address the limited resources and domain-specific constraints often encountered in time-series data domains. As such, it offers a unique set of challenges and opportunities for further exploration. Leveraging pre-trained language models and domain knowledge through graphs can significantly contribute to the development of more engaging, complex narratives in various domains. This research introduces a novel application of the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network to tackle the challenging task of Japanese word segmentation. Building on previous work, which utilized Conditional Random Fields, this study aims to improve word segmentation outcomes. Employing character-based models, this work demonstrates that LSTM can be an effective tool for this task, even when training with as little as one character at a time. When augmented with partial word-based training, the accuracy of the LSTM model surpasses that of the Conditional Random Fields model. Notably, this approach performs exceptionally well on words that incorporate Japanese characters known as "kanji." While word segmentation outcomes show room for improvement, this study achieves high precision rates of up to 92% on certain word categories. Additionally, the researchers investigated how to enhance the model's ability to correctly identify particle words, which serve as grammatical modifiers. To accomplish this, they exploited the sequence information inherent in words, as well as the frequent co-occurrence of words observed in corpora. As a result, the model's accuracy in predicting particles improves substantially, from 64.8% to 85.1%. This research showcases the potential for using character-based LSTM models as a preprocessing step to aid in Japanese word segmentation. When combined with the partial word-based training technique, the accuracy of the LSTM model surpasses that of the Conditional Random Fields model. Furthermore, the researchers found that by incorporating the sequence information within words and frequent co-occurrence of words, the model's particle prediction accuracy increases notably. It is interesting to explore the possibility of using character-based LSTM models to assist in other basic Japanese NLP tasks, such as basic phrase segmentation. This approach may also be applicable to other languages that incorporate sequences of characters in their writing systems, such as Chinese or Korean. On the Stack Overflow platform, users utilize 11,926,354 external connections to share relevant off-site information, augmenting the existing knowledge base. Our research focuses on Stack Overflow, where analysis reveals that links to text-based documentation, tutorials, and other reference materials are most often reshared. This leads to observations such as users contributing identical knowledge across multiple questions, users copying content from each other, and the issue of duplicated information on the platform. To address these findings, potential solutions are proposed to improve knowledge integrity, organization, and the overall quality of the community's knowledge sharing efforts. This way, the efficacy of the community in maintaining and disseminating relevant information can be maximized. Questions and concerns regarding the methodology and potential areas for further investigation are also addressed. Given the shared nature of the resources, it is hoped that this study will stimulate discussion within the Stack Overflow community, ultimately leading to the implementation of new research questions and the development of positive changes in the community's external link sharing practices. Galactic rotation curves show a range of varying inner slopes. Observations suggest a potential relationship between a galaxy's brightness and its central dark matter, indicating the need for a more comprehensive explanation. This study investigates various theoretical models that account for galaxy diversity, specifically comparing a Self-Interacting Dark Matter model with isothermal core to Cold Dark Matter models with/without baryonic feedback. Contrary to standard CDM, SIDM can form isothermal cores, and its effectiveness isn't largely influenced by long-term baryonic feedback processes. Utilizing the rotation curves of 90 galaxies from the SPARC catalog, a thorough model comparison is conducted to improve upon previous methodological issues. Our results show that the best-fitting halo models adhere to standard CDM concentration-mass relations. Although SIDM and feedback-influenced CDM outperform the non-feedback CDM in accounting for rotation curves of galaxies with varying surface brightnesses, neither model has a strong statistical advantage when compared to each other in explaining galaxy diversity in the given sample. Furthermore, a significant isothermal core is required for proper model fit in the case of SIDM. Two distinct types of galaxies, namely those with an abundance of cold gas and spheroidal galaxies, are examined to investigate potential stage-dependent model fitting. Our analysis indicates that the success of either SIDM or feedback-influenced CDM model depends on the type of galaxies, suggesting a potential pathway to distinguish between these models and alleviate the galaxy diversity problem. Our study highlights the potential of utilizing galaxy diversity to distinguish between different theoretical models by analyzing the rotation curves of galaxies in a controlled, model-agnostic manner. This method could be applied to future data, potentially leading to a reliable discrimination between various cosmological models. Clinical symptoms recorded in free-text doctor's notes are inaccessible for further use.
This problem can be resolved by using information extraction techniques capable of learning domain-specific patterns.
However, models trained on a single hospital or institution are unlikely to perform well at other locations due to variations in recording practices.
This diversity of patterns complicates combining data from different sources and training models across domains.
In this research, we focus on reducing the dependency on a specific dataset or domain by using pre-trained models and neglecting domain-specific patterns.
The evaluation of our approach shows that neglecting domain-specific patterns and using pre-trained models enables more effective extraction of symptoms from clinical notes at sites other than where the model was trained. 
This achievement aligns with the goal of domain generalization, allowing models to function effectively across different domains. 
To facilitate comparison, we also developed a new benchmark called ClinSym for extracting symptoms from clinical notes. 
The benchmark comprises of datasets from two hospitals, totaling 43,964 clinical notes, and has been found to contain significant discrepancies between the two sources. 
The code and data used in this research are openly accessible at https://github.com/ai4clinical/ClinSym. 
The benchmark can be used by the community for developing methods to resolve the problem of symptom extraction, and potentially other clinical NLP tasks. 
The results of our research demonstrate that pre-trained models and a 'forget-and-generalize' strategy can together accomplish domain adaptation for symptom extraction. 
This finding opens up the possibility of using the model in a wide range of different domains. 
The next research question will involve using the model to analyze clinical symptoms across the entire spectrum of a hospital's patient base. 
In addition, we will be exploring the potential of using other types of pre-trained models, such as BERT, in resolving this problem. 
It remains to be seen whether employing these models will lead to further improvements in performance. 
Ultimately, we aim to develop a system capable of extracting clinical symptoms from a diverse range of hospital data, and using the model to provide hospital administrators with insights into hospital resources usage. 
In doing so, we are contributing towards achieving the goal of domain generalization through the creation of a valuable clinical symptom extraction benchmark. 
The research has applications in the domain of clinical symptom extraction.

Deep reinforcement learning stands out as a promising AI paradigm for instructing machines via environmental interaction and adaptive learning from their errors. Despite initial expectations, however, its successful application in the automotive industry remains elusive. Following in the footsteps of notable achievements by Google DeepMind in mastering Atari games and Go, we have developed a comprehensive framework for autonomous driving through deep reinforcement learning, given its relevance due to autonomous driving's inherent complexities and environmental dependencies. In particular, autonomous driving poses significant challenges as a supervised learning problem due to dynamic interactions with pedestrians, vehicles, and road conditions. In view of the relative novelty of deep reinforcement learning, few implementations are available for autonomous driving, leading us to propose an original solution in this article. Specifically, we have designed a fully autonomous driving system by integrating decision-making through reinforcement learning and actuation control via neural networks, with simultaneous state estimation through filtering and mapping for uncertain environments. Furthermore, we have incorporated adversarial training for robustness against diverse scenarios, with evaluation and verification by means of simulation and hardware experimentation. Our results indicate that the proposed framework achieves competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we have successfully tested the framework on a diverse range of vehicles, serving to validate its applicability for autonomous driving through deep reinforcement learning. In conclusion, this article presents an innovative, comprehensive deep reinforcement learning-based framework for autonomous driving, along with corresponding experimental results demonstrating its efficacy. This work is made available via a GitHub repository, enabling reproduction of the results and providing an open-source platform for deep reinforcement learning-based autonomous driving implementations. Additionally, the repository contains a detailed tutorial for deep reinforcement learning-based autonomous driving, along with simulation and hardware testing tools. This article may serve as a valuable resource for software developers, researchers, and practitioners seeking to employ deep reinforcement learning for autonomous driving applications. In view of its novelty, we plan to extend this work by exploring new applications for deep reinforcement learning, with potential transmission in prominent conferences, such as ICRA and IEEE TITS. Moving forward, we intend to tackle newly emerging challenges in autonomous driving, marking which involve key advancements in deep reinforcement learning, as observed from existing trends. These anticipated breakthroughs may hold significant consequences, thereby further enhancing the potential for deep reinforcement learning as a universal AI paradigm. Moving ahead, we will leverage our deep reinforcement learning-based framework for autonomous driving to investigate novel applications and make original contributions in this domain. In federated learning, multiple parties collaborate on training machine learning models by sharing local parameters, rather than sensitive data. Despite this setup, model parameter exchanges can potentially expose confidential information, necessitating novel approaches for mitigation. Recent proposals, rooted in concepts such as multi-party computation and homomorphic encryption, often come at a cost of significant computational overhead, rendering them unsuitable for practical application. This work presents an alternative solution by harnessing the capabilities of Trusted Execution Environments to safeguard data and model interactions, introducing Flatee - an efficient federated learning framework across these environments, and demonstrating its robustness and performance through empirical evaluation. This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can automatically determine the system calls a program should be permitted to make and prevent unauthorized system calls from being made. In addition, Timeloops rectifies various shortcomings of static analysis-based techniques, such as the creation of highly precise filters for programs (e.g. web servers), the construction of diagnostic tools and the operation of programs in an immutable environment. Developed using Python and Libvirt, Timeloops executes a sandboxed copy of a program and permits only safe system calls in a sandbox environment. The program's sandboxed system call behavior is monitored by an oracle, which verifies the program's correctness through various types of output, including the correct generation of HTML or the resolution of domain names. Results indicate that Timeloops can be faster and more effective than static analysis-based techniques in creating system call filters. For example, a Timeloops-generated filter achieved a sophistication level 4-6 times higher than that of COPS for nginx, in terms of the number of new, manually introduced system calls. Furthermore, research demonstrates that Timeloops can be relied upon for creating system call filters in safety-critical domains. Specifically, the analysis shows that Timeloops' use of sandboxing can be trusted to block malicious system calls with an extremely low false positive rate of 0.23 per 10,000. This exceptional level of accuracy is due in part to the reliance on Libvirt's seamless three-tier isolation framework for sandboxing. In conclusion, the development of Timeloops marks a significant breakthrough in fully automated system call filtering, paving the way for the creation of robust, safety-critical systems. The underlying code has been made publicly available on GitHub. A live demonstration is also available online. In particular, the following research findings based on Timeloops are available: a package for learning system call filtering policies called timeloops; a containerized web server (e.g. Nginx) with a range of built-in system call filters; a package for evaluating the robustness of system call filters called stress-tester. In addition to these resources, research also demonstrates the effectiveness of Timeloops through a comparison with other prominent system call filtering tools, including AppArmor and COPS. In particular, the research shows that Timeloops can be relied upon for creating system call filters in safety-critical domains due to its exceptionally low false positive rate. Advanced techniques for representing complex data in compact, high-quality forms involve the embedding of product spaces.
We've identified a new challenge - linear classification in complex product space structures composed of different geometric environments, like Euclidean, spherical, and hyperbolic spaces.
To tackle this problem, we first establish a framework for defining linear classification models within curved, high-dimensional spaces that generalize traditional vector-based classification models.
Next, we demonstrate that, regardless of the geometry of the space, linear classification models are capable of accurately predicting a wide range of data distributions.
Building on this insight, we develop new approaches for classification in complex product space structures, providing solutions for domains composed of spherical and hyperbolic spaces.
To validate our methods, we perform experiments that showcase their effectiveness in simulating real-world datasets, highlighting the advantages of our approaches over more traditional Euclidean-based methods. 
Ultimately, we identify new paths for designing linear classification models that excel in complex geometric environments.

In the vicinity of a supermassive black hole, the stellar orbit dispersion resolves into distinct frequency components determined by their orbital parameters. Researchers have found that the spectral characteristics of stellar motions within a galaxy's central region can pinpoint the presence of a supermassive black hole. Recent studies utilizing the parameter $h$--the mean orbital frequency--and the orbital dispersion $\sigma$--the standard deviation of orbital frequencies--have established criteria for identifying black holes through stellar motions. Although previous studies have focused on the weak segregation regime, this paper delves into the opposite scenario where the stellar population's second frequency component dominates. By analyzing the behavior of $h$ and $\sigma$ in the strong segregation regime, we have determined the relationship between these parameters and $m$--the black hole's mass. Our research has established that $m$ can be estimated by considering both the central density $\rho_0$ and the mean stellar velocity $v_0$. Our analysis indicates that $m\propto\rho_0/\sigma^3$ and $m\proportoinv(v_0)^3$. The findings of this research may be useful in identifying supermassive black holes within galaxies experiencing strong segregation. This paper presents a novel, multi-stage image segmentation model, combining the techniques of image restoration and image segmentation. The integration of image restoration aspects enables the proposed model to effectively handle images corrupted by noise, blurriness, missing pixels, and varied color schemes. Specifically, this approach extends the influential Mumford-Shah model, allowing for improved segmentation of gray-scale and vector-valued images affected by noise, blurriness, or missing data. Our model can be efficiently optimized using the alternating minimization algorithm, which converges under minimal conditions. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior segmentation results, particularly for blurry images and those with missing pixel values, outperforming existing state-of-the-art segmentation models. Furthermore, this approach offers a viable solution for restoring corrupted images, yielding competitive results compared to leading image restoration techniques. Notably, the proposed model can be viewed as a method for solving a minimization of variation problem, which provides a flexible framework for developing image segmentation and restoration algorithms. Our code is openly accessible on GitHub, allowing other researchers to replicate our results and build upon our work.

Active galactic nuclei (AGNs), containing accreting black holes at their center, allow for the investigation of black hole mass and spin through the analysis of electromagnetic spectra. Accounting for uncertainties in luminosity measurements, the conversion of values, relativistic beaming effects, and the characteristics of the AGN system, we determine the minimum possible spins of heavy jetted AGNs. This research also provides upper limits on the fraction of dark matter comprised by ultra-light axion-like particles, concluding that, as a single species, such a particle cannot constitute more than 10% of the dark matter in a given mass range ($10^{-21} < \mu \, (\mathrm{eV}) < 10^{-17}$). Furthermore, we derive constraints on the parameters of fermionic and bosonic Voss-Witten particles in various states of instability. Finally, we investigate how the fundamental plane of black hole masses and spins might change in a scenario where ultra-light scalar particles are present, enabling a possible test of this hypothesis with the spins of heavy quasars.
