Firstly, we analyze the steady-state condition under the influence of gravity, and secondly, we integrate the Boltzmann equation by assuming an average angular momentum in a rotating frame of reference. By doing so, we determine how a kinetic energy density related to the cloud's velocity as a function of radius varies. Furthermore, we investigate the role of angular momentum through two key parameters, namely the mean impact parameter and the collisionality measure, which take into account the collision cross-section. As a result, we establish that a kinetic energy density that diminishes with radius is required for accretion to occur. Additionally, we find that a kinetic energy density peaked at the Bondi accretion radius can in fact hinder accretion. Using a steady-state model, we identify the radius at which the fluid becomes non-d dynamical, and show that a kinetic energy density decaying linearly with radius leads to the same black hole mass accreted via the Bondi accretion model. However, masses are inversely proportional to the logarithm of the finite radius. Using a kinetic model with a finite radius, we establish that the boundary conditions are necessary for analytical models to hold. Finally, we investigate the radial current and find that it is influenced by the logarithm of the finite radius, and also that it is independent of the mean impact parameter. Therefore, kinetic energy and angular momentum play crucial roles in black hole accretion dynamics. The methods employed in this research can be applied to investigate the accretion of kinetic clouds onto rotating black holes. Moreover, these results can be utilized as a basis for numerical simulations of black hole accretion by incorporating collision terms. Such simulations can then serve as a means of validating theoretical models under various conditions. Lastly, we propose that a kinetic energy density decreasing with radius could resolve issues arising from Bondi accretion models in cosmological scenarios. These findings expand upon previous scalar model outcomes where the atom was represented by a scalar variable coupled to a scalar field with either Dirichlet or Neumann conditions applied on the boundary. This assessment considers how spontaneous emission rates change when an initially excited atom is accelerated or a slow-moving atom is accelerated. Additionally, the analysis investigates how radiation patterns are affected by an atom's movement when its position is shifted along the axis or perpendicular to the electromagnetic field direction. This investigation also demonstrates that, in the atom's center of mass frame, the emitted radiation always exhibits a dipole pattern regardless of its velocity. However, this dipole pattern can be altered when the atom is moving rapidly enough that a significant portion of its wave function lies outside the electromagnetic field. In such cases, quadrupole radiation emerges as a result of the atom's non-spherical charge distribution. Moreover, when an accelerating atom is in a initially excited state, its movement can give rise to electromagnetic radiation even in the absence of external fields, a phenomenon otherwise observed with fields satisfying certain conditions. This effect is most pronounced for atoms accelerated along the axis of movement and is particularly amplified when the accelerating atom is positioned directly at the mirror boundary, its movement being parallel to the axis. In such situations, the radiation emitted by the accelerating atom is characterized by a combination of dipole and quadrupole patterns. This interaction also possesses time-dependent features that are reversible, where the atom's excitation probability exhibits periodic variations when driven by a mirror-reflecting electromagnetic radiation. A longstanding issue regarding massive star origins involves the environment in which they form.
In this study, we examine the membership and atmospheric properties of OB stars in the outer regions of Westerlund 2, a young cluster in the Large Magellanic Cloud.
The cluster's massive central concentration may influence the formation of high-mass stars, potentially addressing the issue.
The cluster's rich filaments might trap material, fueling the formation of these stars.
However, it is also possible that the presence of a dense core or an unresolved cluster within the observed area contributes to the sample's high-frequency peak.
Moreover, we discover 13 O stars in this outer region: 4 O7O, 5 O6O, and 4 O8O, with masses ranging from approximately 30 to 70 times that of our sun.
Further analysis of this data set, combined with other clusters in the Large Magellanic Cloud, may shed more light on the initial mass function of massive stars.
Ultimately, identifying the core cluster and removing potentially foregent members will help clarify the issues surrounding massive star environments. 
For this purpose, we present a new Gaia EDR3-based membership classification for Westerlund 2, which excludes 4 O stars and adds 2 new members. 
The new member, WD2-O33, holds a membership probability of 100% and has a mass approximately 52 times that of our sun. 
Meanwhile, the Gaia astrometry reveals that the cluster's mean velocity relative to the Large Magellanic Cloud is around 69 km per second. 
Additionally, we report the cluster's significant proper motion in the North-East direction. 
Last but not least, we record a new X-ray source for WD2-O33. 
The unfiltered Gaia DR2 data also suggest the presence of 2 likely non-members: 2 O7O and WD2-O32. 
To verify, we refer to the past X-ray observations, showing that WD2-O32 lacked X-ray emission in 2016, while WD2-O33 and most of the core members had prominent X-ray emission. 
Conversely, the 2 non-core members (including WD2-O33) displayed lower X-ray luminosity. 
In spite of this, WD2-O33's metalline spectrum remains unaltered, suggesting no evidence of velocity variations among the core members.

As a result, conventional IEEE 802.11p estimators experience significant performance decline, particularly in high-speed scenarios. To overcome these drawbacks, researchers have proposed using deep learning-based estimators, yet these estimators either fail to account for the IEEE 802.11p protocol's specific requirements or lack sufficient information to produce reliable channel estimates. To address these issues, this paper presents a novel deep learning-based estimator designed for IEEE 802.11p channels. The proposed solution incorporates the IEEE 802.11p frame structure and utilizes temporal averaging to refine channel estimates, achieving significant improvements over current state-of-the-art estimators. The results show that the proposed estimator yields reliable estimates, facilitates optimal system performance, and achieves superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art estimators in various vehicular applications. Moreover, the results highlight the estimator's capacity to accurately detect transmitted information and remain resilient to jamming attacks. The proposed estimator's source code is publicly available for review and verification. The task of automatically assigning colors to images without human involvement has garnered interest within the machine learning community for a limited time. Colorization is particularly challenging due to its inherently high degrees of freedom; besides predicting color values, it also demands a sense of consistency across space and time. Another related challenge is Single Image Super Resolution, a task that involves transforming and expanding an under-resolved image to exhibit higher resolution and detail, similar to that of a more advanced instrument. By combining these capabilities with rapid, efficient training techniques, we have developed a novel, fully automated system for colorizing and expanding images without requiring manual input. To date, we have tested our method on approximately 14,000 images and have compared its performance with established benchmarks through a range of metrics, including the Mean Absolute Error and the Multi-scale Structural Similarity Index. Our results indicate that the proposed algorithm surpasses current standards in nearly all metrics, yielding an average 30% to 40% improvement in image quality. Furthermore, we have investigated the applicability of our method to the recovery of lost images from deficient observations, a task known as "imagine a picture...", where the missing regions are artificially filled in through inference. Our findings suggest that the proposed algorithm outperforms current standards in nearly all metrics, yielding an average 30% to 40% improvement in image quality. To date, we have tested our method on approximately 14,000 images and have compared its performance with established benchmarks through a range of metrics, including the Mean Absolute Error and the Multi-scale Structural Similarity Index. To validate the relevance of our method to real-world observations, we have applied it to data from the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer and the Pan-STARRS1 astronomical telescopes, yielding improved results in nearly all metrics. We introduce a novel numerical scheme for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) that leverages a neural network solver without relying on gradient information. This approach is grounded in the universal approximation theorem, enabling us to derive existence and uniqueness guarantees for the resulting nonlinear problem. Furthermore, we develop a gradient-free algorithm to train the neural network solver, as the network's parameters cannot be efficiently optimized through gradient methods. To demonstrate the efficacy of our framework, we showcase its application in solving a nonlinear heat equation and a second-order semilinear elliptic equation. The results showcase the accuracy of our neural network-based solutions for various parameter settings. Additionally, we provide evidence that the trained neural network can be utilized as a steady-state solver for time-dependent PDEs. The framework's underlying principles and numerical findings are discussed in detail. The corresponding MATLAB code for the numerical examples is available at https://github.com/Sun-WSgithub/Neural-Network-Solver-in-NNGFBNSS. These waves exhibit unique characteristics, including localized propagation, compact size, and high confinement ratios. Line waves on conventional thin sheets, however, suffer from interference and dispersion due to their lack of structural features. In this study, a novel approach is taken to control line waves using a dual metasurface designed using an anisotropic thin sheet. This metasurface supports two types of wave propagation modes - quasi-electromagnetic and line waves. By manipulating the wave propagation characteristics, the line waves can be steered horizontally or vertically. The experiments confirm that the line waves on the dual metasurface have increased confinement ratios and localized propagation characteristics, surpassing those found in conventional thin sheet structures. These findings open the door for the development of innovative thin-sheet technologies and efficient devices. The research further suggests two promising applications - scalable thin-sheet antennas for wireless communication and efficient thin-sheet rectennas for harvesting wireless energy. Traditional methods of covariate-shift adaptation utilize unlabelled data for either determining importance weights or domain-invariant features. Then, a model is trained using only labelled data. We're proposing a novel semi-supervised approach that integrates a model learning from both labelled and unlabelled data. This method draws on information from domain-invariant components of the feature vector to create predictions and uses the model's representations in the unlabelled domain to guide its development. We test our method against established techniques in classification and regression tasks and find it to be consistently more effective across various scenarios. Additionally, we offer a theoretical explanation for its success and provide source code for reproduction of our results at the specified URL. Keywords: unsupervised domain adaptation, importance weights, domain-invariant features, semi-supervised learning. It's noted that this research likely yields no new information for manifolds with a negative Ricci curvature. A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem. To demonstrate its efficacy, we successfully conduct simulations on the half-filled Hubbard model, a representation of which is heavily influenced by the Hubbard model's low-temperature state. Our method enables us to reach an imaginary time $\tau = 1.0$ with $N=100$ sites, a milestone that had been previously unreachable. Furthermore, we leverage our method to calculate a critical density of $x_c \approx 0.739$ on the half-filled Hubbard model. While exact critical densities for the half-filled Hubbard model remain unknown, our results demonstrate that the method's outcomes converge to theoretical exponents. To validate the method's reliability, we verify the absence of system-size-dependent artifacts in our results. In summary, we believe our method will be a ground-breaking tool for tackling the sign problem in many-body systems and related computational challenges. It has the potential to enable simulations of low-temperature many-body systems with realistic electron interactions. To support this claim, we make our code publicly available for others to use. Additionally, we have published a detailed explanation of our approach in an accompanying article. The use of Virtual-Physical Perceptual Manipulations, like redirected walking and haptics, extends VR interaction beyond conventional physical limitations by exploiting the boundaries of human perception, subtly guiding users' movements to enhance interactivity. This research examines the dangers of VPPM exploitation, beginning with a conceptual framework that confirms their existence and then applying speculative design to identify and mitigate threats. Through practical examples, we demonstrate how current VPPM practices can inadvertently create vulnerabilities that may lead to physical harm. This study seeks to highlight the potential consequences of VPPM applications and dissemination as they stand today. VPPM developers and practitioners are encouraged to apply the methods outlined here to identify and address potential risks in their own work. Recent high-resolution observations using VLA and CARMA telescopes have unveiled previously unknown details of proto-stars in binary systems. Specifically, mass measurements for CB230 IRS1 and L1165-SMM1 revealed a significantly higher mass range ($0.1-0.25 \, M_{\odot}$) than those generally obtained from binary formation simulations, which were primarily in the $0.01 \, M_{\odot}$ range. To bridge this gap, researchers conducted numerical simulations of a core's collapse that varied from 1 to 30 $\, M_{\odot}$, while preserving a core's initial angular momentum and radius. As cores from a molecular cloud's velocity gradient gained mass, they entered a rotating core phase, regardless of the relative density, ultimately leading to collapse. This core's collapse and binary system formation resulted in several observable co-moving molecules and the potential for more complex chemical compositions, including CH$_3OH$ and DCN, which could be applied to other binary systems to identify binary formation criteria. Additionally, researchers obtained spatial mass distributions and proto-stellar masses that matched those from recent observations, highlighting the need for accurate core and binary system representations to ensure mass consistency. This led to several key findings: (1) Binary systems that undergo collapse from rotating cores are primarily composed of equal masses, indicating symmetry; (2) proto-stellar masses are influenced by core collapse mass and binary separation; and (3) Binary systems that are generally unequal in mass ($\Delta M \lesssim 0.1 \, M_{\odot}$) can also exist, with their mass disparity increasing as core collapse mass increases. These findings have far-reaching implications for future observations and the study of binary systems. To better reflect binary formation dynamics, researchers suggest incorporating variability in core collapse mass and binary systems to inform future simulations and observations. This could potentially be applied to other systems, such as the formation of stars in clusters, where similar dynamics may apply. Moreover, the binary system model, which was validated using data from CB230 IRS1 and L1165-SMM1, can be employed to estimate the mass disparity in other proto-stellar systems by using the relationship between core collapse mass and binary separation. This raises the possibility of predicting future observations for binary systems based on data from highly resolved proto-stellar systems. This research introduces the m-arcsinh Kernel ('m-ar-K') Fast Independent Component Analysis ('FastICA') approach ('m-ar-K-FastICA') for feature extraction, combining kernel-based dimensionality reduction with ICA to overcome the limitations of previous methods. Although the kernel trick offers a powerful way to tackle non-linearity, its effectiveness can be undermined by a lack of open-source and reproducible kernel implementations, especially in complex datasets. The proposed m-ar-K-FastICA approach uses a readily available and adaptable Python library that facilitates collaboration with scikit-learn, providing a more reliable solution for feature extraction even in data sets with high entropy and non-linear relationships, as demonstrated by its successful application on synthetic and real-world data sets. Furthermore, the approach enables improved performance and increased efficiency by taking advantage of the inherent properties of kernel matrices. In particular, feature extraction results based on the m-ar-K-FastICA approach have shown notable improvements in terms of overall accuracy when applied to well-known University of California, Irvine data sets ('Iris', 'Byrne-Pac-Man', 'Mushroom', 'Waveform', 'Page-blocks'), as compared to alternative methods. Consequently, the proposed approach is expected to contribute to the development of advanced feature extraction techniques for a broad range of applications. Related code is available on GitHub: https://github.com/jbunolar/m-ar-K-FastICA/tree/main. Additionally, pre-compiled Python binaries are available via PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/mar-K-FastICA/. This research is part of a broader effort described in Bunol et al. (2022) arXiv:2109.04330, which introduced the fundamental m-ar-K technique for dimensionality reduction. A recent article by Bunol et al. (2023) arXiv:2201.08551 further explored the m-ar-K method's potential for learning probability distributions, while this current work extends the m-ar-K method to support FastICA. In other related work, Bunol et al. (2023) arXiv:2206.06430 developed a new Gram Matrix Decomposition ('GMD') technique for kernel densities based on the m-ar-K method, which was subsequently applied to improve the accuracy of kernel Density Estimation ('KDE') on various University of California, Irvine data sets, as demonstrated in the 'M-ar-K-FastICA' approach's supplementary material. To address this, we aim to condense these posts into distinct narratives, thereby isolating the core assertions linked to specific topics. By gaining insight into and visualizing these narratives, social media debates can become more informed and productive. To establish a systematic approach for identifying underlying narratives, we propose PAPYER, a comprehensive dataset comprising online comments about public restroom hygiene, marked by an abundance of unfalsifiable claims. By integrating Bayesian learning into adversarial training of deep neural networks, we developed a rigorous framework for training certifiable Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs). This approach combines constraint relaxation and modified cross-entropy loss to achieve robustness to potential attacks. The method, demonstrated through empirical tests on standard datasets, allows for training BNNs that are both accurate and certifiably secure on challenging datasets such as MNIST and CIFAR-10, further providing benefits in uncertainty calibration. This innovation facilitates the deployment of BNNs in applications requiring utmost reliability. The project's source code is available at https://github.com/jbmanzini/bnns_cert. In future research, we intend to expand on this framework by applying it to more complex datasets and exploring ways to significantly reduce the computational costs involved. The theoretical underpinnings of our method, centered on the concept of perturbation liability, offer a valuable framework for understanding the relationships between robustness, regularization, and uncertainty in deep learning models. This led to the development of liability metrics, which can be used to quantify the robustness of NN models even in cases where testing adversarial examples are unavailable. By drawing parallels with classical statistics, we identified key factors that contribute to the liability of a NN model, such as its capacity, degree of non-linearity, and training data diversity. The advantage of this framework is that it enables training robust NN models without requiring knowledge of specific adversarial examples, instead relying on an estimation of the liability that arises from the expected worst-case loss in training data. The method was demonstrated through empirical tests on standard datasets, showcasing its ability to achieve robustness on MNIST and CIFAR-10 without needing actual adversarial examples. This contrasts with current techniques that rely on either artificial adversarial examples or precise liability measurements derived from detailed threat models. The project's source code is available at https://github.com/jbmanzini/bnns_cert. Liability metrics can further be utilized to establish a more precise theoretical understanding of the trade-offs between robustness, model complexity, and training error, offering insights into the underlying dynamics of NN models that may prove valuable in future research. Moreover, we found that the liability can be viewed as a concentration function, which may have far-reaching implications for the study of NN models given its connections to regression analysis and empirical process theory. This study investigates the impact of hyperspectral pixel dimensionality reduction on classification tasks. Five methods (PCA, KPCA, ICA, AE, and DAE) are utilized to compress high-dimensional pixels down to 301 dimensions. The resulting pixels are used for classification, allowing a comprehensive assessment of each method's effectiveness based on classification accuracy, compression rates, and reconstruction errors. Our research employed three diverse hyperspectral image datasets (urban, suburban, and forest landscapes), gathered by the Remote Sensing and Spatial Ecosystem Modeling lab at the University of Toronto. Our analysis reveals that PCA, KPCA, and ICA methods preserve pixel signals well but show decreased classification performance beyond 90% compression rates. In contrast, AE and DAE achieve better results at 95% compression but see their performance deteriorate as the compression rate approaches 97%. Ultimately, our findings highlight the importance of considering both compression methods and rates when crafting an effective hyperspectral pixel classification workflow. Although all methods examined (linear and deep learning-based) struggle with pixel classification at extremely high compression rates, the best performance is often achieved with a compression rate between 90% and 95%. Additionally, our experiments demonstrate that PCA, KPCA, and ICA methods are more effective than AE and DAE when using pixels from urban scenes, while the reverse is generally true for suburban and forest landscape datasets. These findings provide a foundational understanding of how different dimensionality reduction techniques affect hyperspectral pixel classification, enabling informed selection of the most effective method based on the characteristics of a given dataset. The corresponding source code and hyperspectral image datasets are available for reproduction of our results at https://github.com/ghelber/HRPSR. The University of Toronto's Remote Sensing and Spatial Ecosystem Modeling lab provided access to their hyperspectral image datasets, gathered using the SpecIm software. Neural networks are highly effective feature extractors but they pose significant challenges due to their large size. Understanding the parameters within various layers is complicated, resulting in the networks often being referred to as 'black boxes.' In contrast, simpler models are more interpretable but they are also much harder to find. Identifying and utilizing a sparse network that can be trained to replicate the same results is a viable option to improve network interpretability. According to the lottery ticket hypothesis, even large, dense neural networks harbor a smaller sparse sub-network that can be trained independently to achieve the same accuracy in the same amount of time. Our objective is to explore the existence of this trainable sub-network in the realm of natural language models, and we will accomplish this by examining and evaluating the most recent model compression techniques, such as quantization, knowledge distillation, and pruning. We will also propose a novel form of knowledge distillation known as 'early bird,' which enables a smaller network to achieve higher accuracy faster, and we will demonstrate the efficacy of this approach with experiments on several state-of-the-art models. Furthermore, we will investigate whether the 'lottery ticket' sub-network can be found in language models, and we will develop a method to identify and train this sub-network efficiently. Although independent training of this sub-network may require more time, our experiments have shown that it is possible to do so in significantly less time, and we have found sub-networks that can be trained in under 50 hours on A100 GPUs. Our work has led to the creation of multiple model compressions, including a 26-layer BERT model that can be trained on A100 GPUs in under 2 hours, and a 32-layer BERT model that can be trained on V100 GPUs in under 4 hours. We have also discovered and trained 'lottery ticket' sub-networks in various transformer models, and we have found that they generally perform better than their dense counterparts when it comes to zero-shot learning. The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to select the most suitable option. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant. We support this claim through an extensive empirical study demonstrating the existence of loss function overfitting, as well as by developing a set of rules for selecting the optimal loss function for a given problem, based on both problem-specific and general characteristics. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of loss function randomness as a potential source of performance variability, suggesting future research directions based on this insight. The proposed research aims to promote a deeper understanding of loss function behavior, facilitating more accurate and personalized predictions, thereby enabling the development of more robust classification neural networks. We expect this research to contribute to the deep learning community, enabling loss function selection optimizations and insights, ultimately leading to improved model performance. The empirical evaluation presented in this study may also be reproduced by other researchers, enabling additional perspectives and contributions. We expect these contributions to expand our understanding of loss function behavior, potentially leading to new loss functions and research directions. Describing the behaviors of complex systems comprised of strongly interacting elements requires concise expressions for their internal relationships. Ensuring the stability of these systems is the primary focus. Parquet theory is capable of achieving a level of self-consistency that encompasses all strictly pair-based interactions among elements. Grounded in a perturbative framework, the theory is, however, susceptible to difficulties stemming from non-linear equations it involves. Developing a new perspective based on a Hamiltonian formulation of parquet theory can help to identify suitable approximations that may not have been previously considered. This alternative framework also enables a direct connection between the theory's solutions and concrete system properties, thereby facilitating a clearer understanding of the nature of these solutions. Building on this framework, a specific type of approximation can be introduced that leverages a graph transformation to decompose the system into manageable components, ultimately yielding a relatively simple form for the Hamiltonian. Within this context, the Hamiltonian can be seen as a diagonalized representation of the original system, where various higher-order interactions are absorbed into the Hamiltonian's off-diagonal elements. This particular type of approximation effectively encapsulates all relevant pair-based and triplet-based interactions, in addition to a limited form of quartet-based interactions. It is demonstrated that this approximation is capable of achieving a level of accuracy at the same level as previously established standards in parquet theory for a few benchmark systems. Its performance in more complex systems remains to be determined. Another approximation type, where the Hamiltonian's off-diagonal elements are minimized, can be applied to systems where their impact is relatively small, thereby yielding a simplified picture of the system's internal relationships. In this context, the resulting theory is found to be comparable to a previously established model based on a perturbative expansion. A distinctive relationship between the two approximations is established, where the difference between them is primarily attributed to a difference in their respective perturbative expansions. This relationship leads to a diagnosis criterion that can help identify when a particular approximation is suitable and when it may need to be supplemented with additional corrections. These findings provide a new perspective on the nature of approximations within the parquet framework and the underlying structure of the system, where various approximations may hold varying degrees of validity. This new perspective also enables a systematic classification of approximations based on their level of accuracy and their underlying dependence on the system's internal structure. Lastly, a previously overlooked aspect of the system is identified, which may contribute to difficulties in achieving a stable description, particularly in relation to bound objects. In the US, various safety organizations have adopted text-based systems for processing community members' incident reports, which necessitated a closer look at interactions between community members and dispatchers through these platforms. To investigate, researchers analyzed the system logs of LiveSafe, a community safety tool, combining quantitative and qualitative methods to identify patterns in the conversational flow. By developing a data framework that captured common incident-related information, researchers discovered dispatchers requested specific details from users, which varied based on incident types. Furthermore, emotion analysis and regression testing revealed disparities in the emotional support provided by dispatchers across different organizations and incident categories. Notably, dispatchers who showed emotional support received higher response rates and faster responses from users. These results have provided significant knowledge to practitioners and system designers, inspiring the development of AI-powered tools to enhance human service quality. Future iterations will focus on incorporating the discovered hidden facts into the incident management system to facilitate better human-computer interactions. Additionally, researchers intend to investigate the impact of emotional disparities on overall safety organization performance. This study presents a novel approach to uncovering actionable insights from system logs, promoting a deeper understanding of the underlying interactions within complex systems. With their analysis, researchers can inform the design and improvement of essential software tools for optimizing community safety. A publicly available dataset containing 102,741 incident responses from 33 safety organizations has been made accessible through https://github.com/jjang7/live-safe-interactions. This dataset can be utilized by researchers and practitioners as a ground truth for discovering common patterns in user-dispatcher interactions and developing new features for enhancing the live safe system. Furthermore, researchers can examine various aspects of conversational flows, such as response rates, emotional support, and incident types, to identify their own hidden facts. Additionally, AI-powered tools can be developed to facilitate better human-computer interactions by addressing the discovered hidden facts. These tools may include custom-made Python packages for emotion analysis and regression testing, which can be incorporated into the incident management system to expedite the process. A planned iteration of this project will involve implementing these AI-powered tools within live safe to evaluate their practical effectiveness in improving conversational flows. This research aims to contribute to the existing literature on human-service systems by providing a comprehensive understanding of the underlying interactions within these systems. By sharing their findings and a publicly available dataset, researchers can inform the design and improvement of IncMan, promoting a deeper knowledge of the underlying interactions within community safety organizations. To achieve this goal, researchers analyzed LiveSafe system logs, focusing on incident responses to uncover hidden facts.

Label-efficient active learning algorithms query specific, representative samples to be annotated by a human. Present techniques either utilize a model's uncertainty or rely on diversity measures, such as clustering or reconstruction, to choose unlabeled examples. However, model uncertainty-based methods are susceptible to outliers and diversity-based methods may overlook key information. To address this, we introduce a semi-supervised active learning approach that simultaneously considers both uncertainty and diversity in a minimax framework. Our method incorporates a network that minimizes entropy and an entropy-maximizing classifier, while a discriminator is trained to distinguish labeled and unlabeled data. We then select the samples with the highest entropy that the discriminator identifies as unlabeled for human annotation. Experimental evaluation on image classification and semantic segmentation datasets demonstrates superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. The proposed approach is available on GitHub. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we have created a corresponding video. Its source code can be accessed at this link: https://github.com/moebiusstripping/labelrunner.

These groupings, or partitions $\mathcal{P}_t$, split a continuously increasing set of items $\{1,2,\dots, Rt\}$. Prawitz identified a key feature of Gentzen's intuitionistic natural deduction as the inversion principle, typically paired in proof-theoretic literature with the recovery principle. This paper presents an alternative, by reformulating both principles into a single requirement, referred to as the harmony condition, within the context of the Computational Ludics framework. This new framework illuminates the underlying notions: that the inversion principle embodies containment, while the recovery principle serves as its converse. Additionally, this paper derives and demonstrates the equivalence of the harmony condition with two further conditions defined in the Computational Ludics framework. Furthermore, this study extends the harmony condition to accommodate multiple formulas and explores its implications on connectives, notably on the contraction property. Lastly, this paper exemplifies the harmony condition in action by reconstructing the cut-elimination theorem for the multiplicative exponential logic using an inductive method rooted in Computational Ludics. By leveraging the harmony condition, this paper proves cut-elimination for any multiplicative exponential logic without employing proof normalization. This approach also enables a constructive method for an algorithmic elimination of cuts. Although this paper focuses on multiplicative exponential logic, the results can be extended to other modal logics as well. Additionally, the results can be adapted to deal with multiple formulas simultaneously. This study was initially presented as a research paper at the CIC, LMC, LAMPAS, and CALCULEM workshops. Similarly, the results were initially described as an extension of the notion of inversion through the means of 'harmonious' extensions, which is a distinct and false interpretation. However, this text presents a correct understanding of the results. Moreover, the results were initially presented as a novel framework, but here it is recognized as an extension of the Computational Ludics framework. This text also presents a correction of the initial broad scope of applications, by acknowledging that the results were specifically tailored to address issues within the context of the Computational Ludics framework. A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Through data visualization techniques, we create an interactive interface for users to label these regions, thereby effectively conveying visual cues to human labelers. To ensure optimal labeling quality, we apply a training process on a subset of samples obtained from a prior agent exploration phase. We also introduce a novel metric to gauge the effectiveness of visual representations in conveying reward information. Experimental results on multiple continuous domains demonstrate that our approach significantly enhances labeling quality and enables agents to achieve comparable performance with a reduced number of human labels compared to traditional comparative evaluation methods. For example, in a 3D navigation task, our approach allows agents to achieve similar performance with approximately 0.1% the number of comparisons required by comparison-based methods. The time efficiency of our approach is attributed to the increased information per label and the ability to distribute labeling tasks across multiple users, including non-experts, which significantly reduces the total time required to train an agent while maintaining similar performance. Specifically, in a 3D navigation task, the total time needed to train an agent using our approach is approximately 0.7% of the time required by comparison-based methods. Source code and demonstration videos for the proposed method are publicly available at https://github.com/shrutiroopesh/Visual-Assisted-Reward-Learning. A typical strategy for modelling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this method has the advantage of using threshold-independent extreme value parameters, it comes with the challenge of parameter interdependence, making estimation more complicated. We introduce a novel transformation that reduces the Poisson process parameters, as if they were part of a standard parameter set, thereby facilitating the application of classical methods to estimate the parameters. We demonstrate through simulations that this transformation also enables efficient maximum likelihood estimation of the extreme value parameters. We further show that the transformed parameters behave symmetrically and have a specified distribution, allowing for the implementation of Bayesian inference using standard prior distributions. We present examples of Bayesian inference methods for estimating return levels, as well as a case study on modelling extreme wind speeds in Gibraltar. The methodology is implemented using an open-source R package, called extparam.

In the field of offline reinforcement learning, we focus on adversarial robustness, a critical consideration in RL that deals with the challenge of learning a nearly optimal policy when a fraction of data in the training set has been compromised by an adversary. Our study begins by examining a worst-case scenario involving the worst possible data manipulation and establishes a threshold for the number of compromised data points that can be tolerated without impacting policy optimality. Furthermore, we introduce specific bounds on both the loss and confidence of these malicious data points. Building on these findings, we develop a new approach, based on a modified version of the offline SARSA algorithm, designed to withstand the threat of data manipulation. This method is both easy to implement and adaptable to various problem settings. Through our experiments, we illustrate the effectiveness of this approach in a variety of scenarios, and we evaluate its robustness by comparing it to existing methods such as TRPO and SARSA, as well as an approach focused on minimizing the impact of data manipulation, called AdaBandit. Notably, our results show that our proposed approach excels in environments with a limited number of compromised data points and can perform similarly to TRPO and AdBandit in environments with no data manipulation. Additionally, we provide theoretical guarantees for our approach, ensuring its robustness in various critical aspects. These contributions create new avenues for exploration in the field of robust offline RL. All of our code and experimental data are publicly accessible at https://github.com/xinwang1988/robust_offline_rl. This study demonstrates that, in the context of a one-dimensional heat equation featuring dynamic boundary conditions, there exists a necessary and sufficient condition for controllability in the case of abrupt changes in control. This condition is based on the concept of logarithmic convexity of the boundary domain. When the boundary conditions are stationary, this formulation reduces to a requirement for the boundary domain to be convex. To achieve this outcome, we first establish a characterization of impulses that can effectively reach every possible state within the boundary boundary, which is facilitated by a data-dependent decomposition of the boundary into accessible and non-accessible areas. Subsequently, we show that, in the presence of dynamic boundary conditions, it is possible to optimize the target state to one that is achievable through the use of logarithmic convexity. Ultimately, we provide a logical characterization of integrable impulses that can effectively drive the system from an initial non-reachable state to a feasible state. This characterization is grounded in the concepts of barrier functions and non-impulsive controllability. Interestingly, when the control is applied to the boundary rather than the interior, this study reveals that logarithmic convexity of the boundary domain is both necessary and sufficient for controllability in the case of abrupt changes in control. Moreover, we show that, in the absence of dynamic boundary conditions, it is possible to deconvolve the boundary domain, leading to the realization that convexity of the boundary domain is both necessary and sufficient for controllability in the case of abrupt changes in control. This outcome is likely to be a significant contribution to the field of optimal control, given its potential applications in various fields such as materials processing and biological studies. Additionally, this study features numerical simulations that demonstrate the practical application of logarithmic convexity in optimizing the composition of a rod while incorporating dynamic boundary conditions. Furthermore, we provide a concrete example that illustrates the difference between logarithmic convexity and traditional convexity in the context of (1.1)- (1.4). Finally, we offer a series of open problems and potential areas of research exploration, including the extension of our study to coupled physical systems, the application of logarithmic convexity to the control of coupling terms, and the connection of logarithmic convexity to the concept of geometric controllability. This study is structured into an introduction, two main theorems, an implementation and verification, an extension to the multi-dimensional case, a connection to the concept of geometric controllability, a series of open problems and potential areas of research exploration, and a conclusion. driven by different tunneling processes. Despite the diversity of driving

engines, we present a mathematical model based on the tunneling rates 
into adjacent energy levels. These levels comprise a initial state, a state 
driven by tunneling and a localized state characteristic of the matrix,

fluctuations. By solving this equation, we find that the average velocity 
of these molecular motors depends on their respective tunneling rates, 
temperature and electronic tunneling properties. Furthermore, we propose 
that non-conservative forces, resulting from the interaction between these 
molecules and their environment, are responsible for driving the Brownian 
motion. To demonstrate the generality of this model, we apply it to both 
biological and artificial molecular motors, illustrating its universal 
application. Additionally, we suggest that this model can be used to 
calculate the propulsion speed of these molecular engines before their

biological molecular motors, powered by electron tunneling, can move at 
speeds exceeding that of Brownian motion driven solely by thermal energy.

movement of molecular motors in mesoscopic systems, utilizing scanning 
tunneling spectroscopy and optical microscopy to measure their velocity and 
electronic properties. If successful, this research will pave the way for

molecular traffic control and technological applications based on organic 
molecular motors. Additionally, this study may shed new light on the 
biological movement of electron tunneling-based molecular motors in 
living organisms. Lastly, this work presents an opportunity to expand

forces, as observed in real-world scenarios. Therefore, we propose that

field of nanoscale tunneling-based motors. Finally, we highlight the

In this study, we investigate the concept of general convolution by considering the set of all possible $n$-sized vectors with integer values that sum up to a specific value $S$. A function $f$ is applied to the elements of these vectors that satisfy a given condition, and the resulting value is part of a new set that represents the general convolution of $f$ with a given function $h$. An efficient algorithm is developed to compute this general convolution efficiently, outperforming the brute-force method by a factor of $O(\max\{n^{3/2},n\log n\}/\log n, n^3)/\log n$. This algorithm is also proven to be tolerant of errors for the function $f$ with an error margin of $\delta$ for a specific class of functions, and the result is capped at an error margin of $\delta h(S)_{\infty}^{O(n^{3/2}/(\log n))}$. This study also reveals a lower bound for the complexity of computing general convolution with a value of $\Omega\frac{\log n}{\log \log n}$ bits. Additionally, the problem of computing the elements of the general convolution is shown to be reducible to the problem of solving systems of equations within a bounded diagonal, and this latter problem is proven to be soluble in a restricted scenario. Further research is suggested based on these findings and potential connections to other concepts, such as matrix products and linear codes. These results are established using the concept of slicing, and new methods for slicing are developed using techniques such as cutting, which depend on the distribution of low-density vectors. This new technique is proven to be useful in solving systems of equations within a bounded diagonal and also yields an improved algorithm for computing general convolution, outperforming the brute-force method by a factor of $n^{1+\omega}$ for a small value of $\omega$. This study also investigates the maximum density of slices in objects of a given size and establishes a relationship between this density and the efficiency of computing general convolution. Based on these results and the concepts of linear codes and matrix products, the study proposes new algorithms for a multiple linearly encoded problem and a matrix product problem, and these algorithms outperform the current state-of-the-art by a factor of $n^{1+\omega}$ for a small value of $\omega$. This study also investigates the maximum density of slices in objects of a given size and establishes a relationship between this density and the efficiency of computing general convolution

The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 offered initial insight into its composition, yet a detailed analysis has been lacking due to spectral type objects' high-pressure formation molecules. Utilizing the APOLLO code, which is an advanced radiative transfer model, we conducted a extensive study of GJ 229B, and derived a comprehensive chemical composition of this T-dwarf. Our results from spectral fitting using GJ 229B's emission spectrum allow the validation of the model through comparison with observed data. Furthermore, our analysis of metal-rich ices in the atmosphere of GJ 229B, particularly carbon, oxygen, and nitrogen, revealed significant incorporation at the lower atmosphere levels, contradicting previous assumptions. In contrast, our model showed hydrogen and deuterium abundance aligns with solar values. Our investigation of atmospheric dynamics also provided insights into the chemical separation and phasing of volatile compounds, particularly carbon and oxygen, which facilitated the formation of diamonds and silicon oxides in the interior of GJ 229B. Finally, our analysis of CO and NH3 opacities led us to assume presence of a cloud layer at 1-2 bar, comprising of these molecules. The model generated from our analysis, which represents our best-fit model to the GJ 229B data set, is available for download at http://dx.doi.org/10.1047/journals/jphysiere/2022.02. This model can facilitate future observations or experiments involving GJ 229B with a high degree of accuracy. Conversely, our results can be employed to inform theoretical exoplanet studies, particularly regarding thermal profiles and composition of spectral type atmospheres. In modern research on data-driven systems, a primary focus lies on overcoming challenges presented by high-dimensional complexities, hidden system dynamics, and the presence of nonlinearity.  The dynamic mode decomposition technique has proven valuable in creating models from large data sets, yet the effectiveness of this method is compromised when it encounters significant nonlinearity. Conversely, sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics is able to learn the kernel governing the system's evolution, but it is limited by its inability to distinguish between linear and nonlinear components. In order to improve the dynamic mode decomposition technique and accurately identify both linear and nonlinear components, a new method, linear and nonlinear disambiguation optimization (LANDO), has been developed. By employing kernel learning, LANDO uncovers the kernel governing the system's evolution, thereby allowing it to distinguish between dynamic mode decomposition's linear and nonlinear components. As such, LANDO presents a comprehensive solution for the retrieval of low-frequency linear dynamics and high-frequency nonlinear dynamics from noisy data sets. To validate its use, LANDO has been applied to several systems, including a well-known model of a shear layer system and real-world data obtained from an experimental setup featuring a simulated wave interacting with a solid wall. By comparing results with those obtained using other techniques, the effectiveness of LANDO has been demonstrated. Additionally, LANDO's ability to reduce its degree of nonlinearity has been showcased through its application to a system with a fully nonlinear kernel. Further investigation into LANDO's performance is needed in order to reveal its potential limitations. A related algorithm for retrieving kernels has also been developed, known as filter optimization. This new suite of algorithms, comprising LANDO and filter optimization, presents a robust solution for kernel retrieval and presents a new approach to dynamic mode decomposition. In particular, filter optimization allows the technique to focus solely on retrieving the kernel governing the system's evolution, thereby eliminating any extraneous information. As such, filter optimization presents a new paradigm for dynamic mode decomposition. In this research, we present an alternative approach by focusing on using 3D sketches as input and envisioning a virtual reality (VR) environment for retrieval. We aim to allow users to freely access 3D models through air-drawn sketches in a VR setting. As an initial step, our study contributes four aspects: implementing a tool to collect and retrieve 3D sketches in VR, gathering the first dataset of $167$ sketches in two categories from ModelNet, developing a novel approach to generate synthetic human-like sketches, and evaluating the performance of different approaches. We observed that in the context of sketch-based retrieval, volumetric point-based methods excel due to the sparsity and abstract nature of VR sketches. We believe our work will serve as a foundation for future studies and hope to address the raised challenges in this field. Image-based goal navigation is a difficult problem, requiring agents to navigate to visually identified objectives in unfamiliar environments.
Previous methods often employ diverse memory mechanisms to track navigation history but fail to account for the fraction of relevant information in their memories.
We propose the MemoNav, a novel memory-based navigation framework, designed to improve performance in multi-goal scenarios by selectively retaining and leveraging informative memories.
The model utilizes a set of distinct memories, each associated with a specific goal, and prioritizes the recall of relevant past experiences when confronting new objectives.
The model's effectiveness is demonstrated through navigation tasks in diverse environments, where it successfully incorporate and adapt to varying types of memories, outperforming existing methods even when provided with the best possible memories. The model also exhibits superior generalization and multi-goal capabilities compared to baseline methods. The source code for this work is available at https://github.com/prashant-kr/MemoNav. These coherent states enable us to explore operator growth patterns and entanglement structures in a systematic manner, ultimately verifying that certain fundamental features emerge across these systems, thereby validating our theoretical framework's ability to probe these patterns. Moreover, our work paves the way for further investigations into the distinct characteristics of operator growth within Lie-symmetric systems. These investigations may involve comparing growth rates, evaluating the entanglement spectrum's impact on quantum processes, and developing insights into quantum information applications, all of which would significantly advance our understanding of these phenomena. Lastly, by linking information-theoretic metrics to Lie-symmetric systems, our work enables the exploration of symmetry principles from the perspective of quantum information theory. It thus bridges two distinct areas of research: quantum information theory and Lie-symmetric systems. The atomic structure of the Hoyle state, a state consisting of highly clustered $\alpha$ particles at 7.65 MeV in $^{12}\mathrm{C}$, has been a topic of interest for a long time. The question of whether this system consists of three weakly-interacting $\alpha$ particles in the 0s orbital is crucial and can be answered by analyzing the decay paths of the Hoyle state. The paper provides information about the breakup mechanism of the Hoyle state by employing a novel experimental technique. The investigation of the direct 3 $\alpha$ decay of the Hoyle state, rather than through the $^{8}\mathrm{Be}$ ground state, can be performed through an advanced analysis of the energy distribution of the three $\alpha$ particles from the decay. Using beta-delayed charged-particle spectroscopy on $^{12}\mathrm{N}$ via the Texas Active Target Time Projection Chamber, a highly sensitive measurement of the direct 3 $\alpha$ decay ratio can be made without interference from overlapping events. The analysis using a Bayesian approach reveals that the direct decay fraction is less than 0.043% at the 95% confidence level. This value is in line with previous studies and the present findings suggest a minor non-sequential component with a decay fraction of approximately $10^{-4}$. The measurement of the non-sequential component of the Hoyle state decay without a medium is performed for the first time and the derived upper limit agrees with previous studies. This outcome also exhibits a significant level of sensitivity to the absolute branching ratio, thereby underscoring the importance of further experimental research and a reliable microscopic theoretical understanding of the decay dynamics to unravel the concept of the Hoyle state as an $\alpha$-condensate. The present study demonstrates the capabilities of the Time Projection Chamber in accurately measuring the breakup mechanism of unbound states over a wide range of free parameters. The investigation also highlights the potential of the TPC system in analyzing the decay patterns of various exotic states consisting of clustered systems. The research paves the way for future studies employing the TPC system in examining the sequential and non-sequential components of the Hoyle state and other similar states consisting of multiple $\alpha$ particles. Significant breakthroughs in understanding and computation of fracture instability have been achieved for 2D dynamic fracture. The essence of this advancement is the identification of intrinsic scales at crack tips - nonlinear elastic length and dissipation length scales - which are absent in classical fracture theory. Studies have shown that in brittle materials at high crack speeds, an oscillatory instability emerges, characterized by a wavelength directly proportional to one of these intrinsic scales, which has been observed in line with experiments. Through phase-field fracture models, we find the following features of this oscillatory instability: (i) It also exists in materials with linear elastic behavior near the crack, depending solely on dissipation properties; (ii) It undergoes a type of supercritical bifurcation; and (iii) It's minimally affected by factors like the fracture energy associated with a certain dissipation time. These results support the idea that this oscillatory instability is an inherent feature of fast cracks in 2D, while we also show that an ultra-high speed instability can be attributed to a limiting rate of energy transport near the crack. The numerical framework of the fracture approach used in this study is thoroughly described. It's based on a combination of the phase-field and variational immersed interface methods. The implementation for both brittle and gradient-energy models is outlined, along with a focus on the models' key components. The numerical approach has been tested for both the oscillatory and tip-splitting instabilities, employing a range of inputs including both physical and artificially constructed inputs. The focus has been on the intrinsic scales governing the oscillatory instability, with additional results on factors like the front normal velocity and Remnant Crank Shape (RCS) also presented. The source code used in this study is publicly accessible at https://github.com/numsim2/caaSimFracture. This repository contains the necessary code to replicate the models and algorithms described in this article, with additional support available through issue reporting and contribution. These notes document my process of reviewing equations governing distant groundwater movement for a paper. By "distant," I'm referring to horizontal distances exceeding the thickness of the aquifer. They're based on assumptions discussed later on. These equations aren't an original contribution but rather a reference guide for those working with simplified numerical models of groundwater flow.

I began with Darcy's Law, revisiting the conservation equation for vertical averaging in groundwater flow. Following that, I explored approaches for numerically solving the flow equation. Then, I considered scenarios where the hydraulic conductivity varies solely with depth, simplifying the steady-state flow equation in these cases. Lastly, there's a brief examination of the transient flow scenario. 

It's worth noting that these equations shouldn't be applied to situations involving significant vertical flow or where the time scale is near-or-at-parabolic the flow boundary. Additionally, when applying these equations, one should carefully consider and ensure that sources and sinks are properly balanced. 

Finally, I've included a basic approach for modeling the evolution of the water table over time. This model assumes that the change in water table depth is determined by the average drawdown in the pumping well, taking into account its influence with an infinite extent. This has led to a correlation with the Thiebaud equation, previously observed, but not previously connected. 

I hope these notes are helpful to anyone working on simplified numerical models of groundwater flow. I expect them to be more relevant during periods of low precipitation when the water table is relatively far away from the surface. Trees, which can be shown to possess superior predictive accuracy and more
interpretable results when compared to conventional Decision Trees, as

Current educational tools used in testing can either provide coverage insights comparable to professional tools or highlight instructor-defined test cases that a student has overlooked. While this feedback has some value, it can lead students to rely on guesswork rather than structured testing methods. Moreover, this feedback style does not educate students on the shortcomings of their test suites, potentially making them dependent on the tool's advice rather than relying on their own judgment. As a more effective approach, inquiry-based learning may encourage students to think critically and independently by providing less guidance. Thus, the main objective of this study is to compare the effects of traditional detailed feedback and inquiry-based conceptual feedback on the software testing skills of undergraduate students. An experiment was conducted with 81 students, and the results showed that students who received the conceptual feedback performed better on free-form questions and had a higher overall satisfaction level. Although there was no significant difference in the efficiency of their test plans, this outcome was likely influenced by the learning materials and the lack of a non-instructional group to compare against. Based on these findings, implementing conceptual feedback in educational tools could promote the long-term educational goals of independent decision-making and providing sound testing rationale. To reinforce this effect, instructors are encouraged to build upon the conceptual feedback provided by these tools, helping students to develop more productive attitudes towards testing and fostering a more testing-minded approach. Additionally, future research could investigate the impact of providing conceptual feedback on the effectiveness of educational activities that simulate real-world testing scenarios. It is proposed that this style of feedback could enhance a tester's ability to prioritize and make most use of available resources, as demonstrated in a previous study. To explore this potential, an instructional intervention using the conceptual feedback style could be applied to existing studies that investigate the impact of educational testing skills on a tester's productivity and satisfaction levels in real-world settings. If successful, this could lead to new research avenues that investigate how to cultivate a testing-minded approach in software testing educators. To facilitate this, an instructional survey is planned to examine the current practices of software testing educators in promoting a testing-minded approach and to gather feedback that can be used to develop a set of guidelines that incorporate the conceptual feedback style used in this study. These guidelines can then be used to improve the existing educational materials for testing tools, enhancing their effectiveness in encouraging a testing-minded approach among students. In domains requiring reliability or transparency, explainable AI is increasingly becoming essential for handling the unpredictability of black-box machine learning methods, particularly in healthcare and data protection regulations. However, standard visualizations often fall short due to their inability to differentiate between subtle feature variations or accurately represent the interplay between absent and present features. This issue could be addressed by using more advanced symbolic surrogate models but, since these typically demand symbolic inputs not commonly available in computer vision, we instead explore a new method: Utilizing intrinsic network features, we create a comprehensive, descriptive verbal explanation of a DNN's decision rationale through an analysis of learned features, associated human-interpretable concepts, and an ILP approach resulting in logical rules that facilitate understanding the network's behavior. This approach offers a balance of network efficiency and verbal explainability, enabling the network to generalize its findings across unrelated datasets. Our method also makes the network's decision logic fully accessible, thereby enabling the generation of individualized predictions and the imitation of its behavior in third-party datasets. Ultimately, this research presents a novel technique for verbalizing the network's behavior and demonstrates that, despite being trained on computer vision data, a method based on concept analysis and ILP can successfully identify the network's decision rationale. Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique 30 degree rotated superstructure, not explicable through other mechanisms. This rotation domain percentage significantly increases at lower growth temperatures. It's suggested that slower surface diffusion at lower temperatures favors the remote epitaxial process over faster surface diffusion at higher temperatures. Moreover, careful cleaning of the graphene substrate significantly reduces the occurrence of the rotated domain, implying that impurities may favor the remote epitaxial process. This study demonstrates that precise sample cleaning and thermal processing can greatly influence the epitaxial outcome, potentially enabling remote epitaxy but also competing processes. Well-controlled conditions may be necessary to differentiate between various epitaxial mechanisms. Additionally, a technique was developed to align the lattice of epitaxially grown materials with a specific direction, proving indispensable in proving the existence of remote epitaxy. This technique could be applied to grow materials with specific anisotropic properties. Finally, a van der Waals compound was successfully grown on graphene without showing any evidence of a remote epitaxial process, indicating that such compounds may not be well-suited for remote epitaxy. This study paves the way for further research into the remote epitaxial growth of certain materials, but also suggests that another type of epitaxial process may be more suitable for growing other materials. These results present a nuanced view of remote epitaxy and encourage the exploration of different growth mechanisms. $\boxed{\text{Not proven yet}}$; however, promising findings have been obtained that could lead to the verification of remote epitaxy in the future. This study presents a thorough investigation of the remote epitaxial growth of certain materials, but due to technical limitations, the existence of remote epitaxy remains uncertain at the moment. To resolve this uncertainty, further research is needed, but this study provides promising leads in this area. The authors' investigation into feature extraction techniques also provides insight into how different methods could be applied in practice to extract valuable information from cardiac auscultation sounds. ADHD is a widely prevalent psychiatric condition that has been challenging to diagnose accurately. The advancement in computational capabilities and machine learning methods has enabled researchers to investigate the use of resting-state fMRI imaging data for classifying ADHD. In contrast to prior studies that often relied on the entire brain, this study focused on pinpointing the essential regions for utilizing a deep learning model. By using rsfMRI data from the ADHD 200 global competition, the researchers employed leave-one-site-out cross-validation to derive an integrated outcome. Notably, the study found that using merely 15 crucial regions of interest for training yielded a 70.6% accuracy rate, surpassing the existing benchmark of 68.6% achieved with all regions. Furthermore, the researchers developed a model that selectively weighs the importance of regions during training, resulting in improved robustness when confronted with corrupted data and superior performance on unseen data compared to prior methods. The study demonstrated that focusing on critical brain regions for ADHD classification can enhance deep learning model efficiency and resilience. The derived model also displayed promising predictive capabilities, holding potential for clinical applications. The study's findings can be useful for researchers seeking to streamline ADHD diagnosis by selecting essential brain regions, thereby reducing computational demands. When we reduce this operator to a quadratic stochastic one, we show that it has a unique interior fixed point and examine the long-term trajectory behavior under specific conditions regarding the model parameters. Specifically, we find that the trajectory converges to this fixed point if the infection rate is below a critical value, and in the contrary case, the trajectory alternates between two equilibrium points in the boundary of the state space. Acronyms and abbreviations are frequently employed in everyday writing and speech, 
with the most common domain being English technical and scientific texts. 
These terms enable authors to convey expanded ideas within a shorter form, 
though this may lead to confusion if not properly defined or if definitions are unclear. 
To address this issue, the MadDog system was developed for full-text acronym identification 
and clarification through hyperlinking related definitions within the text. 
By utilizing the expanded definition of one acronym, the system can provide clearer 
answers to questions involving multiple acronyms, thereby enhancing overall understanding. 
Key capabilities of MadDog include: 
(1) acronym identification in both uppercase and lowercase texts, 
(2) definition extraction from physical hyperlinks and embedded HTML content, 
(3) detection and linking of acronym repetitions, 
(4) recognition and connection of acronyms across sentence boundaries, 
(5) hyperlinking of definitions through email, newsgroup, chat, and web-based platforms, 
(6) integration with external knowledge bases for ambiguous acronyms, 
(7) hyperhyperlinking for queries involving multiple acronyms, 
(8) hyperhyperhyperlinking for definitions extending beyond initial pages, 
(9) user-friendly interface and efficient computation via threading technique, 
(10) availability of source code through public donation on the donation-page.

Quantum interference, evident in low-dimensional systems, is one of the most notable manifestations of quantum physics. Historically, quantum interference has been observed in charge transport; however, recent findings indicate that it also significantly affects thermal properties. This insight enables the precise manipulation of heat within microscopic devices through phase-coherence. This study showcases how exploiting phase-coherent edge states in quantum Hall systems allows for the realization of exceptional thermoelectric properties and efficient heat rectification. A multi-quantum point contact tunneling setup with multiple interference paths was used to demonstrate that these systems break electron-hole symmetry. As a result, an electron charge current can be directed from hot to cold or vice versa, and an accompanying heat current is also predicted. These findings can be attributed to a simple and logical physical interpretation. Furthermore, heat rectification can be achieved by combining two quantum Hall systems with distinct filling factors, and this effect can be enhanced through the interference properties of the tunnel junction. These observations open the door for the development of innovative thermoelectric devices as well as highly efficient heat management systems. Additionally, this research may inspire the exploration of related phenomena in other platforms, such as superconductors and topological insulators. Although some aspects of the proposed scheme remain theoretical, these results provide a promising foundation for future research and practical applications. In particular, an efficient heat rectifier could be developed by incorporating two quantum Hall blocks with the same filling factor, but with an extra tunnel junction that allows for adjustable resistance. This could potentially enable the transmission of heat from a cold to a hot source. This research may lead to breakthroughs in heat management and the development of novel thermoelectric devices. On the other hand, an efficient thermoelectric device could be designed using two quantum Hall systems with distinct filling factors and an interference-controlled tunnel junction. Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture a pair of twenty base PCR primers no longer defines a singular object, but rather a distinct, independently managed storage segment with its own index. We've discovered that, although there are limited sets of primer pairs compatible with one another, each segment offers essentially limitless internal storage capacity. Our design leverages this versatility to provide enhanced and versatile data storage properties, including organized hierarchical data and efficient data updates with flexibility. Furthermore, to fully utilize the prefix-based nature of PCR addressing, we've developed a method for converting any indexing system into a compatible PCR format. This enables us to utilize primers that can be variably extended to include desired parts of the index, allowing us to precisely locate specific objects within a segment with minimal scope, resulting in the reduction of sequencing costs by up to 90%. Physicians' written assessments and interviews with patients, stored as unstructured clinical text notes (CTNs), have been analyzed by recent studies using machine learning techniques to forecast diagnoses based on CTNs, but these models face significant challenges in keeping up with rapidly evolving medical conditions and physiciannotations. To tackle this issue, we propose employing CTNs to forecast diagnoses based on patients' previous diagnoses, essentially using historical data to update diagnosis predictions, much like moving average models in financial forecasting. By utilizing semi-self-supervised machine learning methods, we combine both our initial and updated predictions, and can verify the effectiveness of this approach on a large dataset of CTNs from the SpecLab clinic. On this dataset, we achieved significant improvements in accuracy, edge cases inclusion, and clinical notation utilization when utilizing our proposed technique over traditional methods. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our strategy can utilize and generalize from diverse and uneven clinical notation sources, surpassing baseline accuracy even when trained on partially incomplete data. Our results show that semi-self-supervised machine learning methods can successfully incorporate and leverage physicians' written assessments across entire patient populations, and can produce accurate predictions of diagnoses from clinical text notes, even in the absence of comprehensive data.
