Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches. However, current differentiable renderers are either limited by their inability to account for occlusions, light source positioning, or surface normal variations. To address these limitations, we present an innovative, flexible, and accurate approach that efficiently computes shadow areas on 2D images without requiring 3D scene representation. By leveraging a signed distance function, we offer a novel formulation of the rendering problem, which enables the differentiation of non-differentiable elements, like occlusions and light sources. Furthermore, we develop an efficient algorithm to approximate the Eikonal equation, enabling high-quality results with minimal error tolerance. Unlike state-of-the-art methods, our approach can efficiently handle complex, hidden objects, light sources outside the primary view, and accurately predict shadow penumbras. Through experiments on both artificial and real images, our method demonstrates significant improvements in accuracy compared to current standards. Our code is openly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/asharman/DifferrentiableShadow_Computation. Additionally, the generated datasets can be obtained from https://asharman.github.io/Shadow_SDF_Dataset.html. ShaRe, a web-based platform for visualizing and understanding 3D renderings of any object, has also been launched at https://asharman.github.io/ShaRe.html. Recent research on transportation networks has highlighted the need to account for uncertainty and reliability by modeling the probability of origin-destination demand and network flow. Building on long-term traffic data collection, this research develops an innovative framework to estimate the average and statistical relationship of origin-destination demand while considering the day-to-day variability resulting from travelers' independent route selections. The framework also determines the probability distribution of link and path flow along with their associated costs, with variations stemming from origin-destination demand, route choice, and unforeseen errors. By employing iterative least squares and lasso regularization techniques, the framework can iteratively estimate origin-destination demand while maintaining sparse covariance matrices for enhanced interpretability and computational efficiency. Notably, the probabilistic estimation method demonstrates an equivalent level of precision to the best possible estimators with diminishing errors as the sample size increases. The method was tested on two small-scale networks and two real-world large-scale networks, showing consistent and computationally efficient results with fast convergence. The study further confirms the effectiveness of regularization in maintaining a balanced trade-off between fit and complexity. The research demonstrates that incorporating the covariance structure between matrices can yield improved fit and more interpretable results. Furthermore, the proposed framework offers an optimal solution when data constraints are met, with the probability distribution of origin-destination demand serving as a consistent estimator. By utilizing the developed framework, transportation authorities can make more accurate predictions and decisions with the confidence to quantify and express their uncertainty. The research has broader applications, with the tools and approaches presented here applicable to various fields beyond transportation. The study's methods can be adapted for applications such as predicting disease spread or modeling social networks, showcasing the versatility of the proposed framework. This work presents a comprehensive music dataset named MusicTM-Dataset that enhances cross-modal retrieval capabilities by offering a diverse collection of multimedia data. Currently, large music datasets featuring three modalities are scarce, limiting the ability to learn effective representations for cross-modal applications. To bridge this gap, our dataset features a substantial amount of data, encompassing: (1) a massive collection of musical scores, (2) a vast repository of song lyrics complete with poem metadata, and (3) audio recordings extracted from song information. This dataset can be utilized for various tasks, such as cross-modal retrieval, few-shot learning, and domain adaptation, enabling the development of sophisticated methods for generating musical audio from sheet music and poem-based lyrics. Achieving uniform temperature distribution within catalytic fixed bed reactors is critical for both optimal production yield and operational stability.  However, obtaining precise temperature readings simultaneously with good spatial and temporal resolution in these systems remains difficult. Our research utilizes the capabilities of real-time MRI imaging in conjunction with the temperature-dependent shift in water's proton resonance frequency to obtain in situ temperature measurements in a cylindrical fixed bed reactor. The temperature distribution was monitored as the reactor was heated from room temperature to 60°C using hot air, with three-dimensional temperature maps produced as a result. The findings show significant temperature variations along both axial and radial dimensions, corroborated by optical temperature probe measurements, with an average error of 1°C. The presented MRI thermometry technique presents new avenues for the in-depth study of mass and heat transfer in gas-solid fixed beds, further enabling the optimization of catalyst activation and bedding processes. It also possesses potential applications across various industries, including food processing and the production of fine chemicals, for evaluating bed loading and facilitating the scaling of batch processes to continuous operations. Moreover, the technique can be employed to investigate abnormal temperature distributions and their effects on particle agglomeration, further expanding its scope to applications in biotechnology and pharmaceuticals. Lastly, the technique can be adapted for use in rotating and rotating-rack drum reactors to establish a thorough understanding of temperature gradients within this type of equipment. In summary, the presented thermometry technique can be tailored to meet the specific needs of both ex situ and in situ applications in gas-solid fixed bed systems. It offers a viable alternative to current temperature probing methods, providing a highly accurate and spatially distributed temperature measurement that could facilitate the optimization of numerous processes and applications across various industries. To demonstrate its potential for both batch and continuous operations, a subsequent study will be conducted using the developed technique to investigate temperature distributions in rotating drum reactors. This will involve adapting the MRI imaging setup for use in larger-scale systems and determining the precise temperature gradients within rotating drum reactors, thereby providing a comprehensive understanding of the process and potentially leading to new technological advancements in gas-solid fluidized beds. Furthermore, the technique will be employed to establish its validity in both axial and radial temperature measurements, with a particular focus on evaluating its accuracy and resolution in both parameters. Additionally, the study will utilize the MRI thermometry results to develop and implement novel mathematical models for estimating unknown temperature values at specific points in the system. These models will subsequently be employed to guide the operation of fixed bed reactors and ensure optimal temperature distributions throughout the process. Within a cellular environment, proteins and nucleic acids autonomously separate, resulting in the spontaneous formation of membraneless droplets. This process underlies the development of numerous sub-cellular compartments. Models predicting phase separation based on thermodynamic properties provide valuable insights. However, these models fail to account for the inherent organizational tendencies of proteins and nucleic acids. We have investigated how a system containing two interacting proteins, one common to both droplets, behaves during phase separation. The presence of the second protein caused droplets to assemble around a central core composed of the first protein. The droplets then divided and moved towards each other, eventually fusing. This behavior is similar to that observed in biological droplet networks. Furthermore, we have discovered a novel mechanism by which protein interactions influence the formation and behavior of droplets. This research has led to the development of a simplified theoretical model, enabling the prediction of droplet patterns and timescales. The results from our study suggest that intrinsic organizational drives can induce and modulate phase separation, leading to complex and adaptable patterns. (Authors) Peter M. This research involves modeling the mechanical actions of heart muscle tissue using a complex three-dimensional model, which incorporates electronic activity generated by the heart's main pumping unit. Due to the highly non-linear nature of heart muscle tissue, solving the model's system of equations numerically demands a substantial amount of work. Given that models at the tissue level are too complex for current computer processing capabilities, focusing on smaller scale models based on the heart's ventricular muscle is a viable approach. To make this feasible, efficient numerical algorithms are required to solve the model's system of equations quickly. In our study, various scalable solvers are used to solve the model's system of equations for both the full and linearized problems. A wide range of solver combinations, multilevel preconditioners, and iterative methods are employed to compare their performance. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics, where environments frequently shift due to wear of equipment or variations in task premises. In such scenarios, transfer learning becomes essential to achieve success. Nonetheless, developing effective transfer learning methods is hindered by a lack of standardized benchmarks that simulate real-world conditions and allow for controlled experimentation. To address this disparity, we present an assessment framework called L2Explorer, which is a modular, flexible environment for studying lifelong reinforcement learning through diverse problem settings. Our study employs this framework to examine the performance of seven contemporary reinforcement learning methods across three distinct scenarios with increasing complexity. Our research aims to contribute to the advancement of practical, lifelong reinforcement learning solutions. The L2Explorer environment, along with accompanying code and data, is available at https://github.com/jbneumann/l2explorer for reproduction of results. It is also intended to support the development of new techniques. The open-source tool can be accessed via https://l2explorer.ai to explore pre-defined problem settings or by downloading the environment to establish custom scenarios. L2Explorer, inspired by the principles of RoSE (Reinforcement learning In Real-world Settings), mimics real-agent conditions by offering a systematic approach to develop transfer learning challenges through gradual increases in task difficulty. The methodology involves establishing a series of related tasks with varying degrees of similarity and sequential structure, as is the case with our core problem setting, which involves navigating the perimeter of a fixed, real-world environment. The efficacy of six prevailing reinforcement learning methods was evaluated in two additional scenarios: (1) sampling from a real-world distribution of robot trajectories in an indoor environment in navigation, and (2) model-based reinforcement learning for autonomous driving simulation. The findings indicate that the performance of these methods is largely dependent on the specific problem domain and that no single approach surpasses the others across all scenarios. However, the overall results suggest that combining episodic memory for state-action data with online learning and adaptation yields relatively high overall performance. The research also points out the potential of multi-task reinforcement learning to facilitate transfer but highlights several areas for improvement in both the L2Explorer framework and the underlying models. To address this, we propose future research directions that build on our findings and can be answered by further experimentation using the controlled, real-world environment provided by L2Explorer. This study uncovers a broad class of non-trivial and smooth travelling waves that arise in the vicinity of the Couette flow in 2D Euler equation, at low regularity in vorticity $H^s$ for $s<3/2$. The velocity of these waves is directly proportional to their distance from the Couette flow. This finding significantly deviates from scenarios involving highly regular solutions in Gevrey spaces, where it was previously demonstrated that solutions are analytic and have a bounded velocity. This research is particularly notable as it increases our understanding of the behavior of solutions with lower regularity. Moreover, it provides evidence of a barrier to smooth solutions being analytic, thus illustrating the complexity of scenarios where regularity and velocity are trade-off situations. Finally, this work opens the door for investigating solutions with even lower regularity using the reduction method of travelling waves. 

The authors further establish that these waves can persist for an infinite duration of time, provided that their velocity is less than that of the laminar flow; this condition is equivalent to their distance from the laminar flow. This discovery marks the first instance where solutions with very low regularity were shown to be long-lived. Additionally, this research extends the previous results obtained by Chouazni and Planchon (1995) concerning solutions with very low regularity being long-lived, though with a slightly higher velocity threshold. This study further provides an alternative proof using different methods of the results initially obtained by Chouazni and Planchon. 

Lastly, this work also demonstrates that there exists no non-trivial and smooth stationary points near the Couette flow in 2D Euler equation, provided that their vorticity is in $H^s$ for $s<3$. This discovery marks the first instance where the non-existence of stationary points with very low regularity near the Couette flow was proven, thus complementing the previous results obtained by Chouazni and Planchon. This research also shows that there exists no non-trivial and smooth travelling waves whose velocity is greater than a certain threshold near the Couette flow in 2D Euler equation.

Freiman's 3k-4 theorem generally posits that if subsets A and B, of size k and comprised of integers, share a sumset with a size near 2k, then A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. In this paper, we aim to enhance this by limiting the number of possible summands available from subset B. It's shown that if subsets A and B, of size k, meet the criterion that for every four-element subset of B, the sumset A plus that subset doesn't exceed 2k, it follows that A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. This is, essentially, an extension of an earlier result by Bergelson and Sarig. The technique employed involves blending ergodic theory with probabilistic arguments. As a result, one can easily obtain a nonergodic version of this result. It's also demonstrated that the constraints on the number of available summands can be significantly relaxed while still achieving a result in the nonergodic setting. Furthermore, one can obtain a version of this result where only subset A's elements are used in generating the sumsets. Finally, one can obtain a version of this result in zero-density situations. The presented results are, in effect, variations of an earlier result by Ruzsa. The presented results are also somewhat analogous to an earlier result by Bergelson, Hindman, Mills, and Rubin, which can be seen as an ergodic theorem in zero-density situations for the "takes two" case. The technique of blending ergodic theory with probabilistic arguments seems promising for handling cases that involve larger sums and additional complexities. It's unknown whether the obtained results can be extended to the generalized situations. If accurate, this hypothesis offers significant practical value in directing limited medical resources towards high-risk patients by leveraging an economical imaging method. However, confirming this hypothesis proves challenging due to the need for large, well-annotated data sets containing post-imaging severity outcome information. To address this issue, a novel approach is proposed for extracting crucial features from datasets with ICU admission labels, using interpretable models that identify image patterns associated with severe symptoms. By utilizing a large collection of 50,707 COVID-19 X-ray images along with their clinical data, this study validates the hypothesis and presents evidence of distinct patterns between severe and non-severe cases. Additionally, models built with the proposed approach outperform baseline models in multi-class and binary classifications, demonstrating the potential for improving patient outcomes by targeting high-risk patients with limited medical resources. We analyze the transmission eigenvalue problem involving $u$ and $v$ in the Sobolev space $H^1(\Omega)$ associated with $(\Omega, \sigma, \mathbf{n}^2)$. Considering the case where $\Omega$ is a 2 or 3-dimensional ball, and the functions $\sigma$ and $\mathbf{n}$ only depend on the radial distance $r$, we find a sequence of transmission eigenfunctions that tend to concentrate their energies around the boundary of $\Omega$ as the associated wavenumbers $k$ increase without bound. If $\sigma$ and $\mathbf{n}$ are constant, we prove the existence of transmission eigenfunctions that become localized around the boundary of $\Omega$. Our results generalize the recent studies in the mentioned literature and also illustrate the influence of medium parameters $\sigma$ and $\mathbf{n}$ on the localization of transmission eigenfunctions via numerical experiments. Furthermore, we demonstrate the possibility of constructing $T$-solvability sets, which characterize the wavenumbers $k$ for which the given Neumann problem has at least one non-trivial pair of $u$ and $v$ in the Sobolev space $H^1(\Omega)$. Our analysis also sheds light on the well-posedness of the $T$-solvability equation, and we demonstrate that it belongs to a specific type of equation. Our work also involves the application of several known results and the critical Sobolev embedding theorem. Finally, we provide a mathematical expression for the strict inequality of the first transmission eigenvalue $k_1(\Omega,\sigma,\mathbf{n})$ in terms of the first eigenvalue $\lambda_1(\Omega,f)$. Our analysis also illustrates the influence of the phase velocity function $\mathbf{n}^2$ on the first transmission eigenvalue $k_1(\Omega,\sigma,\mathbf{n})$. Additionally, we prove a unique continuation principle for the second transmission eigenfunction $v$ under the assumption that it vanishes on the boundary of $\Omega$. Our analysis also highlights the influence of the real-valued function $\sigma$ on the second transmission eigenfunction $v$. To expand a dialogue system's capabilities and facilitate its practical use, discovering new intent categories from user inputs is essential but remains understudied. Current methods are often inefficient, inaccurate, and require extensive labeling. We address two key research questions for this challenge by presenting new approaches to representing utterances semantically and clustering them effectively. Firstly, we develop a multi-task pre-training strategy that leverages a large amount of unlabeled data in conjunction with labeled external data for representation learning. Secondly, we design a new contrastive loss to capitalize on self-supervising signals from unlabeled data for clustering. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our method over existing approaches on both benchmark datasets and a real-world case study. Our code and pre-trained models are available for reproduction of our work. Additionally, an live demo of our method can be accessed via our website at https://www.iat2019.org/newid.

This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. Optimized hardware is often required in embedded systems, leading to a common operation over integers, Multiple Constant Multiplication (MCM). To achieve this optimization, researchers employ DCMs (Direct Circuits Multipliers) with a hardware-efficient way of calculating MCM results. The efficient use of DCMs is typically guided by a cost function that balances hardware complexity with precision. The focus of this work is on achieving the highest possible number of MCM results using a single DCM hardware implementation. The paper introduces a novel approach to determining the ideal range for DCM values, allowing for a more efficient implementation of MCM operations. The proposed method is supported by an experimental analysis, confirming its better performance than existing solutions. Moreover, the paper provides a practical solution for identifying the optimal DCM values, making the range-finding process more feasible and efficient. To verify the proposed method's performance, extensive experimentation was conducted with various systems, including 32-bit and 64-bit processors, and some specialized hardware. The results demonstrate a substantial improvement in the number of MCM results that can be calculated using a single DCM hardware implementation, specifically up to 16 times more in certain cases. The paper concludes by highlighting potential applications of the proposed method and outlining areas for further research. One such area of inquiry is how the method could be adapted for use in Binary Constant Multiplication (BCM), which may have useful applications in the design of low-power, area-constrained systems. Additionally, the paper raises an open question about the optimal range of DCM values that may hold significant implications in the fields of computer science and cryptography. Specifically, it poses the hypothesis that any two suitable DCM values may be sufficient to calculate any MCM result, which could potentially be verified through reductions in other well-known problems. The paper leaves this hypothesis unverified, but suggests that it may be a valuable area of exploration in the future. Extensive experiments demonstrate the success of this innovative method in achieving state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmark datasets. This work bridges the gap between session-based graph and recommendation, paving the way for future research in this area. In various object categorization tasks, particularly in visually complex conditions, it has been demonstrated that recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can outperform feedforward models.  This research aimed to uncover the specific role of RNN recurrence in aiding object categorization.  We trained RNNs on an object categorization task and discovered through linear diagnostic analysis that auxiliary variables such as object position, orientation, and size are communicated through recurrence and contribute significantly to performance improvement.  This evidence confirms our hypothesis that auxiliary variables are utilized to optimize object categorization in cluttered environments.  Additionally, our results indicate that auxiliary variables are prioritized over primary attributes like object shapes when it comes to processing and integration across time.  This research provides the first evidence of information exchange within hidden layers of RNNs and sheds light on their internal decision-making processes.  Our findings also suggest several further investigations, including the utilization of contrastive multi-object representation learning to distinguish between visually similar objects, and the application of graph neural networks in merging category-level and object-level information.  Ultimately, this research lays the groundwork for the development of more effective object categorization models, while also facilitating the design of more robust I/O systems capable of withstanding visually challenging conditions.  Code for this research is publicly accessible at https://github.com/koaning/cat-rnn.  Experimental data can be found at https://doi.org/10.17632/8874427a2d. Despite numerous studies on non-Hermitian topology, the influence of correlations remains a significant unresolved issue. We conducted an in-depth analysis of correlated non-Hermitian systems, with a particular focus on the topological characteristics of one-dimensional systems. Our results reveal that correlations cause a significant reduction in the topological classification from $\mathbb{Z}\times \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$ for one-dimensional systems with a single synthetic dimension, along with $\mathrm{U(1)}$ symmetry and spin-parity symmetry. We also investigated the properties of an extended Hatano-Nelson chain, which demonstrates substantial correlation effects; interactions abolish the skin effect that exists in the non-interacting system. The findings of this study underscore the instability of the skin effect against correlations, which is consistent with the reduced point-gap topology in one spatial dimension. The discoveries presented here provide novel insights into the topological characteristics of correlated systems, thereby initiating new areas of research within the field of non-Hermitian topological physics. The Hatano-Nelson chain offers an ideal model system to test the predictions of this study; it can be realized in various experimental setups, which involve simulating the Nelson chain using bosonic atoms in an optical lattice. The findings of this study can further be extended by investigating the properties of the Hatano-Nelson chain under external rotations. The results obtained can be generalized to higher-dimensional systems with multiple synthetic dimensions, which possess an enlarged point-gap topology; however, interactions cause a complete loss of this property. The findings of this research indicate that correlations result in the degradation of the topological structure in one-dimensional systems, which is characterized by a single synthetic dimension. The stability of the Hatano-Nelson chain against correlations remains to be investigated; we hypothesize that it will exhibit exceptional stability against interactions. Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel construction methods for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of ring identities is introduced to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, it is shown that GCA pairs are possible in four-dimensional space if certain conditions are met concerning the sizes and their factorization. Additionally, in binary GCM quadruples, possible sizes are postulated as unlimited, which is confirmed for sizes 78x78 and a new 104x104 size is established through a direct construction method. This research further shows that: (i) a GCM quaduple exists for size 26, (ii) a 39x39 GCM pair can be created, and (iii) the existing 13x13 GCM pairs can be expanded to four-dimensional GCM quadruples. Furthermore, it is confirmed that certain sizes provide the best possible GCM configurations. These findings are presented in three separate tables. Prior works on GCM quadruples were confined to two-dimensional spaces; this research breaks that confine, offering a 104x104 size in four-dimensional space. Additionally, it demonstrates that GCM quadruples can also be constructed with circulant matrices in higher-dimensional spaces. This extends existing construction methods using circulant matrices in one-dimensional space to higher-dimensional spaces. Lastly, this research presents an open-conjecture that GCM quadruples may not exist in five or more dimensional spaces. To validate this conjecture, it is first demonstrated that GCM quadruples in five-dimensional spaces up to size 121 can be constructed and, extended to six or more dimensional spaces, no GCM quadruples can be found. Furthermore, it is confirmed that GCM pairs may exist in five-dimensional spaces up to size 121. These findings are presented in two separate tables. Finally, this research offers a computational tool, known as Golay-Net, for generating GCM quadruples and pairs in multi-dimensional spaces. GCM quadruples and pairs generated through Golay-Net are recorded in two public databases, termed GCM-db1 and GCM-db2, as GCM-net databases. These databases can be accessed through the Computational Tool Library at the website: https://computational-tool-library.github.io/Golay-Net/. This research was previously presented at IEEE GlobalSP 2020.

Research on Higgs boson production is conducted, combining CMS data from 13 TeV LHC and previously collected data from 7 and 8 TeV LHC, totaling 104.6 fb^-1. The findings from four-lepton final state analysis provide joint constraints on Higgs boson width and its interaction with electroweak vector bosons. By applying matrix element techniques, production and decay mechanisms of Higgs boson are identified, and its sensitivity is enhanced. The constraints on non-standard interactions with electroweak vector bosons align with the standard model predictions in on-shell and off-shell regions. Assuming the standard model coupling structure, the Higgs boson width is constrained between 0.4 and 5.4 MeV, while the simulated expected range is between -8 and 12 MeV. The constraints on the Higgs boson width remain comparable with the consideration of tested non-standard interactions. When considering the standard model coupling structure, the constraints on the Higgs boson width are consistent with its known value. However, the consideration of tested non-standard interactions results in a loss of precision in the constraint on the Higgs boson width. The constraints on the Higgs boson width remain stronger than the constraints provided by H to ZZ* and H to TT* decays. The constraints on the Higgs boson width and its interaction with electroweak vector bosons increase with the accumulation of 300 fb^-1 of data, and the constraints on the Higgs boson width remain capable of detecting the realistic loss of precision expected in the Higgs boson width due to its anomalous production width. Here, a refined version of that finding is provided with a revised lower bound of $N^{1/3}$. Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can rival Coulomb interactions to give rise to intricate phenomena.
In silicon, precise placement of phosphorus dopants is feasible to address the diverse consequences of this interplay, however this approach depends on wave functions related to crystal symmetry, which quantum tunneling inherently affects.
In this study, lattice-aperiodic valley interference patterns were directly visualized in silicon by employing scanning tunneling microscopy to investigate coupled atoms.
The examination reveals the significance of envelope anisotropy, valley interference and the location of the dopants on Heisenberg's spin exchange interaction in silicon.
The findings indicate that exchange interaction becomes immune to valley interference by arranging in-plane dopants in particular directions aligned with the crystallographic orientation, ultimately retrieving vacuum-like characteristics where the exchange interaction maximizes at approximately 230 meV.
This robust exchange interaction in silicon, paired with its inherent ability to incorporate diverse impurities, makes it an ideal platform for constructing robust qubits utilizing spin-exchange mediation. The study provides comprehensive guidelines for realizing such qubit designs based on the principles of valley exchange and superposition in silicon. The valley-mediated interaction in silicon can be extended to other materials with band structure similarities, such as germanium, where a corresponding exchange interaction of around 160 meV has been predicted. The results presented in this study offer valuable insights for realizing quantum algorithms using spin-exchange mediated operations in silicon and potentially other materials with equivalent band structures. Additionally, the valley exchange effects in silicon can pave the way for developing novel quantum devices that leverage valley degree of freedom for efficient information processing. The research also indicates the potential occurrence of emitters with exceptionally narrow spectral lines due to the interference of valley functions, which could be exploited in the development of high-brightness, tunable light sources. The studies provide a quantitative understanding of emitters with valley interference characteristics that may be essential for high-performance optical applications, ultimately facilitating the realization of valley-controlled emitters with multi-fold enhancements in photon statistics. The proposed research likely opens new avenues for basic research on valley physics in semiconductor systems and may lead to breakthroughs in the development of emitters with adjustable color, high brightness, and related applications. Several disciplines have been influenced by optimization techniques in various real-world scenarios, hence their importance is being increasingly acknowledged by the community. As a result of this growing interest, researchers have been able to develop multiple open-source frameworks for optimization, ultimately contributing to innovation in both techniques and their practical applications. In contrast, there has been less focus on developing a unified platform that can aid in the design, prototyping, and practical implementation of optimization algorithms. To address this gap in knowledge, we introduce a comprehensive framework, known as LibOPT, for implementing various optimization algorithms efficiently. By utilizing LibOPT's robust features and intuitive interface, researchers can quickly develop, evaluate, and compare different optimization algorithms, thereby fostering collaborative progress within the community. Furthermore, LibOPT is versatile, supporting multiple application domains and wrapping popular external libraries to maintain a clean codebase, thereby facilitating the understanding and replication of experimental results. As evidence of its effectiveness, we showcase five recent studies that used LibOPT as their development platform, highlighting its benefits in accelerating research and promoting community collaboration. As a resource, LibOPT is now available to the public, allowing researchers to contribute and further enhance the framework. We invite the optimization community to leverage LibOPT in their future research endeavors. Additionally, a user guide and detailed documentation are available on LibOPT's website, facilitating smooth integration and the customization of optimization algorithms to cater to diverse domain-specific requirements. We expect LibOPT to continue evolving and supporting innovative research in soft optimization techniques. Keywords: open-source framework, soft optimization, optimization techniques, LibOPT platform. Given an algebraic variety X that has a transitive action from the group Aut(X), the highest degree of transitivity of this action is called the transitivity degree. This degree is denoted by the maximum value of m for which Aut(X) acts transitively m times on X. In cases where Aut(X) is m-transitive for any positive value of m, we define the transitivity degree to be infinite. This study involves determining the transitivity degree for specific varieties, such as quasi-affine toric varieties, and homogeneous spaces, while exploring related open problems and conjectures. For instance, we aim to answer whether Aut(X) is m-transitive for m greater than or equal to 2 if X is a projective variety. Moreover, we seek to establish the transitivity degree for projective toric varieties, which represents a key objective of this research. To this end, a project-based approach is adopted, where specific cases are investigated based on the dimension and properties of the variety. For instance, we compute the transitivity degree for smooth projective toric varieties of dimension 2, while providing an upper bound for those of dimension 3 or higher. Additionally, we employ the action of Aut(X) on its minimal model to derive bounds for projective bundles and other varieties. Such models represent a crucial tool of this study, yielding valuable insights into the behavior of Aut(X) given a particular representation of X. To illustrate this point, we examine a projective space of dimension 2, where the action of Aut(X) is shown to be 2-transitive when represented using the projective action, leading to a 1-transitive action when represented using the linear action. This example highlights the dependence of the transitivity degree on the specific representation of Aut(X). As such, our study focuses on exploring and characterizing the transitivity degree for algebraic varieties under different actions, which represents a key area of inquiry. To this end, a key theorem is established, stating that Aut(X) is either 1-transitive or 2-transitive when X is a projective space of dimension 2 or more. Moreover, we demonstrate the existence of a projective space X such that Aut(X) is 1-transitive, yet provides a uniform bound for the degree of any action that is 1-transitive on projective spaces of dimension 2 or more. In non-commutative space-time deformations, the definition of identical particles breaks down. These models are described by non-abelian space symmetries represented by a four-momentum group. Our approach recognizes that for multi-particle states, the total system momentum is the only well-defined property. Calculating the total momentum involves non-commutative composition of individual particle momenta, which become ambiguous. Our results indicate that previous Fock space constructions were flawed due to incorrect assumptions and lack success. We demonstrate that momentum exchange underlies a relativistic covariance principle in the braiding of quantum numbers, solving a persistent challenge in the field. Our framework also resolves a long-standing confusion surrounding the replication of non-abelian space symmetries and identifies potential sources of discrepancy. Our work offers a novel method for resolving identity crises in NCQFT and potentially other models with non-abelian space symmetries. This approach may also be applied to the symmetric monoidal category of non-commutative space-time and extends to the NCQFT sector with infinite dimensions. Our findings are consistent with established theorems in quantum field theory, including the non-existence of a unique Poincar\'e representation in non-commutative space-time and the failure of spin-statistics equivalence. Additionally, our framework is consistent with the principles of special and general relativity and the historical development of quantum mechanics and quantum field theory. We also address other models of non-abelian space symmetries and propose a future research strategy to resolve their associated identity crises. These models include the bicrossed product, the twisted star product, and the monodromy phase space. The framework of our work is general enough to be applied to these models with additional modifications to address unique aspects in each model that compromise particle identity. These aspects include distinct braiding patterns, multiple copies of abelian factors, and unique properties of monodromy phase space. Social media platforms are facing significant problems due to the presence of toxic content like hate speech, off-color language, and misogyny. We examine if controllers obtained using model-based Reinforcement Learning, which employs an environment model to find the optimal policy, remain robust and adaptable when dealing with slight environmental variations. Building upon the concept from PILCO, a probabilistic approach to Reinforcement Learning, our research extends the method to multiple Markov Decision Processes by generating a Gaussian Process model of the underlying dynamics from experience gathered through on-policy sampling. This model is then used to calculate a stochastic optimal policy, which we evaluate in two scenarios: sampling a fixed number of actions and sampling indefinitely. We test our approach on two complex problems: Controlling a quadcopter and managing a power grid, and find that it yields policies that remain effective, adaptable, and resistant to changes when faced with variations of up to 30% in the quadcopter's weight and 100% variation in the power grid's initial state. These policies also demonstrate considerable savings in sample efficiency when dealing with multiple Markov Decision Problems. Additionally, our research reveals that the benefits of model-based Reinforcement Learning become more pronounced when dealing with larger problems of higher complexity. This trend holds true for both single-task and multi-task scenarios. Building upon the model-based approach, our research also suggests several potential applications and functionalities that could further enhance Model-Predictive Control, such as leveraging the controller's confidence level to inform decision-making and developing stop-criteria based on the controller's performance and environmental familiarity. This approach could provide a useful addition to areas like simulation-based learning and learning from demonstrations, further enhancing adaptive control strategies. Finally, our research highlights the model-based Reinforcement Learning method's potential to develop a form of transfer learning that allows sample-efficient generalization across a broad spectrum of tasks. This achievement stems from the method's ability to learn a universal policy that incorporates the underlying structure of multiple Markov Decision Problems through the use of a probabilistic model. This finding could have significant implications for areas like robotics and it is believed that model-based Reinforcement Learning will continue to be a valuable tool in developing adaptive control systems for complex applications. Several key network communication challenges such as caching and computation are interconnected. A centralized caching approach seeks to mitigate network strain during peak wireless network times, whereas distributed computation explores the balance between computation and communication within a distributed system. This paper, drawing inspiration from a study of arithmetic sequences, introduces a comprehensive framework for creating caching schemes. This framework enables connections between caching schemes and numerous combinatorial objects, offering versatility in scheme design. We show that schemes built using a placement delivery array can be expressed through a new approach, and other known schemes can also be accommodated within this framework. Furthermore, we propose a new caching scheme featuring linear subpacketization and near constant transmission rates using a specific type of arithmetic sequence. Additionally, we modify this framework to be applicable to the distributed computation problem. A novel transmission method in the shuffle phase is presented, demonstrating the potential for reduced communication load compared to existing methods with similar file counts. However, the induced data transmission rates during the shuffle and distribution phases may become worse than necessary in extreme scenarios of file dissemination. We offer three examples - two of which involve direct computation and one involving edge computation, to illustrate the utility of this framework. Comparison with existing schemes shows that it can either match or surpass performance in various metrics such as computation complexity, communication load, and data transmission rates. Ultimately, it achieves a balance between these metrics that is both optimal and efficient. Specifically, it accommodates schemes with linear communication complexity, minimal data transmission rates, and efficient data transmission ratios. These results are likely extendable to other areas within the scope of this problem. Related research could be potentially further generalized by this approach. Pulsar halos are large-scale, high-energy emission structures, formed when energetic electrons and positrons break free from pulsar wind nebulae. As a novel category of gamma-ray emitters, pulsar halos serve as optimal probes for examining the diffusion of cosmic rays within the Galaxy's localized areas, as well as their escape from pulsar wind nebulae. Research on pulsar halos has brought to light that their associated diffusion coefficient is substantially lower than the overall average in the Galaxy, thus generating considerable interest among scientists. We delve into the recent developments in the study of pulsar halos, including the distinct properties of these sources, identified pulsar halos, theoretical mechanisms underlying their exceptionally slow diffusion, their pivotal roles in investigating cosmic-ray propagation and particle injection, and the implications on the puzzles of excess positrons and the widespread TeV gamma-ray excess. Lastly, we outline the prospective research avenues based on the anticipation of discovering more pulsar halos and carrying out deeper investigations into the brightest sources. The investigation of pulsar halos is anticipated to provide significant insights that will aid in addressing fundamental questions regarding the unique features and physical processes governing the unusual, high-energy emission from compact astrophysical sources, as well as the dynamic equilibrium between particles and radiation within the Galaxy. The research on pulsar halos is also expected to contribute substantially to the understanding of high-energy particles and radiation, particularly at the localized, self-consolidated pillars of cosmic-ray production and propagation observed throughout the Galaxy. Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.

Our dataset far surpasses existing benchmarks in terms of size and complexity, offering multiple resolutions and aspects that mimic a vehicle's field of view.

Our analysis examines how climate change interest shifts among diverse groups and how their individual interests interconnect. Initially, we track the individual trends, followed by developing a cross-influence model that we then validate using a VAR model. Our results indicate significant fluctuations in the general public's climate change interest, as evident from our creation of a Climate Change Index for Europe and the US. Conversely, these indices show relative stability in media coverage and academic publications over time. Moreover, our results reveal a two-way relationship between climate change interests and financial markets, with a notable lag in the latter. This implies that climate change concerns may influence financial market perceptions. Additionally, we find no clear evidence of a significant influence of climate change interests on financial markets by institutions. It is intriguing that institutions appear to be less responsive to changes in climate change interests. Our findings may suggest that institutions are not adequately incorporating the views of scientists and the general public into their decision-making processes, potentially making them less sensitive to these factors. Our study offers insights for climate change communication strategies, with implications for practice and future research. Specifically, managers of financial institutions, businesses, and non-profit organizations may benefit from aligning their actions with emerging climate change interests, as indicated by scientific and public feedback. This requires adopting a climate change awareness approach that is responsive to the views of their target audience, thereby minimizing the risk of being out of touch with their clients' concerns, ultimately leading to lost opportunities and profits. Ultimately, this research contributes to existing theories on the dynamics of social norms, highlighting the interconnectedness of climate change interests among different groups and the importance of considering these interconnections in managerial and institutional practices. To boost climate change awareness, managers may use the findings of this study, including our proposed Climate Change Index methodology. Specifically, European firms and institutions can benefit from aligning their actions with the views of European scientists, as reflected in the European Climate Change Index. Similarly, US-based firms and institutions can benefit from embracing the views of US scientists, as captured by the US Climate Change Index. By adopting this approach, managers can effectively gauge the interests of their audience, make informed decisions, and ultimately mitigate the negative financial implications of ignoring emerging climate change concerns. From an institutional perspective, this research offers insights for governing bodies on how to effectively convey the views of scientists and the general public, as reflected in our Climate Change Indices. Ultimately, this study can be instrumental in enabling institutions to make data-driven investment decisions that align with the interests of their target audience, ultimately leading to enhanced investment opportunities and profits.

Soft grippers are increasingly popular across various applications due to their capabilities for under-actuation and feature-rich behavior, yet accurately modeling and controlling them poses significant challenges despite their simplicity in appearance. To address these issues, this paper introduces an innovative method that leverages the Koopman operator theory to create an efficient model for grippers. Building upon this model, a controller can be designed using the Nyquist array and robust performance can be achieved through careful parameter optimization. To enable model-based control, this approach relies on a dynamic model derived from the Koopman operator theory. To ensure model accuracy and adaptability to changing conditions, an online update protocol based on recurrent neural networks is integrated, allowing the model to adjust and improve gripper modeling in real-time. Experimental results validate the efficacy of this approach, demonstrating precise and robust control of soft grippers with and without external disturbances. Additionally, the methodology presented can contribute to the development of models and controllers for other flexible robotic systems characterized by non-linear dynamics and under-actuation. High-energy emissions from ancient supermassive black holes can provide a direct look into the black hole activity in the early universe. Specifically, misaligned jets of high-redshift active galaxies can be detected through their radio and gamma-ray emissions, revealing a population that is potentially detectable by telescopes like the Chandra X-ray Observatory. By studying this population, scientists can gain insights into the universe's evolution. Recent research used data from the VLA, ATCA, and VLA-COSMOS, as well as the Chandra X-ray telescope, to investigate a distant active galaxy, J2102+6015. This study provides evidence that J2102+6015 is one of the youngest active galaxies observable from Earth, with its intense emissions of radio and X-rays indicating a young age. In fact, it is one of the youngest of its kind discovered so far, with its intense emissions also suggesting a massive black hole. Furthermore, J2102+6015 displays a 10-kiloparsec-wide jet, with its radio and X-ray emissions aligned in a straight line. Researchers also found that J2102+6015 has a distinct shape, with flat spectra, and it exhibits quasistar-like behavior. Additionally, J2102+6015 has a black hole mass in the range of 10^9 to 10^10 solar masses. Using data from the VLA-COSMOS, researchers found that J2102+6015's intense emissions are exceptional in this dataset, with its radio and X-ray luminosity both exceeding those of its counterparts. This phenomenon suggests that J2102+6015's young age is likely a key factor. Researchers also found that J2102+6015's gamma-ray emissions are within the range that can be expected from its galaxy, with its emissions observable by the Fermi satellite. This discovery adds J2102+6015 to a small but growing list of high-redshift active galaxies whose gamma-ray emissions are also detectable. This study is significant because it provides further evidence that ancient supermassive black holes can have aligned jets of energy, which can be detected through multi-frequency observations. Specifically, the dataset used in this research is a valuable resource for future research into the population of ancient supermassive black holes in the early universe. This dataset can be used to investigate how these black holes change over time, with their jet alignments also undergoing changes. Current methods, both traditional and deep learning-based, primarily rely on single-textual sources such as patient demographics and clinical history. Unlike existing approaches, our proposal leverages both textual and visual data from medical images to inform survival time predictions, which is inspired by the comprehensive understanding of patients' conditions. To achieve this, we introduce a novel multimodal learning framework that integrates textual and visual information to enhance the representation of patients' patterns. Additionally, our method incorporates relevant contextual information, including the distribution of patients' survival times. Experimental results on two publicly available datasets demonstrate the superiority of our approach compared to other deep learning methods. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the significance of incorporating visual modalities in survival time prediction, which is currently an underexplored aspect of this task. To evaluate the practical effectiveness of our model, we employ a diagnostic testing protocol, showing that our approach delivers accurate and robust predictions in real-world scenarios. Lastly, our proposed model, known as LightCLAM, is designed to be efficient and achieve fast prediction times, which is crucial for clinical applications. Researchers found that this phenomenon can be modeled using the concept of Brownian motion. The strength and distribution of SGWMB are directly tied to the frequency and occurrence rate of binary black hole coalescences, and its power spectral density is proportional to the inverse square of frequency. Unlike the more common gravitational wave background produced by binary black holes, SGWMB's characteristics allow it to peak at higher frequencies due to the shorter time frames of many events, and its density declines more rapidly at lower frequencies. These findings enable a new relationship between the frequency and occurrence rate of binary black hole coalescences, and thus, the amplitude of SGWMB. The likelihood of detecting SGWMB through current and future gravitational wave observatories is being explored. The capacity of next-generation gravitational wave detectors to detect SGWMB, and the number of binary black hole events required to do so, reveals promising prospects for utilizing these devices. The findings also enable a new statistical method to analyze gravitational wave memory and provide an initial estimate of SGWMB's amplitude, and a detailed assessment of its detectability is forthcoming. A reliable and efficient communication system known as semantic communication aims to minimize data transfer and ensure seamless connectivity to diverse users and services. A novel approach to semantic communication has emerged that employs an emergent signaling game framework alongside neuro-symbolic artificial intelligence to develop a universal and adaptive understanding of data semantics. In this context, we introduce a neuro-symbolic semantic causal reasoning method that generates a unified semantic framework for multiple communication tasks. Specifically, multiple information carriers can employ this reasoning method to generate a joint and coherent semantic structure across various sending and receiving nodes under limited network conditions. To achieve this goal, we formulate the problem as a structural causal model with latent variables and demonstrate the existence of a unique and universal semantic framework through back-propagation. Through simulations, the proposed method has been shown to yield a coherent joint semantic structure and enable accurate causal inference in complex networks with limited resources. The Natural Language Processing area has garnered disproportionate interest from researchers in the past. A primary factor driving this attention lies in the word prediction challenge, where given a sequence of words in a sentence, a model is tasked with recommending the subsequent word. Researchers have addressed this issue through various techniques, combining either syntactic or semantic analysis methods in the past. However, fully exploiting the potential of combining both approaches remains understudied. In this paper, we propose a pioneering solution to tackle the word prediction task by integrating latent semantic analysis and Naive Bayes classifiers. Our model's efficacy is demonstrated through extensive testing on two diverse text corpora, where we achieve significant performance gains compared to existing models. Notably, our model outperforms current standards in both accuracy and diversity metrics. Our source code is freely available for reproduction of our results. This research contributes to the word prediction field by showing that the synergy of semantic and syntactic approaches can yield better outcomes than methods that isolate single dimensions of meaning. Additionally, we intend for our model to serve as a versatile tool for NLP tasks, capable of being adapted for various word prediction applications in the future. These tasks may involve suggesting word modifications or transforming words in sentence autocomaspeletion contexts. Our model's potential applications extend beyond NLP, where it may be utilized in areas such as language teaching, exposure control, and speech-generating systems. In terms of model evaluation, we complement traditional metrics such as accuracy with a novel consideration of model coherence, including word-related constraints and semantic relationships. This study offers several innovative contributions in this area. First, we offer a fresh perspective on the word prediction challenge, recognizing the distinct contributions of syntactic and semantic word correlations. Second, we introduce a pioneering model that integrates these two approaches, thus providing a more comprehensive understanding of word semantics. Third, we recognize the importance of semantic word correlations, emphasizing the need for future research in this area. A thorough approach is outlined to simulate single-phase flow in fractured porous media. The proposed methodology comprises three core components: generating an accurate 3D mesh of a fracture network, solving governing equations using a high-order numerical method, and implementing high-performance computing strategies. A mesh generation technique that handles problematic cases to maintain high mesh quality is provided. A versatile simulator utilizes process kernels to enable flexible interactions between the fracture and matrix domains. We validate the model through comparison with known analytical solutions and by examining numerical convergence in different scenarios. Two case studies are presented: the first investigates how fractures can impact flow in different configurations, and the second explores flow and transport through a large stochastically generated network of 2579 blocks and 102 fractures. The model demonstrates effectiveness in simulating single-phase flow in complex fracture networks. Further developments will encompass multiple-phase flow and transport applications. The proposed model is expected to contribute to simulations of hydrodynamic problems in natural fracture networks. These problems have significant implications in engineering and scientific fields, such as geothermal energy, enhanced oil recovery, carbon sequestration, and tracing of substances in groundwater. The model can also be applied to other types of fracture network domains, such as rock formations. The code is based on the open-source Mimetic Finite Difference library and is paired with the OpenTools for Fracture Modeling framework, providing a compatible combination for the benefit of the community. The model's compatibility allows for ease of use in existing fracture modeling software, such as TOF-MFD, and enables users to run simulations with minimal modifications. The code is currently compatible with up to 3 fractures per domain and can generate meshes of up to 65536 blocks, with potential for optimization to handle larger problems. The model primarily focuses on steady-state simulations but also incorporates transient solutions, with the expectation that it will be expanded to include additional features in the future. This research centers on low-energy collision avoidance and maintenance of autonomous drone swarms. A formation control method utilizing a centroid-based approach for point set registration is introduced, enabling the synchronization of trajectories without requiring a priori information about the swarm configuration. As each drone within the swarm shares its position with the others, a collective centroid is calculated and used to determine the optimal path, thereby distributing tasks effectively among the drones. A virtual target is created around the centroid, and each drone adjusts its trajectory to converge towards this average position, allowing for automatic correction of deviations within the swarm. During flight, any discrepancy between the actual and desired configurations is addressed through real-time adjustment of trajectories, thereby minimizing energy expenditure and preventing collisions between drones. Simulation and experimental outcomes validate the efficiency and feasibility of this approach. Compared to existing formation control methods, this technique exhibits lower average computational costs and is capable of automatically adjusting the swarm configuration to minimize energy consumption, as demonstrated by simulations. Moreover, experimental results show that this system can effectively correct deviations and prevent collisions, outperforming a comparative method based on local collision avoidance. A key feature of this technique is its ability to distribute tasks effectively among the drones, as evidenced by experiments where the addition of new drones to the swarm caused no interruptions in its operation. Additionally, the feasibility of deploying this algorithm on drones with limited processing capabilities was verified through further reduced-complexity developments of the technique, which were then tested in field experiments using a modified version of this approach, thereby confirming its potential for use in real-world autonomous drone swarms. Overall, this research presents an innovative formation control method for automatic correction of deviations, collision avoidance, and efficient task distribution within drone swarms, thereby expanding the applications of this technology. Finite-time consensus algorithms are also explored to enhance the response speed of the swarm, with experimental outcomes validating the efficiency of this technique. A key feature of this research is the integration of collision avoidance into the consensus algorithm, allowing automatic correction of deviations within the swarm, as demonstrated by both simulation and experimental results showing better performance compared to a related method. Moreover, the feasibility of deploying this algorithm on drones with limited processing capabilities was verified through reduced-complexity developments of the technique, which were then tested in field experiments using a modified version of this approach, thereby confirming its potential for use in real-world autonomous drone swarms. Additionally, the novel applications of this research were verified through the success of experiments using a fully integrated version of the technique, where the integration of collision avoidance into the swarm's consensus algorithm led to significant performance improvements

This research explores various spectral characteristics of the Seidel matrix associated with a connected chain graph, demonstrating that $-1$ is always an eigenvalue, while other eigenvalues may have a multiplicity of at most two. We derive the multiplicity of the eigenvalue $-1$, the minimum number of unique eigenvalues, eigenvalue limits, the characteristic polynomial, and bounds for the Seidel energy of a chain graph, which outperform previously proposed energy bounds by Haemers. We also obtain the minimum Seidel energy for specific chain graphs and present an algorithm to calculate the Seidel energy efficiently. Furthermore, our findings on general chain graphs surpass previously known results on bipartite chain graphs. We support our conclusions with extensive numerical experiments. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between the Seidel energy and other graph parameters. This research is the first to analyze the Seidel matrix specifically for chain graphs. As an extension, our methods can be applied to bipartitioned graphs with no isolated vertices. Our findings on chain graphs set a new standard for research. We have also created an available code on GitHub for the algorithms discussed in the paper. This research was formally presented at the 15th International Conference on Graph Theory and Applications. We've developed a unique, detailed two-parameter set of finite-band Jacobi elliptic potentials that correspond to the non-self-adjoint Dirac operator, seamlessly linking two well-known limit cases, each associated with the absence or presence of elliptic parameters. To thoroughly analyze the Dirac operator's spectrum, we've made connections between periodic/antiperiodic eigenvalue problems for the operator, equivalent tridiagonal operator actions in weighted Hilbert spaces and relevant Heun equation connection issues. This, in turn, ties into four related non-self-adjoint, unbounded tridiagonal operator eigenvalue problems which we've solved, revealing real eigenvalues and establishing essential, simple features. This, consequently, allows us to gain insight into the Dirac operator's spectrum by considering two sets of eigenvalue problems for non-self-adjoint, bounded multiband Jacobi matrices, each corresponding to distinct values of the elliptic parameters. This analysis yields data on the location and nature (real/complex, analytic continuation) of the Dirac operator's spectrum, thereby providing a powerful, generalizable approach to studying finite-band point interactions and related non-self-adjoint Dirac operator spectral properties. This involves establishing a direct correspondence between our finite-band Jacobi elliptic potentials and relevant tridiagonal operator spectral considerations, thereby making available the wealth of knowledge on general tridiagonal operators, as detailed in the supplementary material. This, in turn, is shown to be equivalent to the spectral theory of four related non-self-adjoint, unbounded multiband Dirac operators, each corresponding to distinct values of the elliptic parameters, as discussed in the supplementary material. This comprehensive approach provides a universal way of studying non-self-adjoint Dirac operator spectral properties for systems with any number of bound levels. Furthermore, our data includes information on eigenvalue multiplicity and reveals that in the case of two-level systems, nearly all real eigenvalues are unique, whereas in systems with three or more levels, there inevitably exist multiplicity-two real eigenvalues. This, in turn, necessarily holds for any finite-band system with more than one level. In addition to these findings, we've made relevant connections to relevant second-order Whittaker differential equations, as discussed in the supplementary material. RSUs are a vital component in V2X, facilitating communication with users; however, congestion areas are often poorly served due to high data traffic, weak signals, and interference, which can be addressed through the use of vehicle relays. To enhance the network in these situations, this research utilizes stochastic geometry to develop an innovative analytical framework for the performance evaluation of vehicular networks incorporating RSUs, vehicle relays, and mobile vehicle users. Our two-dimensional analytical model effectively considers the spatial interdependence of RSUs, vehicle relays, vehicle users, and road infrastructure using a Cox point process. By assuming relay backhaul to RSUs over reserved wireless channels and user association with the closest RSU or relay, we calculate the probability that a typical user is linked to either an RSU or a relay, determine the SIR coverage probability of a typical user, and subsequently, calculate the average effective transmission rate of a typical user within the network. This method enables the quantification of the increase in average effective transmission rate resulting from the deployment of relays. Through numerical analysis, we address the impact of parameters like the intensity of relays, user mobility, and signal strength, confirming that relay deployment significantly enhances the network by increasing the probability of coverage, reducing the network's interference, and ultimately boosting the transmission rates of users. As a result, this model offers valuable insights for network planners and designers into the effects of vehicular relays on the performance of vehicular networks. Wikipedia's ultimate goal is to be an authoritative reference on various topics.  However, due to a limited number of editors and a vast amount of articles, only 0.6% are considered of high quality according to their established criteria. To enhance article quality through machine learning, we must first label individual sentences as high or low quality, yet this process relies on human annotations that are time-consuming and often yield inaccuracies. To resolve this, we developed an automated system that examines semantic modifications in Wikipedia edits to create labels, considering the pre-edit version as an example requiring improvement, and high-quality sentences as instances that need no improvement. By employing our labels in machine learning models, we found that performance improves over using labels generated through random edits. We also discovered that our method produces more accurate labels compared to a method that bases quality on the number of edits an article has received. To validate our approach, we compared our labels to human annotations and found a correlation of 0.56, while the random edit method had a correlation of 0.46. We further demonstrated the efficacy of our labels in enhancing machine learning performance by achieving a 5% improvement in average F1 score when using our labels over random edit labels in training a text classification model to distinguish high and low-quality sentences. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by transferring knowledge from a high-capacity teacher model to a smaller student model. Traditionally, this process relies on training data, but research has shown that teacher models can also be learned through black-box optimization using query-efficient evaluation methods. Despite these advancements, existing techniques still rely on having access to the teacher model's parameters, allowing the student to learn from the teacher's original training data. A recent approach, decision-based black-box learning, enables transferring knowledge even if the teacher model is simply a decision function, without providing any additional information. Building on this innovation, we introduce a zero-shot knowledge distillation method that allows the student to learn from the teacher's decision mappings, even in scenarios where the teacher's original training data is not accessible. This method leverages the teacher's decision boundaries to estimate the posterior probabilities of the training dataset, which can then be used to train the student model. Our approach is particularly useful in scenarios where the teacher model is a third-party or a microservice, where providing the original training data or model parameters may be impractical or insecure. Our experiments show that the proposed method achieves competitive results on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 benchmarks, demonstrating its efficacy as a robust knowledge distillation method. Additionally, we find that our approach can successfully transfer knowledge in low-resource settings, and provide theoretical insights on the conditions that must be met for successful knowledge transfer. Our code is publicly available on GitHub. Keywords: knowledge distillation, black-box learning, zero-shot learning, decision-based learning, query efficiency. Additionally, our framework allows us to extend known cases of T-duals, including non-trivial examples in dimensions of $6$ and $10$. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision. This paper proposes a metric function that yields an optimal performance on average, which significantly reduces decoding computations while maintaining superior error-correction performance for polarization-adjusted convolutional codes. When using our proposed metric, the PAC code decoding computations are comparable to conventional convolutional codes with sequential decoding. Moreover, our results demonstrate improved error-correction performance for low-speed upper-layer protocols such as DTX and MCS selectors in wireless systems. Two computational methods are suggested to reduce PAC code decoding complexity: one involves approximating the metric function and the other utilizes the trellis structure of the convolutional codes. These optimization techniques significantly reduce computational load by as much as 90% without sacrificing performance. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed solutions outperform current approaches in terms of both error-correction performance and computational efficiency. To confirm our design's validity, we have conducted a thorough simulation of its nonvolatile behavior, revealing two stable equilibrium points separated by a negative differential resistance region. Additionally, we have examined how well our design's characteristics align with an ideal single-electron trap model. Our results demonstrate that systems with short charge relaxation times and narrow size variations can exhibit a single-electron transistor behavior, while those with longer relaxation times and larger variations can display a single-electron trap behavior. Most notably, we have observed that our single-electron trap design can withstand small variations in relaxation times and can also be optimized for distinct operating voltages. These findings suggest that combining these two molecules could enable the development of an energy-efficient, compact single-electron memory or switch technology.
