In the 2000s, commodity trading advisors experienced notable gains, largely driven by their trades in commodity futures. But their fortunes have shifted dramatically since the 2010s, with underwhelming returns. One plausible explanation for this downturn may be the presence of short-term reversal traders, who allegedly exploit CTAs for financial gain. In a recent study, an artificial market model was devised by incorporating both a commodity trading advisor (CTA) and a short-term reversal trader (SRT). The aim was to establish whether these SRTs were detrimental to CTA profitability. Notably, the research yielded the opposite outcome - in markets with both types of traders, CTA profitability and activity actually increased. Consequently, a heretofore CTA-dominated market became even more profitable for CTAs. The researchers also discovered that an CTA-SRT pair could generate superior profits relative to markets with either type of trader in isolation. Moreover, an CTA-SRT alliance produced results that were more predictable and stable than those of either component alone. The notion that SRTs harm CTAs appears to be an urban legend, with coexistence potentially yielding greater financial gains. The possibility of an CTA-SRT partnership giving rise to stable and predictable investment opportunities has not been previously considered. The research provides an comprehensive framework for examining potential alliances between apparently competing investment strategies, offering valuable insights for the assessment of new investment approaches. Ultimately, the findings may also be applied to other domains, including self-learning systems, where a possible discovery awaits. Identifying the application protocol is a crucial process in network security monitoring that demands a quick and accurate assessment to support detailed inspection. Although pinpointing the application protocol can be challenging, solely relying on static characteristics like port numbers can be insufficient. As a result, security professionals have developed innovative methods to enhance dynamic protocol identification. In this research, we focus on the most widely used open-source network monitoring tools and examine their approaches to identifying application protocols. We analyze and compare the techniques used for dynamic protocol identification in seven major systems, including Suricata, Bro, Argus, Nessus, OSSEC, Nmap, and Libpcap. Through meticulous testing and validation, we determine the most effective methods used by these tools and test them against a comprehensive dataset consisting of over 1,000 network traffic samples. In addition to this, we craft specific traffic samples designed to deceive the systems and manipulate their accuracy rates. Our findings show that while the accuracy of static protocol identification is generally high, the accuracy of dynamic methods varies significantly. Importantly, we uncover that all seven tools are susceptible to sophisticated attacks, and our analysis reveals that falsifying HTTP headers is an effective means of manipulating dynamic identification. Furthermore, we identify potential vulnerabilities in using HTTP meta-info and pinpoint specific challenges affecting dynamic protocol identification. Our research aims to highlight areas of improvement and potentially pave the way for more sophisticated attacks on network monitoring systems, urging developers to enhance the robustness of their products, and provide valuable insights for hackers into the weaknesses of major network monitoring tools. Ultimately, this research facilitates the development of a systematic approach for crafting advanced attacks on network monitoring systems, and could potentially be applied to other systems as well. In the near future, we intend to expand on this research by investigating the feasibility of these attacks in real-world settings. In a related development, we have made a tool publicly available that generates traffic samples to test the dynamic protocol identification capabilities of network monitoring systems. The tool, known as IDTest, can be accessed at: https://idtest.net. A beneficial approach for gathering user insights while safeguarding user anonymity exists in federated learning. Nonetheless, novel classes emerging from unseen data patterns on various devices challenge this methodology as they are not accessible to the central server or fellow users. In response, we suggest a unified system addressing the associated issues during federated learning. Our system is evaluated in two distinct settings - 1) when users conceal the new class labels, and 2) when users disclose this information, whereupon we simulate user data representations by comparing class similarities, and use clustering techniques to differentiate among them. Our system is capable of handling disparities among users' labels and models as well. Our framework is experimentally verified on two prominent applications: voice recognition and urban sound detection. It exhibits an average improvement in classification accuracy of around 4% on both platforms across multiple updates and different data patterns. Importantly, this performance enhancement is achieved without necessitating any manual configuration. Our system is further shown to surpass existing baselines by a significant margin, achieving comparable results to models trained on shared data. Our code and related information are accessible for others to build upon. Additionally, we have introduced a new unified federated learning framework called UnFeri for audio classification tasks, which can be found at https://unferi.grivera.com. The fundamental ability to count is a prime example of humans' innate capacity for abstract thinking. In this ability, there's typically a notable turning point where children rapidly grasp and master counting techniques. To simulate this cognitive milestone, we developed an AI system using reinforcement learning. By testing this system with the 'give-N' task - where it's given a binary vector and has to pick 'N' items - we discovered that it showed a similar inflection point in learning. Furthermore, our AI, built using the ESBN network structure, was able to learn patterns that allowed it to accurately select items outside of its initial training scope, similar to how humans can apply learned concepts beyond what they initially learned. By comparing its learning processes with those of human kids, we found that its progress wasn't simply a result of the amount of training it received, but rather the complexity of the tasks it was working on. This finding is significant because it shows that the rise in performance isn't necessarily caused by the same factors as the decrease in errors, which has implications for understanding both artificial and human intelligence. To study this phenomenon in more detail, we developed a theoretical model that explains the relationship between task complexity and learning. When we combined this model with real data collected from both our AI and 4- to 6-year-old children as they learned to count, we found an extremely close match. This similarity suggests that the underlying learning processes of these two very different groups are very similar. Crucially, our work shows that it's possible to model the developmental learning - a key concept in cognitive science that explains how intelligence emerges and changes over time - using sophisticated AI systems. This demonstrates that there are fundamental equivalence principles at play, where AI can be used to understand human learning processes, and implies that advanced machine learning techniques could be used to create more human-like, adaptive learning systems. These could potentially be used to make a wide range of other machines, from self-driving cars to intelligent home assistants, more clever and capable of learning new skills on the go. Finally, our findings also open up new avenues for exploring the underlying learning theories that attempt to explain human intelligence, such as the widely-held idea that advanced cognitive abilities are necessarily controlled by centralized processes. The striking similarity between our AI and human learning suggests that this theory might not be entirely correct, and that future research could be directed towards developing new theories that better fit these observational results. Bloom filters provide quick approximations of set membership while consuming minimal memory. These filters help engineers prevent time-consuming actions, such as accessing a disk or the network. A potential substitute for Bloom filters is the cuckoo filter, which often needs less storage and processes information faster. A different solution, the Bloomier filter, has been proposed as an expansion of the Bloom filter. A modification to this concept has also been explored, particularly by Dietzfelbinger and Pagh. Their variation of the Bloomier filter can serve approximate membership queries efficiently, though no comprehensive testing of it exists to date. A different filter was developed, the xor filter, as an implementation of their idea, offering more effective efficiency and speeds. Notably, the developed xor filter can surpass both Bloom and cuckoo filters in performance, all while consuming even less storage space than these solutions. A compact variant of the xor filter was also designed (xor+), resulting in storage needs similar to or smaller than already compressed sequences while providing similar speeds to those seen in Bloom filters. As such, the developed xor filters can serve as an efficient and flexible alternative to existing solutions for storing approximate membership queries. A range of testing was performed to validate the effectiveness of the designed xor filters for different types and sizes of data, as well as machines with varying processing capabilities. As a result, the development presented here can be expected to improve performance in programs, especially when working with databases or network traffic. A code base with implementations of the described xor filters has been created and released under an open-source license, allowing for reproduction of the results and potential integration into projects. This methodology stands out for its inherent ability to select a suitable time frame, which is automatically identified by analyzing past market activity and determining the state of highest trading efficiency. To facilitate implementation, a straightforward algorithm extracts relevant data from transaction sequences, sorting them in real-time and providing insights within a predefined window size. This methodology's primary benefit lies in its ability to supply current market trend information, regardless of the chosen window size, thereby enabling traders to make informed decisions when looking ahead to the near future. This work presents FLVoogd, a refined federated learning technique that allows servers and clients to cooperatively prevent Byzantine attacks while maintaining user anonymity. Specifically, servers utilize DBSCAN with S2PC to cluster the legitimate data majority without acquiring private user data. Concurrently, clients create duplicate models and engage in distance-controlling testing to tailor their local models towards a centralized standard. Our framework is both autonomous and adaptive, as servers and clients require no manual parameter adjustments. Furthermore, it operates efficiently without obstructing performance. Evaluation on various datasets demonstrates that FLVoogd effectively prevents Byzantine attacks and precludes data exposure, thereby aligning with ANON's parameters. Finally, our framework exhibits enhanced accuracy and robustness relative to competing methods. The code for this research is publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/Amr-Abdelmegid/FLVoogd.

The identification of sub-Neptune exoplanets receiving irradiance levels similar to Earth's revitalized the prospect of discovering potentially habitable worlds over the coming decade, with some temperate planets potentially harboring liquid water oceans, provided they do not possess massive H2/He envelopes that would cause them to be excessively hot. Characterizing the masses of these envelopes in planets larger than Earth, especially those with masses between 1-4 Earth masses, remains a challenge to assessing their habitability potential. We demonstrate that observable solubility equilibria or thermochemical reactions could be utilized to measure this mass range. Large massive envelopes would lead to observable changes in the atmosphere's deuterium-to-hydrogen ratio, while smaller masses can be inferred from transit spectra analysis featuring features characteristic of water-rich supercritical fluids. Conversely, planets with smaller masses are expected to exhibit specific absorption features related to water, methanol, and other volatile compounds. By analyzing the equilibrium between soluble gases such as CO2 and H2O, we can also estimate the planet's total volatile content, thereby differentiating between various thermal models of planetary differentiation. Ultimately, combining these novel methods for identifying massive volatile contents, alongside analyses of nano-second optical flashes and gravitational microlensing, will enable us to distinguish between habitable and non-habitable exoplanets with a high degree of certainty. We propose that characterizing the masses of temperate sub-Neptunes can be achieved through a multi-disciplinary approach combining transit spectroscopy, asteroseismology, and gravitational microlensing, with a notable emphasis on spectroscopic features that are within our current technological reach, such as those exhibited by water, methanol, and NH3. These features are expected to be more robust against interpretation uncertainties and are likely to be detectable with the upcoming James Webb Space Telescope. Additionally, we demonstrate that characterizing the thermochemical segmentation of planetary interiors via spectroscopic features can be accomplished through machine learning algorithms, thereby enabling us to identify characteristic patterns in temperate sub-Neptunes' transmission spectra. These patterns would allow us to distinguish between planets formed through different stellar masses and to gauge their compliance with core-accretion models. In essence, we outline a comprehensive strategy to assess the habitability potential of various temperate sub-Neptune exoplanets using spectroscopic features that can be measured with our current technology and the upcoming James Webb Space Telescope. This paper reports on the findings from the 2022 Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) challenge.
The competition highlighted an underinvestigated area in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology: accurately reading previously unseen text in real-world images during model training.
The dataset compiled for the competition comprises a diverse collection of 326,385 images, encompassing 4,864,405 text instances.
To address the challenge, a distinct validation and test set was created, comprising scene text that was not present in the training data.
The competition featured two recognition tasks: a holistic approach to reading full text and a focused task involving cropped text segments.
The analysis of baseline models and those submitted by competitors revealed a significant disparity between their performance levels in the newly introduced setting.
The proposed dataset will play a crucial role in further research to enhance the development of more versatile scene text models capable of providing more reliable and robust predictions. A specific type of chaos expansions can effectively analyze differential equations with uncertain factors by approximating random equilibrium states associated with such equations. This study integrates principles from validated calculations to provide precise error assessments alongside findings about chaos expansions representing random equilibrium states. This approach also develops a new framework for validated tracking, which entails accurately calculating separate solution branches in parameter-dependent systems and generalizes seamlessly to multi-parameter tracking. To demonstrate the proposed methodology, this research achieves the precise calculation of random equilibrium cycles in the Lorenz system, as well as solution branches and 2-dimensional planes of steady states in the Swift-Hohenberg equation. Additionally, this technique is applied to a system of coupled map equations to visualize and accurately calculate 2-dimensional planes of random equilibrium states in multi-scale systems. This methodology offers a theoretical framework for addressing challenges associated with the numerical analysis of differential equations that incorporate random elements, as well as generalizing findings from the analysis of such equations. This approach further integrates the principles of numerical analysis and probability theory to provide a reliable theoretical foundation for addressing questions related to the existence, location, and preservation of random equilibrium states in differential equations with uncertain factors. The increased use of sensors in industrial settings has led to the widespread collection of high-dimensional data, despite this comes with its own set of difficulties. Notably, gathering a comprehensive set of readings is challenging due to the inherent limitations of manufacturing sensors, thereby affecting accuracy. Moreover, industrial systems may exhibit multiple failure patterns, and identifying the primary cause is essential. Considering these complexities, designing effective monitoring systems for industrial processes becomes a complex problem. To tackle this issue, an adaptive algorithm that addresses partial data collection and multiple potential failure patterns has been implemented. By leveraging a Bayesian approach with independent Gaussian processes, a Bayesian changing point detection method is developed to identify failures and determine the primary cause. Furthermore, an adaptive method that dynamically selects data subsets is implemented to mitigate the effects of missing readings. Finally, simulated data based on an air-purification system is used to evaluate the accuracy and effectiveness of the developed method. Compared to existing techniques, this method showcases better performance in failure isolation and reduced effects of missing readings. As such, this algorithm holds significant potential for implementing failure-free and high-performance monitoring systems in industrial processes. A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our experiments on multiple document types across three different fields have shown that selective labeling can cut labeling costs by tenfold, without a noticeable decline in accuracy. Furthermore, by integrating our active learning approach, we observed an improvement in model performance after each iterative round of training, achieving exceptional results on documents with high levels of visual complexity. To facilitate the development of deep learning models capable of extracting data from visually complex documents, we have created a publicly accessible large-scale dataset known as the "Business Document Understanding" dataset. It consists of 42,000 documents collected from 1,200 domains, making it one of the largest resources of its kind. Our approach and dataset are both designed with the goal of reducing costs associated with data labeling, while enabling the creation of highly accurate models for extracting data from documents. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, we have achieved a level of performance known as the "State-of-the-Art" on two prominent datasets, all while using a model trained on our Business Document Understanding dataset. Our model achieved this level of performance without requiring any extensive training on the target domain, simply by being given a small collection of 1,000 documents for fine-tuning. Our work offers a cost-effective solution for labeling visually complex document datasets, while simultaneously achieving exceptional levels of model performance. The details of our approach and dataset are provided to support the development of efficient data labeling methods and the advancement of deep learning models in the document understanding field. The EuS/InAs interface has gained attention due to its potential to introduce magnetic properties in a semiconductor material crucial for the development of quantum devices. Using a computational model that incorporates machine-learned data and density functional theory, we have studied how varying the bonding configuration at the interface impacts the electronic properties. Across the examined configurations, we observed that the energy levels at the interface in InAs are positioned higher than those in EuS. Furthermore, we discovered novel states that arise from the interaction between the two materials, and are localized at the interface due to charge transfer. The arrangement of atoms at the interface significantly influences both the energy position and distribution of these states. While an induced magnetic effect is evident in InAs, the magnetic moment is relatively weak. Additionally, we have analyzed the potential impact of these findings on spin-valve devices. Our research demonstrates the importance of understanding and controlling the configuration of atoms at interfaces to achieve efficient magnetic oxidation of semiconductors. Based on our calculations, a specific bonding configuration could enable stable magnetic properties in InAs when combined with EuS. Our study provides a foundation for further research into the magnetic properties of semiconductor materials. Deep, wide, and complex Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are increasingly being employed in Click-Based Interaction (CBI) interfaces to enhance user experience and access data quickly, especially on mobile devices. The rapid model updates demanded by CBI are costly in terms of computation and memory, making storage and retrieval of the full model impractical in some cases. through the application of constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs). These
models ensure that the system's actions adhere to specified rules. We develop a new
algorithm for CMDPs that balances reward and constraint compliance by calculating
the optimal policy using a primal-dual approach. This method initially estimates the
value function, then generates the corresponding policy. The approach's primary
benefit is its ability to solve CMDPs with partial state information without
requiring a perfect state information. We also demonstrate that under certain
conditions, a single iterative application of the algorithm suffices to reach a
stationary point. The algorithm can be applied to scenarios with partial state
information by incorporating auxiliary variables. We illustrate the effectiveness
of our approach through simulations of an aircraft fuel management problem. The
resulting fuel savings average 4% compared to the current operational procedures.

This research outlines a method for recognizing handwritten mathematical symbols when not using an actual input device, offline. The approach involves segmenting symbols accurately into over 300 categories. Since many complex mathematical symbols require both horizontal and vertical projection to be fully isolated, but since handwriting on paper often results in connected symbols, this problem becomes particularly challenging. To tackle this issue, the proposed technique incorporates a novel symbol transformation technique to split connected symbols into individual symbols. Following this, a Full-Convolutional Network is applied to process the transformed symbols, and a subsequent Hidden Markov Model is used for segmentation. Results indicate significant gains in performance for the full set of mathematical symbols recognition. The code and data for this project can be accessed via the following link: https://github.com/nishkalgrt/MATH SYMBOL_RECOGNITION.

Nereid, a satellite of Neptune that holds the record for the largest orbital discrepancy, has an irregular shape and a non-axially aligned orbit. In 2020, the New Horizons flyby provided the first close-up images of Nereid, revealing its elongated, irregular shape and polar dimensions. In the near-infrared spectrum, Nereid's reflectance exhibits a notable absorption feature around 1.5 $\mu$m, suggesting the presence of non-homogeneous ices on its surface. By applying a simple spectral model to two featureless bands, we determined the proportions of magnesium iron silicate and amorphous water ice on Nereid's polar regions, where temperatures are sufficient to retain ice. The resulting ice concentrations show a polar dichotomy, with lower ice content in the warmer, equatorial regions (around 10%) compared to the polar regions (around 40%). This ice content in Nereid's polar regions is notably higher than in other outer solar system objects, making it an intriguing marker of non-thermal ices, similar to their presence on other irregular moons like Hyperion and the North Pole of Jupiter's moon, Icy. This study provides crucial constraints for any model aiming to explain Nereid's irregular orbit, as well as its shape and polar dichotomy in ice content. Traditional offline data solutions often result in sub-optimal policies when the coverage condition isn't met, which frequently occurs with offline data. The pessimism principle resolves this problem by limiting actions with little state-dependent data usage. Presence-absence data is represented as binary vectors or matrices consisting of present markers separated by a binary vector or matrix containing only ones. This data type is commonly found in ecological studies, where the markers denote various species present in different locations. Due to the rich structure it possesses, researchers often apply clustering methods to analyze such data. Clustering methods were applied to five-dimensional binary presence-absence data generated artificially, revealing that the applications resulted in uninterpretable clusters. Consequently, we examine various methods for converting binary data into real-valued representations and propose a novel approach based on the hyperplane Hough transform. Furthermore, we evaluate the performance of six clustering methods including our proposed technique on artificially generated presence-absence data and demonstrate its superiority through experimental comparison. Additionally, we demonstrate the feasibility of our proposed method on an actual dataset obtained from microbial community composition, where the resulting clusters showed coherence with existing classifications. Our method has been implemented and made available for public use on our GitHub repository. It has also been transferred to packages.uq.edu.au/package/clustbin. Furthermore, the RStudio environment includes a implementation of our approach in the clustbin package. It is also available through Bioconductor under the clustbin package. Moreover, the source code for our method has been shared on our GitHub repository. We advocate for utilizing presence-absence data directly in clustering analyses rather than converting it into real-valued representations. The UM-IU@LING system for the 2019 SemEval OffensEval Task is the subject of this paper. We adopted a dual-strategy to detect and classify hate speech in social media posts. Our method specifically for subtask C demonstrated effectiveness in identifying the victim of abusive content with a macro F1 score of 0.5248, and placed 27th out of 65 participants. Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively utilized in both engineering and medical fields for creating detailed images of internal structures within various subjects and objects. Since most X-ray sources emit X-rays of multiple energy levels, which vary in their absorption rates, the process of reconstructing images typically involves a reverse ray transformation process. Omitting these variations may result in image distortions such as beam hardening, which poses additional challenges. In certain settings, the dual effects of radiation and electronic signal degradation caused by devices such as CCD cameras contribute to image degradation. A proposed variational model effectively accounts for these two distinct types of noise as well as the polyenergetic X-ray source, and further distinguishes between materials with unique attenuation characteristics. In support of this proposal, the model's performance is verified through both numerical simulations and practical experiments. The numerical results validate the model's accuracy in denoising and decomposing materials, and the experimental data show an improvement in image quality when compared to traditional single-energy and CCD model-based approaches. Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) with limited resources is a complex challenge, largely due to the scarcity of labeled data and limited language knowledge (dictionaries and language models). A specific obstacle is encountered in deciphering historical ciphers, which often employ fictional alphabets to conceal the contents. To overcome this problem, this study develops a novel data creation approach rooted in Bayesian Program Learning (BPL). Unlike conventional generation methods that require extensive annotated images, our approach produces realistic handwriting from just one sample per alphabet symbol. After creating these symbols, synthetic lines are produced for training leading Handwritten Text Recognition models without the need for line segmentation. Our proposed method's effectiveness is validated through experiments using simulated data from real historical documents. Notably, it surpasses conventional synthetic line generation methods, while a trained language model aids in correcting its initial errors. Ultimately, this study's goal is to create a full system for deciphering ciphers without knowledge of the used language, where possible solutions were discussed at ICDAR 2019 and ICDAR 2021. For this study, specific insights were shared at ICdar 2020, 2021, and 2022. Related code can be accessed at https://github.com/alvareny/program-handwriting. We have developed a novel storage approach that significantly decreases the required memory, allowing us to compute three-nucleon interaction matrix elements with larger spatial dimensions up to 17 nucleons. With this, we have achieved a breakthrough, enabling the construction of a converged, ab initio potential energy landscape for heavy nuclei. Our findings demonstrate that the previously assumed finite-range nature of the 2nd Tjon anomaly actually represents an artificial boundary. We have also obtained the first fully converged estimate (precision ±50 keV) of the neutron's 2-body correlation energy. Most importantly, our research results facilitate a genuine multipoles-based description of the nuclear interaction, paving the way for a direct, phase-shift-driven simulation of the neutron's scattering on heavier nuclei. The calculated correlation energy value is consistent with experimental data, and we anticipate that our work will lead to improved understanding of the neutron's low-energy structure. The converged Scattering Lengths will also enable a precise prediction of the neutron's Deuteron Form Factor at very low energy. Moreover, our research will enable the development of a genuine multipole-scattering model for the neutron on lighter nuclei, and we expect to obtain precise estimates of neutron form factors in the momentum range Q^2 ≤ 100 fm^2. The convergence of our ab initio potential will also enable novel applications in nuclear physics, particularly in the realm of dense nuclear matter where the finite spatial dimension of conventional potentials might become a limitation, and could impact the construction of Dual-Field Effective Field Theories where a finite spatial dimension is inherently included. The code used for our calculations, and the detailed technical details of our methodology are fully described in arXiv:2203.07069. We have also developed a novel Storage Approach that significantly decreases the required Memory, enabling the computation of I2 on nuclei with up to A ≈ 100; the details are presented in arXiv:2203.07070. Both papers present a comprehensive overview of our methodology and discuss the implications of our research on the understanding of neutron-nucleus interactions. The method involves the use of a Casimir operator that determines the amplitude up to certain ambiguities. A specific set of four-dimensional 'zigzag' integrals is found to accurately describe the leading logarithmic structure, with the result matched to the AdS/CFT correspondence for two loops. Moreover, an underlying universal framework is suggested, where the amplitude is completely described by a set of holomorphic preamplitudes through a process of 'duality transformation'. The result holds a high degree of symmetry, which can be seen in its expansion using Witten diagrams and the basis of 'zigzag' integrals. High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access. Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities. Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type. Given the potential parallelization benefits, we developed DynaSOAr, a GPU memory allocator designed for the SMMO model. This allocator dynamically manages memory for a given application's objects, allowing for efficient and parallel access to a variable number of objects within a given range. Multiple iterations of DynaSOAr's implementation, utilizing CUDA and open-source, led to significant performance gains of up to 3.3x and energy efficiency improvements of up to 2.3x in various benchmarks. To further open doors for parallelization across a range of applications, we created ParOO, a programming framework that automatically converts SMMO code into a parallelizable form with efficient memory access. This breakthrough allows applications with object structures to take advantage of massive parallelization potential on SIMD devices, enabling new performance breakthroughs. Both DynaSOAr and ParOO showcase the feasibility of efficient and scalable object-oriented programming on SIMD devices, unlocking new possibilities for a wide range of applications. They also demonstrate the capability for significant performance improvements through novel approaches to memory allocation and parallelization. This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The resulting digital temperature value is obtained by converting the frequency ratio in the sensor module's digital backend. With a simple and efficient analog-digital conversion technique, the proposed design achieves a significant improvement in energy efficiency, resolution, and thermal error accuracy compared to prior works. Furthermore, the design's wide operating voltage range and minimal die size enable its application in diverse processes. Experimental results from eight test dies demonstrate a 0.24°C resolution, a 1.4°C maximum error margin, and an energy consumption of 1.06nJ per conversion at 1.8V. The die area required for this design is just 0.021mm^2. The proposed temperature sensor also boasts a compact back-end digital circuit, consuming low power with a frequency of over 1.5GHz and featuring a 6-bit binary counter, a shift register, and a comparative rheostat-based current converter. Quantum entanglement serves as a cornerstone for quantum information science and technologies. In optical applications, a common form of entanglement known as polarization entanglement typically arises from postselection methods, which are accompanied by destructive photon detection, limiting their usability in various applications. In this research, a new strategy is proposed to create entangled states of polarized photons without requiring postselection, instead employing a cut method based on heralding to prepare entangled states. By utilizing quantum scissors based on linear optics and single-photon emitters, we demonstrate that our method not only preserves but also enhances the purity of entangled states, while also allowing for adjustable parameters that mimic the characteristics of a Bell projection for perfect entanglement. What is more, our approach is compatible with a wide range of quantum systems beyond optical interactions, making it feasible to prepare entangled states through the harnessing of various nonclassical resources. By applying this method to a system of two spatial modes, for example, our results reveal that the purity of entangled states can be increased by leveraging a two-photon addition process. In practical applications, our research offers an innovative means of creating entangled states that are stable, continuous, and available in real-time. The proposed setup can be used to generate entangled states of polarized photons, as well as other types of entangled states, thus providing a crucial foundation for the development of quantum information technologies. Additionally, our research offers a means of observing quantum correlations without detection, thereby pushing the boundaries of entanglement research. The conceptual framework of our strategy, known as the cut method, can be applied to a variety of entanglement scenarios and may provide insights into the fundamental characteristics of entanglement. In particular, we find that entanglement in the form of polarization entanglement can be created through a quantum scissors based on single-photon emitters without requiring Bell projections, demonstrating the versatility of the cut method in preparing complex quantum states. Furthermore, we explore the limits of our entanglement production apparatus, revealing that it can come close to achieving perfect entanglement through a two-photon addition process using single-photon emitters. In an extension of our research, we consider the interaction between two photons generated by a quantum scissors based on single-photon emitters, thereby throwing light on the behavior of entangled states in the absence of detections. The theoretical primordial black holes that may have formed in the early universe are proposed as a possible type of dark matter. If these black holes exist, they can potentially be identified through specific star-related signals resulting from gravitational lensing. A simulation tool called PopSyCLE allows users to study this phenomenon and predict the occurrence of detectable microlensing events. To assess the likelihood of detecting primordial black holes using PopSyCLE, we modified the code to account for a dark matter halo composed of these hypothetical black holes. Our population model includes key factors, such as the ratio of dark matter to primordial black holes and the average mass of these black holes. Using PopSyCLE, we simulated various scenarios to estimate the number of microlensing events that could occur towards specific stars. Our population model was validated by reproducing previously published results and by demonstrating that PopSyCLE can accurately account for the effects of uncertainties in galaxy models. Furthermore, we employed PopSyCLE to study the influence of different systematic errors on the analysis and found that it can successfully simulate various event distributions. However, due to computational constraints, our study had to exclude events involving multiple stars. Nonetheless, we were able to show that PopSyCLE can efficiently simulate a wide range of realistic scenarios and provide reliable estimates for the analysis of microlensing data. Ultimately, our research aims to contribute to ongoing research into the existence of primordial black holes and their potential role in the universe as dark matter. Additionally, we hope that our population model and modifications to PopSyCLE will benefit other studies in this field. A conventional imaging scenario hinges on three essential elements: a light source that illuminates and scatters off the subject of interest; a means to detect this scattered light; and a detector that can resolve spatial information. However, the typical ingredients of imaging may be insufficient for delicate biological specimens or sensitive samples due to the inadequacy of available light-detecting capabilities and potential harm from light interaction. To overcome these limitations, we have developed a quantum imaging protocol that achieves all this by leveraging the unique properties of a Michelson interferometer and combining it with induced coherence-based nonlinear interferometry, coupled with the use of a single-pixel imaging method. By doing so, we have successfully performed interaction-free imaging of a structured object using undetected photons, thus pushing the boundaries of quantum imaging to the point where object interaction and photon detection are minimized. This innovation lays the groundwork for utilizing single-pixel imaging to examine delicate samples at wavelengths detectable by standard silicon detectors. Additionally, the resource efficiency of our scheme makes it suitable for space-based quantum imaging applications. Our results represent a significant advancement in quantum imaging, bringing it closer to the point where photon interaction and detection are minimized. This capability could be employed in a wide range of applications, such as using satellites to monitor celestial objects with out-of-band wavelengths. Furthermore, the proposed scheme offers an attractive solution for imaging sensitive samples at wavelengths within the visible spectrum by minimizing object interaction and detection nonlinearities. This potential application makes our scheme an interesting candidate for multifarious applications, such as monitoring living cells using coherent visible light to analyze their behavior. To verify our theory, we have successfully performed single-pixel imaging using the 808 nm wavelength, which is within the range detectable by standard silicon detectors, and has reached a minimum value of 1.05 for the ratio of object interaction to photon interaction. Our research has achieved a substantial reduction of 99.99% in object interaction without significantly increasing the ratio of photon interaction. This achievement enables us to perform quantum imaging on delicate samples at wavelengths within the range detectable by standard silicon detectors using a Michelson interferometer combined with the unique properties of indistinguishable photons. We carry out a finite-time scaling analysis near the detrapping point in a three-state quantum walk model. The coin operator is adjusted using parameter $\rho$ that controls the speed of wavepacket dispersion. The initial state is a symmetric superposition of two coin operator eigenstates with mixing angle $\theta$. One eigenstate corresponds to full wavepacket spreading at $\theta_c(\rho)$ where none of the wavepacket remains near the initial position. At the detrapping angle, key metrics such as survival probability and participation ratio exhibit one-parameter scaling behavior. Moreover, we demonstrate that these metrics follow universal dynamical laws that apply across various quantum walk models. The results are verified numerically using the unitary quantum process simulator (UOPSIM). Based on the obtained results, it is suggested that the participation ratio decays exponentially in time, at least for small and intermediate values. The findings may be useful in designing quantum-based detection methods and also contribute to resolving long-standing debates surrounding the participation ratio's asymptotic behavior. UOPSIM code is publicly available at https://github.com/qm-qm/3-state-quantum-walks.git. UOPSIM is a Python 3.x-based tool that executes slow quantum walks on multiple GPUs. It leverages CPU-GPU data sharing for increased efficiency and provides a shared memory interface for ease of use. The package includes a trio of functions that execute the three-state quantum walk model under varying initial conditions, employing wavepacket spreading controller $\rho$ and mixing angle $\theta$. The functions also enable the simulation of wavepackets with a controlled amount of initial coherence. The project closely replicates the experimental conditions described in the original research. A corresponding IPython notebook document detailing the simulation process is also included in the repository. It demonstrates how to set up and execute the quantum walk model in UOPSIM, comparing results to the original research. The project offers a versatile research tool that can be used to study one-dimensional quantum walks with a controlled amount of initial coherence. It is suitable for research in wavepacket spreading, participation ratio, and long-lived states due to its compatibility with diverse coin operators, adjustable initial states, and the ability to extend it to higher-dimensional scenarios. Moreover, the project can serve as a valuable educational resource for introducing students to quantum walks, leveraging real-world numerical experiments and simplifying code based on the original research. The project can be useful in resolving debates surrounding the participation ratio's asymptotic behavior and may be extended to model detrapping in diverse physical systems using the UOPSIM framework.

Additionally, these features excel as k-NN classifiers, with self-supervised ViT models reaching a 78.3% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet when using a compact architecture. Notably, our research highlights the significance of incorporating a momentum encoder, employing multi-crop training, and using small patch sizes when utilizing ViTs. Recently, large-scale text-conditioned generative diffusion models have received considerable attention for their impressive ability to generate detailed images from text input alone, yet achieving high-quality results typically requires multiple iterations. To facilitate text-guided image generation, users must frequently adjust input prompts, but even small modifications can lead to vastly different generated images, restricting artist control. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the Stable Artist, an image editing technique allowing artists to exert precise control over the image generation process. Its key component is semantic guidance (SEGA), enabling the diffusion process to be directed by multiple, varying semantic axes, thereby permitting refined edits to images and changes in style, composition, and artistic vision. Furthermore, SEGA facilitates the exploration of latent spaces, providing insights into the complex concepts, like 'carbon emission,' learned by the model. We illustrate the Stable Artist's capabilities through multiple tasks, demonstrating its ability to create high-quality, conditionally stable images. The source code for our method is available at https://github.com/aleksandrabrancelov/the-stable-artist.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have brought about a significant transformation in the field of reversible steganography. A key foundation of reversible steganography relies on predictive modeling that can be achieved using deep neural networks. However, critical inaccuracies persist when dealing with data outside the scope of a model's training and noisy data. To address this challenge, we introduce the concept of uncertainty in predictive models rooted in the theoretical framework of Bayesian deep learning. Bayesian neural networks are essentially intelligent systems that recognize their own shortcomings. To accurately quantify uncertainty, we approximate the posterior predictive distribution by leveraging Monte Carlo sampling combined with stochastic forward passes. Furthermore, we illustrate that predictive uncertainty can be separated into aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties, both of which can be learned through unsupervised methods. Experimental findings demonstrate that the application of Bayesian uncertainty analysis results in improved steganographic performance with regard to capacity-distortion metrics. A comprehensive framework for Bayesian steganography is presented, encompassing cover frequency analysis and a novel approach for measuring uncertainty based on predictive marginals. To verify our findings, we employ rigorous threshold-based analysis, including extensions for multiple compression methods and diverse datasets. To streamline experimentation, we introduce a versatile steganographic framework known as 'StegANO', which integrates the integration of complementary steganographic techniques previously proposed in our study. A thorough examination of our approach reveals promising avenues for further research in the intersection of steganography and deep learning, specifically focusing on the utilization of variational inference and generative models. Human vision can distinguish objects and actions using spatial or temporal data, but integrating these aspects remains unclear. This study demonstrates how the human visual system can effectively combine spatial and motion information, enabling recognition in scenarios where individual sources are insufficient. Researchers achieved this insight by analyzing'minimal videos' - brief clips that facilitate reliable object, part, and action recognition, but are unrecognizable when spatial or temporal constraints are compromised. Unlike existing deep networks, humans exhibit more adept performance in these complex configurations, highlighting missing dynamic vision mechanisms in current models. Building on this finding, the authors developed 'VesselNet' - a simple, efficient model capable of synergistically combining spatial and temporal features. VesselNet employs a novel flow-constrained self-attention mechanism that mimics the human visual system's integration of spatial and temporal cues. In experiments, VesselNet surpassed state-of-the-art models on multiple benchmarks, while its training objectives also guided the development of a neural network that approximates human minimal videos, confirming the advantages of leveraging both spatial and temporal information in dynamic recognition models. These videos were annotated by individuals with disabilities and were found to facilitate reliable object, part, and action recognition, but are unrecognizable when spatial or temporal constraints are compromised. In contrast, deep network models were shown to perform poorly on these videos, leading researchers to develop a novel training approach called 'flow-constrained self-attention' that mimics the human visual system's integration of spatial and temporal cues. The resulting model, 'VesselNet', was then tested on multiple benchmarks and found to surpass state-of-the-art models in various tasks. In a black hole-white dwarf binary system, we examine electromagnetic and gravitational waves emitted during a process where a white dwarf loses mass to a black hole through tidal forces. We simulate this scenario using a quantum hydrodynamic model and represent the white dwarf as a zero-temperature Bose-Fermi droplet. When the white dwarf approaches its point of closest approach to the black hole, it loses a portion of its mass, causing the black hole to experience an influx of matter. This mass accretion leads to the generation of intense bursts of electromagnetic and gravitational radiation, echoing patterns observed in recently discovered X-ray sources. The energy emitted from the accretion process initially manifests as brief, high-frequency bursts at each close approach, but eventually, the surrounding disc becomes a sustained source of radiation, emitting electromagnetic and gravitational waves in a continuous pattern. We investigate the properties of this radiation, including its spectra and polarization, as well as the patterns of orbital movement, and demonstrate how they are impacted by variations in the white dwarf and black hole masses. Modern motion deblurring methods based on deep learning utilize paired synthetic data for training frameworks, aiming to directly convert blurry inputs to clear outputs. This artificial blurring method enables the use of pre-blurred images, thus alleviating the need for extensive synthetic data. The ultrapower of any ordered set is created as a refined version of the set itself by taking into account infinite sequences of elements from it. This process involves dividing the sequences into classes according to a set of rules defined by an ultrafilter, leading to a set that always satisfies a fundamental property of ordered sets. It turns out that a set's openness determines its ability to fulfill the open completeness property in the refined version, whereas its original cardinality dictates whether the refined version is complete. Specifically, a set has open completeness if and only if its cardinality is less than or equal to the continuum, whereas its completeness is determined solely by its cardinality. Interestingly, a set of size Aleph1 can exhibit open completeness, whereas a set of size Aleph1 cannot guarantee completeness. Lastly, a set of size Aleph2 is required to exhibit completeness, illustrating how a set's cardinality determines this property. To summarize, a set's openness determines open completeness, whereas its cardinality determines completeness, with a set needing a cardinality of Aleph2 to guarantee completeness in its ultrapower. Moreover, a set can have an open completeness of size Aleph1, but cannot guarantee completeness, demonstrating how a set's cardinality determines this property. Finally, a set requires a cardinality of Aleph2 to exhibit completeness, illustrating the significance of a set's cardinality in this context. However, the computational resources required to evaluate every possible model against a large dataset are excessively expensive, rendering them impractical to execute. As a result, existing benchmarking approaches utilize select, representative datasets, but this limited method restricts extensive analysis and introduces bias towards models that perform well on those chosen datasets, thus overlooking each dataset's distinct features. In response to these challenges, we aim to establish a new framework that integrates dataset profiling into the model selection process, providing more accurate model assessments. To justify this need, we address two critical questions: do scientific datasets have the potential to alter the ranking of competing models relative to traditional, generalized datasets, and could optimized, resource-efficient model evaluation enhance benchmarking reliability. The purpose of this research paper is to derive optimal estimates for the first eigenvalue of the first Robin eigenvalue problem involving the anisotropic $p$-Laplace operator. This problem seeks to minimize a specific functional over all nonzero functions in the Sobolev space, and involves several variables and constants, including $p$, a bounded mean convex domain $\Omega$ in $N$-dimensional space, and a smooth norm $F$ on this space. We discovered lower and upper bounds for this eigenvalue in terms of these variables and constants, and found these estimates to be sharpest when the domain is a half-space and the norm is Euclidean. This result was further generalized to the $p$-Laplacian operator and we proved the estimates to be sharp in this case as well. This research involves the study of anisotropic problems, including the anisotropic Minkowski problem, and provides new results in this area. Specifically, we proved that the first eigenvalue is achieved and depends continuously on the norm $F$. We also found that the first eigenvalue is larger for the anisotropic $p$-Laplace operator compared to the isotropic $p$-Laplace operator. This result was further generalized to the $p$-Laplacian operator and we found the first eigenvalue to be larger for anisotropic compared to isotropic cases. This research was motivated by a conjecture provided in the first eigenvalue problem chapter in Chapter 7 of the book "Anisotropic Problems in Physics", edited by P. Strzelecki. This research was supported by funding from the Polish National Science Center, award number 2017/26/D/ST1/00411. This research was also conducted under the umbrella of the collaborative grant "Anisotropic problems in physics and geometry", awarded by the Fondation Hans Sigurdsson. This research involved the participation of P. Strzelecki, C. Keaten, M. Warholm, and B. Weng. This research provided new results and improved existing ones in the area of anisotropic problems. Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how GCNNs generate trainable features discloses that GCNNs rely on an extended version of the Correlation Matrix Rank (CMR) theory to extract top-ranked features from the data, making this method feasible for mapping complex patterns. We further show that GCNNs' capacity for distinct classification can be quantified using the Inter-Class Distance (ICD) metric, effectively measuring the success rate in distinguishing combined data classes. As our analysis highlights the pivotal role of the L2 regularization in enhancing GCNNs' classification performance by reducing noise and data dependency, it suggests a novel strategy for automatically scaling GCNN models according to the data size for optimal results. Additionally, we propose an intuitive method using the Norm-Based Size Estimator (NBSE) for determining the ideal GCNN model size suitable for a given dataset. Experimental findings validate our analysis and NBSE predictions, demonstrating that the proposed framework offers a clear understanding of the inner workings of GCNNs, enabling the automatic scaling of models for top-notch performance. A recently developed neural dependency parsing method has achieved remarkable results across various languages and domains. However, its high reliance on large, annotated datasets has proven costly and impractical to obtain. This paper proposes a novel self-training technique that mitigates this data annotation constraint by leveraging the parser's own output to improve performance. Specifically, the Deep Contextualized Self-training algorithm integrates external sequence models, derived from the parser's application to unlabelled data, into the parser using a sophisticated weighting system. Comprehensive experiments have been conducted across multiple languages in diverse settings, and the results clearly indicate that our approach outperforms traditional self-training and state-of-the-art semi-supervised learning methods by a significant margin. Moreover, our results show that the parser's performance can be enhanced by integrating models from unsupervised and supervised sources equally, indicating a uniform benefit accrued from combining unlabeled data and small amounts of annotated data. With its exceptional performance on large, medium, and small datasets, as well as its non-target language results, the Deep Contextualized Self-training algorithm proves to be a versatile solution for neural dependency parsing that can effectively address both abundant unlabeled data and small amounts of annotated data. Many software systems have adjustable settings through run-time options, such as input parameters, allowing users to modify them to fulfill different purposes, such as reducing the system's footprint or improving security, yet these configurations often go unused in a specific system instance. In our research, we devised an experimental approach to automatically eliminate unnecessary settings during compilation to optimize a system's efficiency. Our method involves the systematic elimination of irrelevant settings at source code level, guided by heuristics that identify which settings could affect a system component's behavior. Initially tested on a small benchmark of cross-platform libraries, our technique successfully eliminated up to 71% of all possible settings for a library component with minimal overhead, and with promising results, we plan to continue investigating and refining this approach. Furthermore, we found that our method also applies to other types of adjustable settings, such as those impacted by code changes, expanding its potential applications to other domains. To advance this research, we will follow these incremental goals: (1) delve deeper into the theoretical underpinnings of our technique; (2) further validate our approach by increasing the diversity of our benchmark; (3) develop more sophisticated heuristics to eliminate irrelevant settings; (4) examine how well our method generalizes to other types of adjustable configurations; (5) explore the feasibility of automatically adjusting code sections to correspond to a system instance's configuration for better security and efficiency. By addressing these questions and continuing our investigation, we expect to make significant contributions to the field of software efficiency and security. The source code for our research is publicly available at https://github.com/jjosa10/SpecPy. SpecPy is a specification tool for Python packages that allows specifiable settings to be easily added, removed, and filtered. Additionally, the SpecPy library includes a command-line tool for automatically eliminating unused settings from a Python package with minimal overhead. The SpecPy library is compatible with pip and can be installed using the command `pip install specypy`. The benchmark of library settings used in our research is also available on GitHub at https://github.com/jjosa10/SpecPy-Benchmark. This repository includes a collection of source code files that can be used to replicate our experimental results, as well as additional benchmark libraries. The SpecPy library and the benchmark of library settings can be utilized by other researchers as a starting point for similar studies on the efficient and secure management of software systems. Light dark matter particles, particularly those weighing less than a GeV, offer an attractive explanation for the observed galactic rotation curve discrepancies, making them direct targets for experimental investigation. Directly detecting such lightweight particles, however, poses a significant challenge, as they are easily overlooked among the numerous electron and gamma-ray background reactions. Researchers have proposed a new direct detection strategy that could successfully identify sub-GeV dark matter through an indicator of nuclear interactions. By operating a detector at lower voltage where electrons generated from nuclear interactions have longer lifetimes, the experiment can filter out standard model background reactions. Additionally, the technique can distinguish between dark matter signals and background through distinct seasonal variations. Such a direct detection experiment could achieve a dark matter detection sensitivity five orders of magnitude better than that achieved in XENONnow, with a corresponding increase in the detection probability by four orders of magnitude. As a result, the experiment could reach a minimum detectable cross-section of $10^{-17}$ cm$^2$/GeV on a $20$ kg mass scale at $100$ keV neutrino energy, offering an improved detection capability. Furthermore, the experiment's design can also enhance the detection capabilities of solar neutrino, double Compton scattering, and other rare nuclear processes, offering potential breakthroughs in these areas. Finally, the experiment's direct detection method could successfully identify sub-GeV dark matter particles with masses ranging from a few GeV to a few hundred MeV. Researchers have also explored the potential of using axion-like particles, which can also be detected through the experiment's direct detection method. Specifically, the experiment could directly detect axion-like particles with a mass range of $10^{-12}$ to $10^{-16}$ eV, or a pseudo-scalar mass range of $10^{-10}$ to $10^{-14}$ eV, with corresponding electric dipole moments ranging from $10^{-12}$ eV/cm to $10^{-16}$ eV/cm. This research introduces HUMBI, a large, comprehensive multiview dataset showcasing diverse human body expressions while accounting for everyday attire. The primary objective of HUMBI is to enhance modeling accuracy by capturing five essential bodily signals, such as gaze, facial expressions, hand gestures, posture, and clothing variations across a range of subjects. The creation of HUMBI involves utilizing 107 synchronized high-definition cameras to capture and capture high-definition footage of 772 individuals, representing various demographics and styles. Using these multi-view images, we apply advanced 3D mesh modeling to accurately reconstruct and represent diverse human body expressions from multiple viewpoints. The proposed dataset demonstrates exceptional efficiency in learning and reconstructing a complete human model, effectively supplementing current pose and face-based datasets such as NTU-RGB+KE, U3D-KE, and CFNet. Furthermore, we present a novel benchmark challenge centered around five key focus areas: (1) extending current ke, pose, and face-based datasets to encompass comprehensive three-dimensional human representations, (2) enhancing learning-based approaches with explicit regularization strategies to better capture the underlying structure of the observed data, (3) developing novel evaluation metrics to assess representation fidelity and utility, (4) designing novel machine learning paradigms to effectively learn from multiview images, and (5) designing novel machine learning paradigms to effectively learn from 3D meshes. The HUMBI dataset is accessible at http://humbi-data.com/ for research purposes. Despite the growing need for models in non-English languages, natural language processing has long been Anglo-centric, and translating neural models between languages can be costly and time-consuming in terms of data labeling, development time, and expertise. We propose a universal approach to effortlessly and effectively transfer neural models from English to other languages. Our method utilizes weak supervision in the form of task representations and can adapt existing neural models to new languages with minimal modifications, as long as there's unlabeled parallel data and a loss function based on task representations. We put our framework to the test by transferring an English sentiment classifier to three foreign languages and discovered that it surpasses the performance of numerous strong baselines while matching or even exceeding state-of-the-art results obtained through more resource-intensive and complicated methods. Moreover, our framework successfully captures rich, semantically significant representations across languages despite the absence of direct supervision. The code and data can be accessed via https://github.com/song1201/NTRT.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is well established in model-free methods using shared policy networks,
our research focuses on the benefits of shared dynamics models. We find that,
contrary to expectations, learning a single dynamics model for multiple tasks
can actually lead to poor performance and reduced task efficiency. Our study
reveals that this underperformance is caused by the adverse effects of task
interference in model-based learning. To prevent these adverse interactions, we
develop a novel method called the Dynamics-Structure Learning Agent (D-SLA), which
learns task-specific and task-free dynamics models in parallel. D-SLA uses
these models to select the most beneficial samples for reinforcement learning,
resulting in improved learning efficiency and higher task reward. Our research
includes analysis of both theoretical and empirical results, which demonstrate
the benefits of limiting interactions between tasks in model-based learning. D-SLA
is evaluated on a range of simulated multi-task environments and found to
significantly outperform existing model-based multi-task reinforcement learning
methods. Additionally, we provide a connection to prior work on adversarial
multi-task learning, explaining why learning a single dynamics model can be
incompatible with that approach. Further extensions of our research are explored
in the form of additional ideas and problems. Overall, our research provides
insight into preventing adverse interactions between tasks in model-based learning
and offers a practical solution to improve learning efficiency and reward in a
variety of tasks. Key words: multi-task reinforcement learning, model-based methods,
shared dynamics models, theoretical analysis, practical performance improvement.

We have improved the performance of heat engines working within specific timeframes, employing a time-varying energy function in conjunction with experimentally grounded limitations on the bath temperature and the scale factor. A broadly applicable geometric proof has demonstrated that the maximum efficiency in these systems can be achieved by alternating between the maximum and minimum permissible temperatures and scale factor values. For situations where the scale factor range is restricted and the system's thermal state closely matches its equilibrium values at temperature plateaus, this protocol also ensures maximum output energy production. These findings are valid for a wide range of physical systems, including an overdamped heat engine driven by a particle in an optical tweezers setup characterized by a scale factor related to the stiffness. We have further demonstrated that deviations from the optimal protocol can be utilized to identify the correct scale factor range and temperature values in experimental setups, thereby filling a gap in existing theoretical knowledge regarding this particular system. Additionally, this protocol may also be applied to other multi-level systems and could have significant practical implications in various biomedical applications. A practical implementation of this protocol in an optical tweezers setup has shown promising results, with the experimental efficiency closely matching the theoretical values, particularly at scale factor values near the optimal range. This approach offers a comprehensive strategy for optimizing heat engines in various biophysical and chemical systems. This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space. Furthermore, our results are tailored to accommodate functions exerting a specified level of control over their Dirac operators, thereby bridging Clifford algebra and differential forms theories. To achieve this, we develop expressions for controlled functions u(gamma) and establish a logarithmic estimate on u(gamma)(z) within a specified region of R^n+1. Additionally, we exploit these estimates to demonstrate a meaningful extension of the theorem to functions u(gamma) and 1/f(gamma), where f represents an appropriately chosen positive function. Consequently, this achieves a connection between the theories of Clifford and differential forms. In this context, our study also addresses an unresolved question posed by the 2008 Clifford conference. While our approach draws upon some aspects of Hadamard's original argument, the novel estimates developed here necessarily underpin the modified theorem will be the primary outcome. This hadamard-clifford analysis integration, featuring its distinctive logarithmic character, will serve as a crucial pillar in the construction of a Clifford algebra-based asymptotic theory for the Dirac operator. Such a theory will provide a direct means of linking the properties of the Dirac operator with those of differential forms. To summarize, this work has successfully established a bridge between the theories of Clifford and differential forms, achieved through the development of meaningful estimates for controlled functions u(gamma) and a meaningful extension of the three circles theorem to these functions. This was accomplished while maintaining the distinctive logarithmic character of Hadamard's original theorem. We identify that the intrinsic encoding properties of these maps align with those of the Dyck system from the study of languages, and this correspondence serves as the foundation for an in-depth analysis of their invariant measures. Through initial investigation, we confirm the existence of two distinct ergodic measures with maximal entropy for these generalized baker maps, and also reveal the underlying cause for the failure of certain entropy-based approaches. Additionally, we provide a direct computation of the entropy of the Dyck system, and provide supporting evidence that the behavior of the generalized baker map shares many key similarities with that of the Dyck system. Furthermore, we extend our findings to explore the properties of distributions resulting from the encoding of areas under these generalized baker maps, and apply these results to develop a theoretical framework for understanding the observed two-stage approach toward a maximum entropy state in various experiments. In the process, we address a previously unstudied question regarding the ergodicity of one particular invariant measure, and provide a method for constructing ergodic Markov chains with optimal approachability of maximum entropy, and also develop a method for approximating this optimal approachability based on finite ergodic Markov chains. Lastly, we provide a direct computation of the entropy of a particular 2D ergodic Markov chain, and establish a maximum entropy state as a limiting behavior for certain averaging methods applied to random trajectories of a 3D conservative system. A pressing concern is whether the Standard Model of particle physics adequately accounts for the scalar sector observed in nature or if it is a subset of a more complex model featuring additional particles. A critical method for resolving this query involves scrutinizing extended scalar models using future high-energy collider facilities, including the potential proton-proton collider with 27 and 100 TeV center-of-mass energy, and advanced lepton colliders at 80 and 100 TeV. A comprehensive study of this type would involve thoroughly examining various theoretical models featuring diverse scalar interactions and multiple new particles, coupled with a thorough evaluation of the theoretical and experimental aspects of these models. This review aims to provide an in-depth introduction to these theoretical models and their potential detection using future collider data. A companion document offers a detailed analysis of the potential for these colliders to detect non-SM physics. Following the presentation of the SM predictions for various processes in the scalar sector at future colliders, the additional signatures expected from these models are examined. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's effectiveness in modeling quasi-periodic signals. Additionally, the PDCNN adaptation mechanism facilitates the generation of synthetic speech with broad frequency ranges. The open-source code for QPNet can be accessed via the GitHub repository: https://github.com/aiqa0/QPNet. The model was mainly tested on speech data but can be applied to generate signals from periodic and quasi-periodic signals with limited pitch control. With a few modifications, QPNet can generate synthetic speech with broad frequency ranges. Additionally, the model can be utilized in voice cloning and audio generation scenarios. Furthermore, the use of quasi-periodic networks could be utilized to analyze and generate signal types such as chirps and other quasi-periodic signals.
